bullets: AdaptiveVPI is a new benchmark for testing web agents against visual prompt injection—malicious instructions embedded in webpage imagery. It adds adaptive attackers that know the defense and tests hidden destinations, such as phishing links in the underlying webpage code, rather than limiting evaluation to visible screenshot text. Why it matters: If you are choosing defenses for a browser agent, this changes the test from detecting fixed visible attacks to checking whether the agent remains safe when attackers adapt and harmful destinations are not visually apparent. That can distinguish defenses that recognize suspicious pixels from defenses that also constrain resulting actions. Evidence: E002. Medium confidence.

MASSys is a new benchmark that reruns identical multi-agent workflows across different serving systems and load levels. Its source description reports that a workflow’s speed ranking can reverse even when the models, prompts, and task stay fixed, making the execution environment part of the measured result. Why it matters: If you are comparing multi-agent architectures for deployment, this means a result from one serving setup may not transfer to another. Including serving system and load as controlled evaluation variables can prevent a product team from selecting a workflow whose apparent advantage disappears under its intended infrastructure. Evidence: E020. Medium confidence.

ESM-Bench is a new benchmark of 60 coding-agent tasks drawn from six Earth system model repositories. It tests changes where an agent must preserve software interfaces and the physical assumptions represented by scientific code, and it includes physics bug fixes, process changes, parameterization choices, and parameter optimization. Why it matters: If you are evaluating coding agents for scientific software, ordinary test passing may not establish that a patch preserves the modeled science. ESM-Bench offers tasks and patch-review criteria aimed at separating syntactically valid maintenance from changes that remain consistent with the physical model. Evidence: E003. Medium confidence.

WARD is the clearest new example in this feed of a recurring move away from final-answer scoring. It evaluates longitudinal clinical agents at checkpoints as evidence accumulates, separating evidence use, patient-state updating, and action selection; separate new releases similarly decompose experimental planning and state-changing tutoring behavior. Why it matters: If you are selecting an agent for a workflow where mistakes compound over time, a final success rate cannot reveal whether the system noticed evidence, updated its internal assessment, or chose a timely action. These designs support failure-specific acceptance tests and make remediation decisions more targeted. Evidence: E018, E012, E034. Medium confidence.

TrialAgentBench is a new benchmark with nearly 3,500 tasks for clinical-trial analysis and sequential drug-development decisions. It uses simulated trials with known underlying truth, addressing settings where real trials are costly, involve people, and do not reveal what would have happened under an unchosen alternative. Why it matters: If you are evaluating agents that recommend expensive sequential experiments, simulation permits scoring decisions against known outcomes and alternatives that real operational records cannot expose. This can change suite selection from retrospective imitation of historical choices to controlled testing of decision quality over multiple steps. Evidence: E016. Medium confidence.
bullets_zh: AdaptiveVPI 是一个用于测试 Web 智能体抵御视觉提示注入的新基准；视觉提示注入是指嵌入网页图像中的恶意指令。它引入了了解防御机制的自适应攻击者，并测试隐藏目标，例如底层网页代码中的钓鱼链接，而不是将评估局限于截图中可见的文本。Why it matters: 如果你正在为浏览器智能体选择防御方案，这会将测试重点从检测固定、可见的攻击，转变为检验当攻击者进行适应且有害目标在视觉上并不明显时，智能体能否保持安全。这可以区分仅能识别可疑像素的防御方案与还能约束后续行为的防御方案。Evidence: E002. Medium confidence.

MASSys 是一个新基准，它会在不同的服务系统和负载水平下重复运行完全相同的多智能体工作流。其来源描述称，即使模型、提示词和任务保持不变，工作流的速度排名也可能逆转，这使执行环境成为测量结果的一部分。Why it matters: 如果你正在比较用于部署的多智能体架构，这意味着来自某一种服务配置的结果可能无法迁移到另一种配置。将服务系统和负载纳入受控评估变量，可以避免产品团队选中某个工作流，而该工作流表面上的优势在目标基础设施中却会消失。Evidence: E020. Medium confidence.

ESM-Bench 是一个新基准，包含来自六个地球系统模型代码仓库的 60 项编码智能体任务。它测试的代码变更要求智能体既保留软件接口，也保留科学代码所体现的物理假设；任务包括物理缺陷修复、过程变更、参数化方案选择和参数优化。Why it matters: 如果你正在评估用于科学软件的编码智能体，仅仅通过常规测试可能不足以证明补丁保留了建模所依据的科学原理。ESM-Bench 提供的任务和补丁审查标准，旨在区分语法上有效的维护与仍然符合物理模型的变更。Evidence: E003. Medium confidence.

WARD 是本次信息流中最清晰的新例证，体现了评估方式持续摆脱仅对最终答案评分的趋势。它会随着证据不断积累，在多个检查点评估纵向临床智能体，并分别衡量证据使用、患者状态更新和行动选择；其他新发布的基准也以类似方式拆解实验规划和会改变状态的辅导行为。Why it matters: 如果你正在为错误会随时间累积的工作流选择智能体，最终成功率无法揭示系统是否注意到了证据、更新了内部判断，或及时采取了行动。这些设计支持针对特定故障的验收测试，并使补救决策更具针对性。Evidence: E018, E012, E034. Medium confidence.

TrialAgentBench 是一个新基准，包含近 3,500 项用于临床试验分析和序贯药物开发决策的任务。它采用底层真实情况已知的模拟试验，以应对真实试验成本高昂、涉及人类参与者，且无法揭示在未选择的替代方案下会发生什么的问题。Why it matters: 如果你正在评估为高成本序贯实验提供建议的智能体，模拟可以依据已知结果和替代方案对决策进行评分，而真实运营记录无法呈现这些信息。这可以让评测套件的选择从对历史决策的回顾性模仿，转向对多步骤决策质量的受控测试。Evidence: E016. Medium confidence.

evidence_items.summary: We present OWE-Bench (OpenWorldEngineer-Bench), a benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering tasks written by domain experts in software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and scientific computing. Tasks range from optimizing kernels and designing an aircraft, to identifying the faults responsible for an earthquake. Each task requires significant domain knowledge and engineering work, with models averaging hundreds of millions of tokens per task. Solutions are scored on practical measures such as speed, cost and accuracy, both on provided cases the agent could test against and on hidden cases that an engineer would expect from the task description. The best-performing frontier model so far, Claude Fable 5.2, scores 54.6% and averages 211 million tokens per task. We highlight two findings. First, when models are given more time, they use more test-time compute and achieve higher scores. Models also scale differently with test-time compute: GPT-6 Astra achieves higher scores at shorter time limits and at equal token use, while Claude Fable 5.2 uses more tokens at longer limits to achieve the highest overall score. Second, each model scores lower on hidden cases than on the provided cases, by an average of 18 points, which we call the deployment gap. Models also fail to predict the deployment gap, overestimating their performance on hidden test cases by an average of 21 points. We hope that OWE-Bench grounds progress toward agents whose engineering solutions perform as well in deployment as they do in testing.
evidence_items.title: OWE-Bench: A long-horizon benchmark for measuring real-world engineering

evidence_items.summary: Overview This repository contains the research data, computational engine, experimental records, statistical analysis scripts, and reproducibility materials supporting the manuscript entitled “A standards-aware AI copilot architecture for highway geometric-design quality assurance,” under revision for the ASCE Journal of Computing in Civil Engineering (Manuscript ID: CPENG-8885). The research proposes a hybrid deterministic-generative expert system for highway geometric-design quality assurance (HID-QA), separating deterministic compliance calculations, grounded large language model (LLM) explanations, and workflow-based decision routing while retaining professional engineering decision authority with qualified engineers. Version 2.0 — Research Extensions Version 2.0 extends the original repository (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22044826) by incorporating additional prospective experiments, independent computational verification, corridor-clustered statistical analyses, and expanded methodological and engineering qualification documentation. The original historical experimental evidence, computational engine, benchmark geometries, and encoded reference classifications are preserved. Repository Contents HID-QA-50 benchmark comprising 50 constructed highway corridors. Eight encoded geometric-design checks, producing 400 check-level reference classifications. Frozen deterministic computational engine and encoded engineering criteria. Archived August 2026 Grok 4.6 experimental prompts and completions. One hundred prospective agent sessions conducted in November 2026 under two different computational information-access configurations. Prospective model completions and sanitized native request-level execution records. Historical and prospective scoring scripts. Corridor-clustered statistical analyses and confidence interval calculations. Independent computational recoding of the eight geometric-design checks.
evidence_items.title: A Standards-Aware AI Copilot Architecture for Highway Geometric-Design Quality Assurance: HID-QA-50 Dataset, Computational Engine, Agent Evaluation, and Reproducibility Package

evidence_items.summary: These files were used for training and evaluating TmProt 1.0, a protein melting temperature (Tm) predictor based on LoRA-adapted ESM-2 embeddings (Pailozian K et al., 2026). The source code is available at https://github.com/loschmidt/TmProt. The record holds the dataset files (each CSV has a matching FASTA file), tmprot predictions.zip (per-protein predictions of all compared models) and tmprot lora adapters.zip (the three trained ESM-2 LoRA adapters). MANIFEST.json lists row counts and SHA-256 hashes of the dataset files; each zip has its own README and manifest. Columns of the dataset CSVs: ProteinID (protein identifier), sequence (amino-acid sequence), Tm (melting temperature, °C), stage (train/val/test split), cluster# (homology component) and Is Melter (measured melting point or non-melter, Meltome pool only). The other fields are source metadata and preprocessing annotations. Each FASTA file mirrors the sequence column of its CSV, and its headers start with ProteinID . Training dataset: Meltome pool train meltome.csv , val meltome.csv , test meltome.csv , meltome clusters.csv (each with a FASTA file) The training data come from the Meltome Atlas (Jarzab A et al., 2020; PRIDE PXD011929, licence CC0), which covers 13 organisms. Only lysate measurements were used. Sequences were required to be 20–2,000 amino acids long and free of ambiguous residues (X, B, Z). Proteins that matched one of the independent evaluation sets by UniProt ID or by sequence similarity were removed. The resulting pool has 46,698 proteins; 36,855 have a measured melting point and are used for regression, and the other 9,843 showed no melting transition and were used only for clustering ( meltome clusters.csv ). The pool was clustered with MMseqs2 at 25% identity and 80% coverage, and whole clusters were assigned to the training, validation and test sets.
evidence_items.title: Training and evaluation datasets, model predictions and adapters for the TmProt tool

authors: Haichuan Zhang, Zhiyuan Zhong, Shih-Chieh Dai, Xinyu Sun, Guanhong Tao
evidence_items.summary: Multimodal web agents automate website interactions but remain vulnerable to visual prompt injection (VPI), where malicious webpage content manipulates their visual processing and induces unintended actions. Although several defenses focus on detecting injected instructions in screenshots, malicious destinations such as phishing URLs embedded in HTML can remain hidden yet accessible through agent interactions. Existing evaluations have also not sufficiently examined adaptive attackers who know the defense mechanisms. To address these limitations, we introduce AdaptiveVPI, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating adaptive VPI threats in web agents. Specifically, we present a dataset of 360 webpage instances spanning 6 distinct hijack strategies across 10 real-world websites, with malicious destinations not visible in screenshots. We design an adaptive attack framework that iteratively refines malicious instructions based on feedback from the defense mechanism being evaluated. We also introduce three metrics to measure the extent of agent hijacking at three different levels. Across 10 defense configurations for computer-use agents and 11 defense configurations for browser-use agents, our adaptive attacks achieve average success rates of 91.87% and 91.99%, respectively. These results reveal a gap between current VPI defenses and realistic threats and highlight the need for defenses designed with adaptive attackers in mind.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Web Agent Defenses Against Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection

authors: Koutian Wu, Yuxuan Cao, Gengchen Mai, Zeping Liu
evidence_items.summary: AI coding agents that modify Earth System Model (ESM) code must preserve both software interfaces and the physical assumptions encoded in them. We introduce ESM-Bench, a benchmark of 60 developer-commit tasks from 6 repositories: Noah-MP, CLM5, SUMMA, ParFlow, MOM6, and VIC. The v5 corpus contains 17 physics-based bug fixes, 16 process-representation modifications, 13 parameterization-scheme selections, and 14 parameter-optimization tasks. Each task includes a scientific objective, parent-commit source files, a reference diff, and three stored prompt variants. An artifact audit confirms that all 60 reference diffs apply to their supplied starting files. We define an eight-item patch-review rubric and audit five archived patch fixtures against the implemented local checkers. None of the five fixture diffs applies to its supplied starting files, yet three text-pattern checkers return a pass. A ParFlow expression replay disagrees with the reference slopes, and a MOM6 pattern check detects an omitted update. Inspection also identifies a retained VIC reference assignment that overwrites the intended vegetation-specific albedo. These findings expose limits of reference patches and local proxies as correctness evidence. The release provides a reproducible corpus and diagnostic tools; complete expert validation, comparative agent performance, and full-model execution remain unmeasured on v5.
evidence_items.title: ESM-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Whether AI Agents Understand Earth System Model Physics and Code

evidence_items.summary: Precise language control requires embodied models to follow instructions governing both task outcomes and execution. Although recent methods train policies to follow increasingly detailed commands, existing benchmarks often assess instruction following alongside perception, planning, and generalization to unfamiliar scenes. Higher task success therefore offers limited evidence of closer adherence to instructions. We introduce RoboInF, a benchmark measuring how reliably manipulation policies adapt their behavior to changes in an instruction. For each of eight tasks, six to twelve expert-validated instruction branches vary the requested goal, procedure, or manipulation detail while holding the initial scene and robot state fixed. Task-specific checkers verify the terminal goal and use recorded trajectories, contacts, and event sequences to assess compliance throughout execution. The accompanying RoboInF-4K dataset pairs 4,242 expert demonstrations with simulator-derived annotations of motion and contact. We evaluate leading manipulation policies ($\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenWAM) and inference-only agents (GPT-6 Astra and Qwen3.8-Flash). All four models exhibit a gap between task completion and faithful execution, indicating substantial room for fine-grained instruction following.
evidence_items.title: RoboInF: A Benchmark for Instruction Fidelity in Robotic Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: Professional documents are a long-context workload that retrieval-style benchmarks do not capture. In a ten-domain enterprise collection, a task's evidence is spread across a source document of median length 27 pages (mean 48.8, maximum 873); a third of tasks rest mainly on charts, drawings, and maps; and 70.9% require two or more reasoning hops. We post-train Kimi-K2.7, an open-weight foundation model, at its full context window on 1,465 expert-authored tasks with atomic rubrics from that collection, training rank-32 adapters with one round of privileged-context on-policy self-distillation followed by two rounds of rubric-reward reinforcement learning. We render each PDF as text for training and as extracted text plus selected page images at evaluation. The smoothed RL training reward rises from 0.37 in the first tenth of the run to 0.67 in the last. On the 100-task GDP.pdf holdout, served in a 262,144-token window, strict pass (all rubric criteria met) more than doubles after the second round, from 11.0% to 24.5%, with gains across input lengths up to 240K tokens. Mean tokens generated stay flat (9,803 to 9,733), so the gain does not come from longer outputs. GPT-5.6 Sol's leaderboard strict pass is 30.7% at a measured 3,422 tokens. On 220 out-of-domain GDPval tasks, where the model runs as a long-horizon tool-using agent, mean rubric reward rises from 0.571 to 0.746 after the third round and zero-credit tasks fall from 54 to 10, while messages per task fall 18%, from 70.9 to 58.2. In paired trajectories, the third round replaces a context-thrashing retry loop with one up-front check of all sources, and verification extends from checking that files exist to checking what they contain. We argue that long-context evaluation of agents should report accuracy jointly with tokens and turns, and that datasets of long documents should ship text and image renderings alongside each PDF.
evidence_items.title: Post-Training Agents for Long-Document Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Intensive care units (ICU) generate long, dense and evolving streams of clinical information, where physicians must repeatedly reassess patient states under time pressure, underscoring a clear need for reliable AI decision support. Existing ICU benchmarks typically treat historical clinician actions as ground truth. However, these actions are made under incomplete information and limited temporal context of the underlying patient state, and may therefore be suboptimal, making it difficult to assess the true reasoning capabilities of AI systems. We introduce RealICU, a hindsight-annotated benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) under realistic ICU conditions, where labels are created after senior physicians review the full patient trajectory. We formulate four physician-motivated tasks: assess Patient Status, Acute Problems, Recommended Actions, and Red Flag actions that risk unsafe outcomes. We partition each trajectory with 30-min windows and release two datasets: RealICU-Gold with 930-window annotations from 94 MIMIC-IV patients, and RealICU-Scale with 11,862 windows extended by Oracle, a physician-validated LLM hindsight labeler. Existing LLMs including memory-augmented ones performed poorly on RealICU, exposing two failure modes: a recall-safety tradeoff for clinical recommendations, and an anchoring bias to early interpretations of the patient. We further introduce ICU-Evo to study structured-memory agents that improves long-horizon reasoning but does not fully eliminate safety failures. Together, RealICU provides a clinically grounded testbed for measuring and improving AI sequential decision-support in high-stakes care. Project page: https://chengzhi-leo.github.io/RealICU-Bench/
evidence_items.title: RealICU: Do LLM Agents Understand Long-Context ICU Data? A Benchmark Beyond Behavior Imitation

Contents (wflo/): README.md — Instructions for reproducing the experiments, statistical tables, and figures. algorithms.py — Implementations of WARO, WARO-S, GMR, WFLOA (with equation-to-code mapping), DEEM, GBO, EO, PSO, HOA, and RIME, plus the exact O(hM) incremental wake evaluator. run experiments.py, pilot.py, sens conv.py — Scripts to execute the pilot study, main benchmark experiments (E1–E4), and wind-direction resolution sensitivity checks (15°, 3°, and 1° spacing). analysis2.py — Statistical analysis script computing paired percentage effect sizes, 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, Holm-corrected Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and Friedman ranks. results/ — Raw .npz files containing final turbine coordinates, per-turbine expected power, total expected power, convergence histories, and CPU times across all 10,620 paired runs (E1: 5,400; E2: 1,260; E3: 3,600; E4: 360). tables/ — Aggregated result files (.json, .csv, .md) corresponding to all main and supplementary tables. figures/ — High-resolution PNG figures (fig wind.png, fig rank.png, fig convergence S1.png, fig convergence S2.png, fig box.png, fig cpu.png, fig layouts.png, fig wake models rank.png, fig direction.png).

evidence_items.summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems perform strongly on native-English benchmarks, yet their accuracy degrades sharply when the input speech comes from under represented non-native accents. Nepali-accented English is particularly under-served: existing resources either focus on native Nepali speech, cover broader multi-accent settings without dedicated Nepali evaluation, or provide only limited Nepali-accent coverage. This paper presents a Nepali-accented English evaluation dataset designed to support robust ASR benchmarking under accent mismatch. The corpus was collected through a web-based platform that did not collect directly identifying metadata and contains recordings from 57 speakers. Each session follows a fixed 22-prompt protocol consisting of 11 phonetic prompts, 10 domain prompts, and 1 spontaneous prompt, providing complementary coverage of pronunciation, topical vocabulary, and natural speaking style. In addition to transcribed speech, the dataset includes participant metadata for coarse exploratory subgroup analysis and speaker-level manual recording-quality labels. Manual quality assessment shows that 50.9% of sessions are clean and 42.1% contain only mild noise. As a descriptive reference, open-source ASR baselines are substantially worse on this corpus than the corresponding LibriSpeech test-clean values reported in official model cards, reaching 38.15-55.00% WER on the collected set versus reported 2-4% WER on LibriSpeech test-clean. These baseline results position the corpus as a practical held-out resource for evaluating accent robustness and out-of-distribution generalization on Nepali-accented English.
evidence_items.title: A Nepali-Accented English Evaluation Dataset for Automatic Speech Recognition

evidence_items.summary: Dietary decisions require identifying a food's nutrient content and considering individual dietary needs, but recognizing food from an image alone does not provide this information. Visually similar foods can have different nutrient profiles, so selecting the wrong food record can lead to incorrect decisions even when nutrient rules are applied correctly. Furthermore, satisfying nutrient constraints does not necessarily establish a food's relevance to a person's intake. Evaluating these challenges together requires connecting food images, nutrient records, and individual intake histories. To support this evaluation, we introduce UMAMI (Unified Multimodal Assessment of Meals and Intake), a multimodal dataset and benchmark linking independently collected food images with nutrient profiles and respondent health and intake records. Using this dataset, we construct three diagnostic tasks covering visual nutrient question answering, personalized food recommendation, and condition-aware food substitution. Paired instances and input controls examine how visual identity and respondent context affect decisions. Our experiments identify errors in both food-record selection and nutrient-rule application, while showing that higher rule compliance does not necessarily improve alignment with subsequent recorded intake. These findings highlight the need to evaluate how multimodal systems select and use structured evidence for dietary decisions. The dataset, code, and dashboard are available at https://umami-benchmark.github.io.
evidence_items.title: UMAMI: A Multimodal Benchmark Dataset for Evidence-Grounded Dietary Decisions

evidence_items.summary: Accurate teak-tree segmentation from high-resolution drone imagery is critical for sustainable plantation management, yet lacks dedicated benchmarks. We introduce TeakTreeNet, a comprehensive dataset and evaluation protocol for binary teak-tree segmentation at native 2cm resolution. Four state-of-the-art architectures: U-Net, PSPNet, DeepLabV3, and SegFormer were rigorously benchmarked across scratch and ImageNet-pretrained settings with three-seed reproducibility. SegFormer establishes new SOTA performance with F1 0.938 +/- 0.002 (Teak), IoU 0.968 +/- 0.001 (Teak), and Accuracy 0.986 +/- 0.001, outperforming all pretrained CNNs. Domain-adaptive training suffices, as the scratch SegFormer outperforms ImageNet pretrained baselines, avoiding large-scale pretraining overhead. Comprehensive analysis reveals Transformer's superior boundary delineation for dense plantation scenarios. TeakTreeNet provides researchers with 6391 expertly annotated drone patches (224x224) and establishes reproducible evaluation protocols, enabling direct comparison of future methods. Our benchmark demonstrates SegFormer's optimal balance of accuracy, efficiency, and deployability for operational forestry monitoring of teak plantations for India's western tropical forests.
evidence_items.title: A High-Resolution UAV Benchmark Dataset and Baseline Evaluation for Teak Crown Segmentation in Western Ghats Tropical Forests

evidence_items.summary: ESG analysis requires complex language understanding across diverse sources, including corporate reports, news, and disclosures, for tasks such as ESG relevance detection, action interpretation, impact analysis, and question answering. However, existing ESG datasets are fragmented by task and source, with heterogeneous formats and annotation schemes, limiting their use for training general-purpose ESG LLMs and unified evaluation. In this work, we construct ESG-Instruct, a 30,000-instance ESG instruction dataset built from public ESG resources, and ESGU-Bench, an ESG understanding benchmark covering six representative ESG tasks. Based on these resources, we further develop ESGPT, an 8B ESG-specialized LLM, and evaluate it against diverse open-source and API-based LLMs. Experimental results show that general-purpose LLMs exhibit substantial performance variation across ESG tasks, while ESGPT, despite its relatively small scale, achieves the best performance on multiple ESG tasks. This work provides unified data and benchmark resources for training and evaluating ESG-specialized LLMs.
evidence_items.title: ESGPT: A Data-Centric ESG Language Model with Unified Instruction and Benchmark Resources

authors: Ryo Kuroki, Amin Mansouri, Philippe Schwaller
evidence_items.summary: Evaluating large language model (LLM) agents on scientific tasks typically reduces to final-task accuracy, which obscures where reasoning succeeds or breaks down. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic evaluation framework for hypothesis-driven adaptive experimental planning in closed-world system identification, instantiated in kinetic mechanism identification. The framework goes beyond final accuracy in two ways. First, we evaluate exploration behavior by quantifying the extent to which agents exhibit space-filling or corner-seeking patterns in the experimental design space. Second, we decompose the reasoning process into four interpretable steps: belief update, hypothesis discrimination, discriminative experiment design, and predictive reasoning under interventions, each scored separately on reasoning traces. Across ten LLM agents, we find that stronger agents outperform both adaptive (Bayesian optimization) and non-adaptive (Latin hypercube) baselines and exhibit exploration patterns inconsistent with naive heuristics. Decomposing reasoning reveals that the stronger agents score consistently well across all four steps, whereas weaker agents often succeed at belief update and hypothesis discrimination but are less reliable at translating them into actionable designs and sharp contrastive predictions. Independent expert annotations support predictive reasoning under our stated validation criteria, while evidence for discriminative experiment design is positive but less consistent. The results suggest a gap between recognizing plausible hypotheses and translating them into contrastive predictions, with more tentative evidence for a corresponding experiment-design bottleneck. The benchmark website is available at https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Accuracy: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Hypothesis-Driven Experiment Planning in LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Giving an AI agent a wallet lets it buy data and services on a client's behalf. Trust then depends on how it spends money and what that spending achieves. We introduce Agent Money Benchmark (AMB) to test whether agents spend a client's money well, starting with purchases of information for financial decisions. We link seller quotes and payments to final answers, evaluating 12 models on 80 payment tasks with simulated sellers and 76 research questions using live data. Purchases settled in USDC on Solana mainnet via x402, a protocol for paying per web request. Three of the 12 models passed 79 of 80 payment tasks without payment or budget errors. Nine fell for a seller's trap at least once; repeat charges and above-list quotes accounted for 79% of scam events. We estimate waste from data and inference costs, counting failed payment tasks in full and research answers in proportion to missed points. With spending split equally between tracks, estimated waste ranged from \$21.0 per \$100 for Claude Fable 5.2 to \$70.8 for GPT-6 Luna.
evidence_items.title: Agent Money Benchmark: Can AI Agents Be Trusted to Spend Money?

evidence_items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/24492277. SUMMARY This paper introduces the first publicly released benchmark for evaluating how well accessibility assessment approaches — in this study, five large language models — can judge the accessibility of scholarly PDFs. The authors selected 35 highly cited papers, used Adobe Acrobat Pro to create controlled variants of each, and produced a dataset of 125 PDFs spanning seven WCAG 2.2 / PDF/UA-derived criteria (alternative text quality, semantic tagging, logical reading order, table structure, functional hyperlinks, color contrast, and font readability), each labelled Passed, Failed, Not Present, or Cannot Tell. Labels were checked by one accessibility specialist. Five models (GPT-4-Turbo, GPT-4o-Vision, Claude-3.5 Sonnet, Gemini-1.5-Pro, Llama-3.2-Vision-Instruct) were then run zero-shot against criterion-specific extracted inputs, three times each. GPT-4-Turbo achieved the highest overall accuracy (0.85, Table 3); all models were much weaker on the Not Present and Cannot Tell labels, and several fabricated content — most strikingly Claude-3.5 generating alt text in 32% of Cannot Tell cases and then evaluating its own fabrication (§5.2). A qualitative comparison with five automated checkers (§6) leads to a sensible proposal for a three-tier hybrid workflow. This is a useful, transparently documented benchmark on an important problem. My concerns are with the validation chain underneath the headline numbers: how separable two of the four labels actually are at the input level, how many independent judges stand behind the ground truth, whose reading experience that ground truth represents, and how much of the measured accuracy was tuned on, or is an artefact of, the evaluation protocol itself.
evidence_items.title: PREreview of "Benchmarking PDF Accessibility Evaluation A Dataset and Framework for Assessing Automated and LLM-Based Approaches for Accessibility Testing"

evidence_items.summary: This dataset provides a multi-regime empirical benchmark evaluating deterministic on-chain Control Barrier Function (CBF) safety shields for continuous reinforcement learning in autonomous vehicle navigation. The archive contains 1,800 evaluation episodes conducted across three random seeds (42, 123, 777) and three distinct operational test regimes: nominal highway cruising, dense spatial corridor bottlenecks, and adversarial sensor-actuator disturbances. The dataset includes aggregated cross-seed statistical comparisons, 24 comprehensive evaluation run logs, 1M-step episodic training metrics, immutable smart contract intervention audit trails, empirical Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) gas profiling distributions (100 runs), and pre-trained neural policy checkpoints. These artifacts enable researchers to study formal safety shielding, evaluate out-of-distribution policy collapse, reproduce zero post-shield constraint violation benchmarks, and verify real-time execution bounds in safety-critical autonomous systems.
evidence_items.title: ChainShield-RL: Multi-Regime Safety Benchmark and On-Chain Control Barrier Function Dataset for Autonomous Vehicles

authors: Haiyu Xu, Yiyang Chen, Jiayi Zhou, Jiaming Ji, Juntao Dai, Yaodong Yang, Boyuan Chen
rationale: Matched: agent~benchmarking, benchmark, evaluat, training data
evidence_items.summary: Edge cases are not the long tail; they are the norm. An embodied system deployed across changing environments, bodies, objects, and tasks will routinely encounter combinations that were absent from its training data. General-purpose physical intelligence therefore requires world models that reuse prior knowledge, predict consequences, and adapt with little or no additional training. Yet current evaluations of conditional video generation emphasize visual quality, prompt alignment, or isolated physical plausibility, leaving systematic generalization difficult to measure. We introduce AxE Bench, a benchmark that organizes condition changes along eight factors of the acting agent and of its environment, and pairs every original condition with controlled variants that change one side or both. WBench-plus applies the same structure to an existing multi-turn benchmark, pairing each WBench scenario with variants on the environment side, through its world setting or camera behavior, or on the agent side, through its interaction instructions. Additionally, to score generated futures, we develop an evaluation harness that combines vision-language reasoning with targeted computer-vision evidence, converting each video into temporally localized events and comparing generated events with reference events in both time and semantics. We summarize each model with the AxE Score, event Fidelity weighted by its Stability across original-variant pairs. Across twenty models, generated events match reference events far more often in timing than in content: no model exceeds a Fidelity of 13.01, the highest Stability is 0.55, and the highest AxE Score is 7.10. Together, these components turn world-model generalization from an informal aspiration into a falsifiable evaluation program for real and simulated interactions. Our project website can be found at: AxEBench.github.io
evidence_items.title: AxE: Benchmarking Agent-Environment Generalization of Video World Models via Grounded Events

authors: Andrzej Nov\'ak, Yiyang Zhao, Dolores Garcia, Eric A. Moreno, Jeffrey Krupa, V\'ictor Bres\'o-Pla, Samuel Bright-Thonney, Lukas Heinrich, Michael Kagan, Philip Harris
evidence_items.summary: Agentic systems are increasingly being explored for automating experimental high-energy physics measurements, but the correctness of their results can today be reliably evaluated only via extensive expert review. To address this, we propose a method to perform detailed quantitative evaluations of agent-driven analyses through the use of blind analysis and injection tests, which are critical in a typical expert review. Agents develop a data analysis pipeline on a public dataset, while the evaluation is performed on programmatically generated sealed private datasets where signals are injected and simulation settings varied within realistic detector uncertainties. By requiring agents to provide a single workflow that is evaluated across these "sealed worlds", we are able to test the accuracy and robustness of the workflows. We demonstrate the approach on four tasks built from CMS open data and present it as a way to reliably benchmark scientific work in experimental high-energy physics. At the time of writing, the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, reaches 60% of the score of the expert reference analyses on average, ahead of GPT 6 Astra at 38% and Claude Opus 5.5 at 31%. In individual sessions on one of the tasks, Gemini 4 Argon exceeds the reference. The benchmark is hosted at https://hep-ex-bench.github.io
evidence_items.title: HEP-Ex-Bench: Evaluating Agentic Performance in High Energy Physics Experiment Data Analyses with Sealed Worlds

authors: Bradley Segal, William Bolton, Philip Torr, David Clifton, Lei Clifton
evidence_items.summary: Clinical drug development is a long-horizon, high-stakes process requiring sequential decisions based on information that costs money and time to acquire. AI agents have demonstrated capabilities for scientific analysis, but there is no established way to evaluate them on these decisions, as real trials are expensive, involve people, and never reveal the counterfactual. We introduce TrialAgentBench, a benchmark for evaluating AI agents on clinical trial analysis and drug development decision-making using simulated trials where the truth is known, embedded within the data records of a fictional drug sponsor. We publicly release nearly 3,500 tasks, varying from analysing a single trial to managing multi-phase programmes with budget and time constraints. We score each analysis by rerunning its code on new trials, and each programme by the value its decisions achieve. Across 24 closed- and open-weight models, the strongest agents can analyse raw, messy trial records to within 6% of a process-aware analysis, even when an assumption is violated, with 95% confidence intervals containing the true effect 94--95% of the time. Over the prior year, the best model improved from 19% above this analysis, with serious misses on 15% of tasks, to 3.5% and 1%. What limits them is decision-making from evidence under uncertainty: when to correct, what evidence to buy, when to stop. The strongest agents are overly careful, correcting on 83% of tasks with equal recording errors, where it is unnecessary. On drug programmes, the best agent has substantial headroom, reaching 48% of the value an oracle achieves against 58% for a rule-based developer, with others falling 24 to 66% short. Model generations show ongoing improvements in handling data and evidence, with substantial variation. The strongest models can act as competent analysts, but do not yet make reliable long-horizon decisions.
evidence_items.title: TrialAgentBench: Evaluating AI Agents for Clinical-Trial Analysis and Long-Horizon Drug-Development Decisions

authors: Kuan Zhang, Zhihao Yang, Yukun Chen, Xingyilang Yin, Mingyu Ouyang, Yue Su, Xiangnan Wu, Jiaming Li, Longze Chen, Run Luo, Zirong Chen, Lu Wang, Yiming Li
rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: Interactive intelligence requires agents to act on observations and adapt to the consequences of actions. Studying these abilities calls for diverse, challenging tasks under controlled conditions. We introduce GameDojo, a controllable interactive gameplay benchmark of 120 boss encounters across 20 games for evaluating model capabilities, learning algorithms, and agent harnesses. Coding agents reconstruct the environments and write gameplay scripts, producing GameDojo-Data with 600 hours of gameplay trajectories. Experiments reveal substantial challenges for frontier models, especially in real-time interaction. Training on GameDojo-Data brings GameDojo-4B to frontier performance, with the strongest real-time performance. We also find joint training improves individual tasks, and learned policies transfer across bosses. Together, these findings establish GameDojo as a challenging and valuable interactive gameplay benchmark for the community. Our project page is at https://gamedojo-benchmark.github.io/ , and our code is at https://github.com/THUSI-Lab/GameDojo .
evidence_items.title: GameDojo: Benchmarking Real-Time Interactive Agents in Video Games

authors: Chao Ding, Yidong Jiang, Junzhi Ning, Juncheng Wu, Yuhan Wang, Renjie Lu, Minjia Yuan, Gaopeng Wang, Liyang Wang, Pengcheng Chen, Dong Yin, Meiping Wang, Jinru Ding, Yuyin Zhou
evidence_items.summary: Large language models for longitudinal clinical care must revise their assessments and actions as patient information accumulates. However, benchmarks centered on isolated responses or final task outcomes provide limited insight into intermediate failures in evidence use, state updating, and action selection. We introduce WARD, a benchmark for evaluating how clinical agents translate accumulating evidence into patient-state judgments and timely, safe actions. WARD comprises 4,560 clinical tasks across seven clinical output domains, organized into 240 checkpoints from 40 longitudinal clinical trajectories spanning 95 hospitalizations. Its Longitudinal Track evaluates these tasks under controlled cumulative evidence. Its Interactive Track evaluates end-to-end, tool-mediated clinical management across 271 verifiable evidence items and 141 reference transitions. Across 12 models with scorable checkpoint outputs, evidence recognition consistently outpaces downstream state and action decisions, with linked-evidence nonresponse reaching 74.47--90.90\%. Models also struggle to retain and update information over time, while in the Interactive Track only 11.46\% of executed actions advance a reference transition. These results reveal a persistent evidence-to-state-to-action gap and highlight the need for process-level evaluation of longitudinal clinical agents.Code and data: https://github.com/Dingsuper-creator/WARD.
evidence_items.title: Seeing Is Not Acting: WARD Diagnoses the Evidence-to-State-to-Action Gap in Longitudinal Clinical Agents

evidence_items.summary: The deployment of large language models in operational settings demands evaluation of judgment under institutional constraint. We introduce DiscernBench, a benchmark for evaluating cooperative discernment: the ability of an agent to determine whether to comply with, refuse, or escalate a request in an institutional setting. DiscernBench comprises scenarios derived from real-world incident reports across domains such as aviation, law enforcement, and emergency management. We evaluate eight LLMs across three decision-making configurations and analyze both final decisions and the intermediate judgments produced during multi-agent deliberation. Under disagreement, Final Responders exhibit model- and role-dependent aggregation patterns in which a lone specialist recommendation can disproportionately influence the collective decision, a phenomenon we term Minority-Signal Override. Role-specialized multi-agent deliberation raises average over-escalation from 3.79% under direct single-agent judgment to 28.27%, with the direction and magnitude of minority-signal influence varying substantially across models and specialist roles. These results reveal distinct collective decision behaviors that are not captured by final-answer accuracy alone. Trustworthy multi-agent systems therefore require evaluating not only individual specialist reasoning, but also how conflicting judgments are transformed into collective decisions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Disha1001/DiscernBench.
evidence_items.title: DiscernBench: Evaluating Cooperative Discernment of LLM Agents in Institutional Settings

authors: Haoyuan Zheng, Dongting Li, Hancheng Ye, Qinsi Wang, Mingyuan Ma, Yuncheng Yao, Yifei Wang, Baijun Zhou, Zishan Shao, Tingjun Chen, Hai Helen Li, Danyang Zhuo, Yiran Chen
evidence_items.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) usually coordinate heterogeneous models and tools to solve complex tasks, creating a growing need for reliable evaluation. However, a multi-agent workflow that is fastest in one serving environment can lose its advantage in another, even when its models, prompts, and task remain fixed. This makes a benchmark result conditional on how the workflow is executed. We introduce MASSys, a benchmark for measuring this dependence in multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems. MASSys executes the same candidate-task pairs across serving substrates and load regimes, using five workload families spanning software repair, research synthesis, financial analysis, interactive control, and diagram generation. It records task quality alongside delivery, latency, cost, resource pressure, and failure evidence. In a controlled motivation diagnostic, the Star workflow falls from first to fourth in mean-latency rank under KV-cache pressure, while Chain rises from fourth to first. The substrate sweeps further show that increasing load creates long runtime tails and timeout pressure. In several task families, quality among evaluated outputs changes less than effective quality over submitted jobs: the system delivers fewer usable results even when the surviving outputs remain competitive. Tool and runtime traces reveal that these outcomes involve both model serving and non-model execution. Together, the results motivate evaluating MAS designs over explicit operating conditions and reporting which tasks are delivered, how well they are solved, and where execution breaks down.
evidence_items.title: The Evaluation Substrate Matters: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Serving Substrates

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have offered a new path for misinformation detection, but the reliability of model-generated auxiliary information and the applicability of detection results in new scenarios have yet to be verified. Some representative studies and related methods have been classified into three types in this paper: content-driven, context- and relation-driven, and knowledge- and evidence-driven methods. Factual reliability, generalisation reliability and the reliability of explanations and evidence are introduced. According to the comparison of previous experiments, semantic augmentation, simulation of user behaviour and logical reasoning can all improve the detection rate in specific circumstances; however, the level of improvement differs depending on the dataset and model parameters. This suggests that method selection should depend on the available information and the specific detection scenario, rather than classification scores alone. Based on the above results, this article analyzes and evaluates issues such as data contamination, synthetic data bias, and external evidence reliability, providing reference for the selection and evaluation of detection methods.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model-Driven Misinformation Detection: Methods, Trustworthiness Evaluation, and Challenges

organizations: Chonnam National University
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Heart-sound denoisers are often judged by reconstruction fidelity under artificial noise, leaving diagnostic preservation after transfer insufficiently characterised. We built a multi-corpus benchmark rather than proposing a new architecture. Criterion-based panel construction defined an executable panel of ten learned denoisers trained on a common source corpus, four classical filters and an identity control. We evaluated five 300-recording arms from four phonocardiogram corpora (1,333 unique recordings). Paired comparisons covered 18 artificial-corruption conditions and their no-added-noise passthroughs in three arms, plus two original-recording arms without paired clean references, using four fixed classifiers. Uncertainty used patient clustering where identifiers were available, recording clustering otherwise, and a parent-recording sensitivity analysis for PaHS. Mean AUROC change was +0.014 on the denoiser-development corpus but -0.085 and -0.081 on two external corpora. On external no-added-noise inputs, some learned denoisers reduced AUROC by up to 0.380 and attenuated approximately 91\% of magnitude within detected cardiac-event regions on BMD-HS. On original BMD-HS recordings, the largest AUROC reduction was 0.387, with a 0.767 sensitivity loss at the pre-denoising threshold. Development-distribution benefit therefore did not establish diagnostic preservation after transfer. Target-corpus task effects, no-added-noise behaviour and fixed operating points should be evaluated before integration into a diagnostic pipeline.
evidence_items.title: A multi-corpus benchmark reveals limits of diagnostic preservation in heart-sound denoising

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in spatial omics have enabled tissue atlases spanning serial sections, donors, and experimental technologies. Aligning these datasets is essential for comparing spatial organization, reconstructing three-dimensional tissue architecture, and registering sections to a common coordinate framework. However, systematic comparisons of alignment accuracy, computational efficiency, and usability remain limited. Here, we benchmarked 15 tissue alignment and registration algorithms using experimental and simulated spatial transcriptomics datasets across pairwise alignment, three-dimensional reconstruction, cross-resolution alignment, and atlas registration tasks. We assessed spatial-domain and cell-type correspondence, spatial gene-expression similarity, computational scalability, and usability. Simulated datasets with known spatial coordinates additionally enabled direct evaluation of geometric accuracy and reconstruction stability. No single method performed best across all settings: performance depended on the task, spatial resolution, and tissue characteristics, and strong pairwise alignment did not necessarily translate into reliable three-dimensional reconstruction. Evaluation metrics captured complementary aspects of alignment quality, highlighting the importance of using multiple criteria for comprehensive assessment. These findings provide practical guidance for method selection and identify priorities for improving the accuracy, scalability, and accessibility of spatial omics alignment.
evidence_items.title: A systematic benchmark evaluation of algorithms for 3D tissue alignment and registration with spatial omics

organizations: Department of Electronics and Information Technology, Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Lublin University of Technology, Nadbystrzycka 38A, 20-618 Lublin, Poland

evidence_items.summary: This study presents an exploratory benchmark of object-detection architectures and explainability methods for dermoscopic skin lesion images. It compares model performance and explanation properties under a controlled, dataset-specific protocol, without assessing clinical effectiveness or screening readiness. Thirty-two model variants spanning seven detector families (YOLOv8, YOLOv9, YOLOv10, YOLOv11, YOLOv12, YOLOv26, and RT-DETR) were evaluated on four lesion classes—basal and squamous cell carcinoma (BCC + SCC), invasive melanoma (MI), melanocytic nevus (N), and pigmented benign keratosis (PBK)—as well as negative images of healthy skin. Models were filtered by recall, mAP@50–95, and inference time, then prioritized using a study-specific per-class score that emphasized malignant-lesion recall. This descriptive procedure selected a common reference detector for paired XAI comparison and was not subject to statistical inference. YOLOv8m was designated as the reference (recall 79.3%, mAP@50 81.9%, inference time 4.2 ms; BCC + SCC recall 69.4%). Because each detector was trained once and selection used test-set results, these findings neither provide an independent post-selection estimate of YOLOv8m’s generalization nor establish its superiority. A paired comparison with instance-segmentation models trained on the same data found no significant differences in recall or mAP@50 across 22 architecture variants, whereas detection was significantly faster on the study hardware. Seven XAI methods were compared using 337 true-positive detections from the reference detector. Under the original evaluation protocol, LayerCAM achieved the strongest localization and robustness at low computational cost, whereas LIME and D-RISE showed the strongest faithfulness. Additional evaluations confirmed the high localization performance of LayerCAM using polygon annotations but revealed the influence of detection geometry, feature level, and architecture-related factors.
evidence_items.title: An Exploratory Technical Benchmark of Object Detectors and Explainability Methods for Malignancy-Prioritized Skin Lesion Analysis

evidence_items.summary: MLX Benchmarks Structured benchmark results for local hardware and hosted-provider language model evaluations. Rows include both local-device runs and provider results; recorded host and accelerator fields may be absent for provider rows. evidence_items.summary: Existing AI-generated image (AIGI) detection benchmarks predominantly rely on earlier synthesis systems with limited content diversity and conspicuous artifacts, failing to fully reflect the detection challenges posed by high-fidelity images from contemporary models. We introduce AIGI-26, a benchmark of 253,200 images covering 26 recent open- and closed-source generators. Its novel, diverse, and heterogeneous sources provide a basis for systematically evaluating detection methods on modern generated imagery. Additionally, to capture subtle statistical discrepancies across complementary forensic views, we propose the multi-aspect forensic detection network (MAFDNet). Its fixed forensic operators expose complementary texture, local prediction, resampling, and chromatic responses, summarized by a hierarchical encoder using multiscale means and standard deviations. In parallel, a spectral branch captures Fourier log-magnitude and neighboring-frequency phase variation across radial bands and directional axes. Fusing these descriptors combines local inconsistencies with global spectral organization for authenticity detection. Trained on 12,660 AIGI-26 images, MAFDNet achieves 88.5% accuracy and 94.9% average precision on the 240,540-image test set, with only 1.04M parameters and 1.39 GFLOPs per $256\times256$ input. MAFDNet also demonstrates effective cross-dataset generalization on DailyBench and Treasure-37.
evidence_items.title: AIGI-26: A Benchmark for AI-Generated Image Detection Across Diverse Modern Generators

evidence_items.summary: Cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) aims to locate an object indicated by a click point in a ground or drone query image within a satellite reference image. Through a quantitative prompt-sensitivity evaluation, we find that existing CVOGL methods suffer from a prompt-disobeying overfitting problem: when the click point is moved or removed, their predictions barely respond, indicating that the models rely on spurious feature correlations rather than genuinely following the prompt semantics. We trace this behavior to the limited scale of the benchmark dataset, which contains only 4,343 prompt-object pairs per task, so that the models simply memorize the object associated with each scene instead of learning the true prompt-to-object correspondence. To address this, we propose two plug-and-play components. First, we construct the CVOGL-MO dataset by expanding the existing training and test sets with diverse multi-object annotations, mitigating the memorization that induces shortcut learning. Second, we propose the Cross-View Co-Scene Multi-Object Contrastive Loss (CVMCL), which enforces distinct feature representations for different click points within the same scene, compelling the model to follow prompt instructions. We further design a prompt-sensitivity evaluation protocol with prediction-shift metrics, providing the first quantitative measurement of prompt-following capability for CVOGL. Both components are architecture-agnostic and can be integrated into existing methods without any architectural modification. Experiments on three representative backbones show that our components substantially improve prompt-following accuracy on the new multi-object test sets and markedly increase prompt sensitivity. Our dataset and code will be publicly released at https://github.com/Sunny-Fresher/CVOGL-MO.
evidence_items.title: Prompt-Consistent Cross-View Object Geo-Localization

evidence_items.summary: Games are a robust test for large language model agents: they require sequential decisions, adversarial or cooperative interaction, state tracking, reasoning under uncertainty, and long-horizon planning. However, a one-time game benchmark can go stale as models, prompts, environment implementations, and evaluation policies change, and refreshing it is costly: full round-robin evaluation scales poorly in the number of model pairs, and the resulting outcomes live on incompatible per-game scales. We present a framework for continuous evaluation of LLM agents in game settings, organized around three coupled components. First, an adaptive scheduler that maps pairwise Bradley-Terry uncertainty to reduced per-pair match targets, concentrating budget on comparisons that remain unresolved. Second, a Unified Leaderboard (ULB) that reduces heterogeneous outcomes to pairwise evidence and fits a game-balanced Bradley-Terry model by minorization-maximization with bootstrap intervals, so that high-throughput games cannot dominate the aggregate ranking. Third, a game skill-profile methodology that scores each game along diverse skill dimensions, making the capability coverage of the suite explicit and turning game selection into a design decision rather than an artifact of availability. In this paper, we specify the research design and outcome reduction of the current implementation and evaluate the framework on a ten-game suite spanning perfect-information board games, imperfect-information games, and social/language settings, reporting LLM capability profiles, evaluation-cost savings across model-refresh cycles, and an empirical Pareto frontier relating model performance to inference cost. As deployed, the scheduler saved 61.7% of episodes; it counted each episode in the two team games as four records, overstating their savings, and the other eight games save 61.9%.
evidence_items.title: Schedule, Rank, Profile: Continuous Evaluation of LLM Agents in Games

evidence_items.summary: Tandem mass spectrometry provides a high-throughput framework for identifying and quantifying proteins in complex biological samples. In computational proteomics, predicting peptide MS/MS spectra is a critical task, enabling downstream applications such as large-scale peptide identification and quantification. While deep learning architectures have substantially improved prediction accuracy, three evaluation challenges obscure the true progress of the field. First, inconsistent data preprocessing and incompatible model output spaces hinder fair model comparison. Second, flawed data splitting strategies can permit hidden sequence leakage and inflate reported performance. Third, existing evaluations typically lack systematic assessment of heterogeneous zero-shot domain shift and robustness to collision energy and precursor charge. To address these challenges, we propose PepSpecBench, a unified benchmark for peptide MS/MS spectrum prediction. The main leaderboard scores all six predictors on a shared b/y fragmention intensity subtask, so their outputs are directly comparable. PepSpecBench standardizes data preprocessing across complementary public datasets, enforces a strict backbone-disjoint splitting strategy to prevent exact backbone overlap across partitions, and evaluates diverse architectures within a shared fragment-ion representation space. It further introduces a heterogeneous zero-shot domainshift suite and metadata perturbation probes to assess robustness and whether models respond to fragmentation-relevant experimental conditions. Across six representative models, we uncover changes in model rankings across training sources and external test subsets, along with differences in their responses to collision-energy and precursor-charge perturbations. Code and data are available at https://github.com/zwYang2004/PepSpecBench.
evidence_items.title: PepSpecBench: A Unified Evaluation Benchmark for Peptide Tandem Mass Spectrometry Prediction

evidence_items.summary: In recent years, three initiatives have emerged to develop generative language models in Hungary. The motivation behind them is the same. For Hungarian, no model with the given capability existed, or existing English-centric models offered limited proficiency. A detailed examination of the corresponding studies, however, reveals several methodological limitations. First, the reliability of the evaluation protocols is questionable. Contrary to the findings of Csibi et al. [2026], evaluation under the recommended inference settings shows that Qwen3-4B achieves higher scores than Racka-4B, its Hungarian-adapted version. Data contamination is evident in the work of Yang et al. [2025d] and Szentmih\'alyi et al. [2025], potentially biasing the reported results. Second, the training pipelines fall short of current best practices in corpus curation and data mixture, which risks wasting substantial compute on low-quality data. The lack of controlled ablations prevents reliable assessment of these choices. Third, none of the three papers assessed forgetting or capability loss. Testing the adapted models on a subset of the original benchmarks indicates performance decline in all three cases, especially Racka-4B. These observations emphasize the importance of rigorous experimental design in language model development, given the significant computational and financial costs involved.
evidence_items.title: Made in Hungary: Comments on the performance of generative language models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) play a critical role in modern cybersecurity; however, traditional signature- and rule-based approaches remain limited against zero-day, polymorphic, and adaptive cyberattacks. Recent advances in Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) and Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) have introduced new opportunities for improving intrusion detection through adaptive learning, synthetic traffic generation, autonomous response, and adversarial robustness. This systematic literature review synthesises evidence from 78 studies published between 2018-2026, providing a comprehensive analysis of the emerging role of Generative AI and Agentic AI in NIDSs. The reviewed studies are organised into four major research themes: (i) data augmentation and synthetic attack generation, (ii) adversarial robustness, (iii) autonomous intrusion detection, and (iv) explainable and trustworthy AI. The analysis shows that generative models, including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), diffusion models, and Large Language Models (LLMs), improve synthetic data generation, mitigate class imbalance, and enhance anomaly detection, while agentic approaches based on reinforcement learning and multi-agent systems increase adaptability and distributed decision-making. The review identifies a persistent gap between benchmark performance and operational readiness, driven by limitations in cross-dataset generalisation, computational overhead, adversarial robustness, explainability, privacy preservation, and real-world deployment. To address these challenges, this review proposes a Generative-Agentic Synergy Framework that integrates generative simulation, adaptive detection, agentic response, trust and explainability, and privacy-aware deployment into a unified conceptual framework for designing and evaluating next-generation NIDSs.
evidence_items.title: Generative and agentic artificial intelligence for network intrusion detection: a systematic literature review
