authors: Peilong Zhou, Cangyuan Li, Kaiyan Chang, Ying Wang
evidence_items.summary: Hardware benchmarks for LLM agents all run the design flow forward, from a specification to RTL, a layout or a bug fix. We ask the reverse question: given an implemented artifact, such as a layout, a gate-level netlist or a protected simulation model, can an agent work out what it does well enough to act on that knowledge? We introduce HWRE-Bench, a benchmark for agentic hardware reverse engineering built on one observation. Each step of the forward flow discards information (names, hierarchy, word-level structure, generator parameters, the programming model), and a reverse-engineering task asks the agent to recover what was lost and to prove it with an executable deliverable that the artifact alone cannot supply. Since layout extraction is now mechanical and a correct netlist is already a cycle-exact model, every task carries a mandatory copy-the-netlist control that must score zero. HWRE-Bench spans five tracks (Extract, Abstract, Audit, Interoperate, Modify), four information-loss levels and white- versus black-box access, all on original designs. We report a pilot of 148 rollouts from two agents on four seed tasks under 16 conditions, with stage-annotated trajectories. Agents built their own layout extractors and audited a sanitized layout as reliably as a netlist, at about 27% more turns. Keyless, equivalence-preserving obfuscation changed neither pass rates nor defect-repair scores. Whether agents read the structure at all depended on task framing rather than on necessity, so pass rate alone does not show understanding. Provider safety filters stopped 16% of one agent's runs on the audit tasks. These results argue for deliverables beyond equivalence and for reporting run validity explicitly.
evidence_items.title: HWRE-Bench: Can LLM Agents Understand Hardware They Did Not Design?

authors: Yan Zheng, ShengYun Peng, Xuyao Liang, Xiaoyan Cong, Nuo Chen, Bangya Liu, Zihan Wang, Wenyan Cong, Zhiwen Fan, Zhangyang Wang
evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for spatial tasks such as navigation and manipulation, where they must infer geometry and object relationships from visual input in order to act correctly. Existing benchmarks usually test perception and reasoning in isolation, making it hard to tell whether failures come from visual understanding, downstream reasoning, or the bridge between them. We introduce VeriWorld, a benchmark for spatial reasoning in interactive 3D environments with executable actions and deterministic verification. For task families where all three channels are well-defined, we evaluate matched visual, structured, and combined input conditions on the same instance, environment, and verifier; families without a clean visual/structured/combined split are reported separately. This design supports controlled comparisons of perception, reasoning, and their interaction. Using this setup, we uncover two diagnostic findings. First, models often perform much better when task-relevant information, such as object identity, current state, or target location, is given explicitly than when it must be read from the rendered scene, revealing a recurring visual-to-structure gap. Second, action-space and harness design can change outcomes even under the same task and information condition, showing that interaction protocol is itself a confounding variable. VeriWorld is open-sourced to support reproducible and fine-grained evaluation of spatial reasoning in VLMs.
evidence_items.title: VeriWorld: A Verifiable Visual SWE-Bench for Spatial Reasoning in 3D Environments

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: Effective real-time, full-duplex multimodal interaction requires systems to understand not only what users say, but also the communicative needs conveyed through prosody, facial expressions, gestures, and context, and to generate audiovisual responses that appropriately address those needs. Existing evaluations offer limited insight into whether systems translate an understanding of such unspoken needs into effective responses. We introduce UUBench, a benchmark for assessing how well multimodal interactive systems Understand the Unspoken intent and address users' implicit communicative needs. The inherent subjectivity of implicit intent inference poses a key challenge for evaluation. To address this, we introduce Process-Oriented Scoring, which grounds the assessment of intent fulfillment in observable auditory and visual cues, such as prosody and gestures. Rather than relying solely on a single overall score, it evaluates how well a response addresses the communicative needs conveyed by each applicable primitive dimension. We aggregate the dimension-level scores according to each dimension's relevance to the annotated evidence. Beyond intent fulfillment, Outcome-Oriented Scoring evaluates the naturalness, appropriateness, and human-likeness of the reply itself under audio-only, visual-only, and audiovisual conditions. To make these judgments traceable to observable evidence, we propose a Fact-Grounded Scoring JEV module, which uses structured, timestamped audiovisual observations of the user and the digital human's reply to assess one dimension or criterion at a time. UUBench provides a foundation for assessing whether multimodal interactive systems respond effectively to meaning beyond literal wording, supporting progress toward context-aware, real-time, full-duplex interaction.
evidence_items.title: UUBench: Understanding the Unspoken toward Full-Duplex Multimodal Interaction

rationale: Also found via Hugging Face Papers
evidence_items.summary: Latent world models predict the outcomes of action sequences, but comparing candidate plans through recursive rollout remains expensive at test time. We introduce Fast-JEPA, a latent world model planning framework that advances the success-latency Pareto frontier of predictive search. Fast-JEPA reorganizes predictive computation to support effective action-sequence search at low planning cost. It constructs a goal-directed plan to guide search and directly predicts the outcomes of complete candidates for efficient comparison, avoiding recursive state rollout during refinement. Across PushT, Reacher, Cube, and TwoRoom, Fast-JEPA achieves 96.50% average success rate with 2.41x faster planning than INTACT. Search-budget sweeps show that its competitive success and low latency extend across candidate counts and refinement depths. We further introduce DynaGoal, a benchmark for evaluating world-model planning under dynamic out-of-distribution conditions, execution deadlines, and controlled response delays. Fast-JEPA achieves average success rates of 73.83% on DynaGoal-Shift and 87.67% on DynaGoal-Deadline, demonstrating the practical value of low-latency predictive planning under changing control conditions and execution-time constraints. Our project page is available at https://deepcybo-physai.github.io/Fast-JEPA.
evidence_items.title: Fast-JEPA: Advancing the Success-Latency Frontier for Latent World Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only to power AI agents but also to build them. While many benchmarks assess the quality of LLM- powered agents, few ascertain how good LLMs are at building them. To this end, we introduce AppSci-Bench, where we construct a setting akin to how human Applied Scientists build agents for businesses - through eliciting task requirements from stakeholders, exploring the business's infrastructure, and scientifically improve the target agent by designing experiments and internal benchmarks. AppSci-Bench features seven realistic domains - five new ones (Slides Generation, Order-to-Cash, Compliance Review, Customer Call Insights, and CRM Insights) and two domains recast from tau3-bench (Yao et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2026b)(Airline and Banking) - each with a held-out evaluation suite customized for that task. We evaluate seven frontier models and find AppSci-Bench challenging: the best model, Claude Opus 5.0, only reaches a mean-minimum score of 59.1% across 3 build attempts; other models do significantly worse. Models struggle with eliciting task requirements (only 65% for Opus 5.0), build representative internal evaluations (models saturate their own evaluation 65% of the time but fail to solve the held-out task), presenting challenges for future research. The benchmark code is available here: https://github.com/sanjari-orb/appsci-bench.
evidence_items.title: AppSci-Bench: Can LLMs Build AI Agents and Make Them Better?

evidence_items.summary: Effective polyp segmentation in colonoscopy images is crucial for early detection of colorectal cancer, a leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide. While current deep learning models perform well on traditional Dice benchmarks, border segmentation remains difficult. Most methods use boundary information only as an additional loss signal during training, which prevents the network from explicitly learning border-guided feature selection or mask refinement. This paper introduces BGD-SF PolySegNet, a boundary-guided encoder-decoder architecture that controls three phases of the segmentation pipeline: dynamic multi-scale context aggregation, selective skip-feature fusion, and final mask refinement. The architecture comprises a pretrained EfficientNet-B4 backbone and three proposed modules: Boundary-Guided Dynamic Cascaded Multi-Scale Context Aggregation (BGD-CMSCA), Boundary-Guided Selective Attention Fusion (BG-SAGF), and a Multi-Level Boundary Guidance Head (MBGH). The model is trained on 3,535 annotated images from Kvasir-SEG, BKAI-IGH NeoPolyp-Small, and PolypGen, and evaluated on four held-out benchmark datasets. On the internal test set, BGD-SF achieves a Dice of 0.887, IoU of 0.839, mask-derived Boundary F1 of 0.531, HD95 of 30.32, and ASSD of 18.10, improving Boundary F1, HD95, and ASSD by 15.7%, 27.5%, and 34.6% over the strongest CNN baselines. External validation on CVC-ClinicDB, CVC-ColonDB, ETIS-Larib, and CVC-300 yielded Dice scores of 0.891, 0.776, 0.863, and 0.885, respectively. The model runs at 35 FPS with 22.51M parameters. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests confirm statistically significant mask-derived Boundary F1 improvements over six of seven ablation variants (p < 0.001; small-to-moderate effect sizes, r = 0.215-0.434), demonstrating that integrating boundary guidance as an active architectural component measurably advances polyp boundary delineation.
evidence_items.title: BGD-SF PolySegNet: boundary-guided dynamic selective fusion network for robust polyp segmentation in colonoscopy images

evidence_items.summary: The growing use of language models for forecasting motivates a broader evaluation of their world-model capabilities. Such evaluation must go beyond predictive accuracy to assess hidden-state inference and intervention prediction. Real-world forecasting benchmarks offer limited access to hidden-state ground truth and controlled experiments. We introduce CivWorldBench, a benchmark built on a multi-agent strategy game engine with recorded internal states, controlled observations, and paired intervention rollouts. Its 1,900 decision points from 475 worlds support three task levels: association forecasting, belief inference, and intervention prediction. Reference predictors support attributable evaluation of capability gaps, with an expert harness and empirical ceiling estimates contextualizing scores. Stored trajectories make intermediate predictions verifiable, while agent-play experiments test whether world-model capabilities support decision-making. The main panel comprises eleven frontier language models. Composite benchmark scores correlate with real-world forecasting leaderboards on matched model panels, more closely than with a general-capability index, supporting its use as a proxy for real-world forecasting capability. Strong association forecasts do not consistently extend to belief inference or intervention prediction, and effect magnitudes remain poorly calibrated despite informative direction predictions. Process verification reveals errors missed by final-answer evaluation, and structured reasoning improves intervention prediction for the strongest model in the process study. Agent-play experiments identify useful assisted plans and motivate evaluating decision-relevant capabilities beyond association forecasting. These findings identify hidden-state inference, intermediate-state prediction, and effect calibration as priorities for world-model training.
evidence_items.title: CivWorldBench: Evaluating Language World Models in Structured Multi-Agent Sandbox Worlds

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly evaluated on their ability to use tools, plan multi-step tasks, coordinate with other agents, and operate over extended horizons. Reported benchmark gains often obscure recurring failure modes documented across otherwise unrelated evaluation efforts. This paper synthesizes 27 benchmark, taxonomy, and audit papers (2023-2026), spanning 19 distinct benchmarks, into a cross-cutting taxonomy of agent limitations. To our knowledge, this is the first synthesis that integrates evidence across tool use, planning, long-horizon reasoning, multi-agent coordination, safety, and measurement validity into a single, unified taxonomy of LLM agent limitations. We identify six failure clusters: (1) tool invocation and parameter-level errors, (2) planning and constraint-satisfaction failures, (3) long-horizon degradation from context accumulation, (4) multi-agent coordination failures, (5) safety and security failures under adversarial or underspecified conditions, and (6) measurement validity problems. The taxonomy was derived iteratively by grouping independently reported error categories into themes corresponding to distinct stages of the agent reasoning-to-action pipeline. Across the literature, we find that failures compound nonlinearly with task length, that strong performance on individual sub-tasks does not reliably translate into end-to-end success, and that additional scaffolding does not consistently improve reliability. At the same time, substantial progress has been demonstrated in single-turn tool use, short-horizon web navigation, and narrowly scoped coding tasks.
evidence_items.title: Beyond the Leaderboard: A Synthesis of Tool-Use, Planning, and Reasoning Failures in Large Language Model Agents

evidence_items.summary: Despite remarkable progress in machine translation, Vision Language Models (VLMs) struggle on historical manuscripts, a domain that stresses core Natural Language Processing (NLP) capabilities: low-resource transliteration, archaic vocabulary, and noisy input signals. We present a systematic framework for evaluating the full image-to-translation pipeline on medieval Latin manuscripts, a setting in which scribal shorthand, ligatures, and parchment degradation expose failure modes that are invisible in clean-text benchmarks. Benchmarking on the CATMuS Latin dataset reveals a specialization gap: domain-specific Optical Character Recognition (OCR) models reduce character error rate by up to 4.3$\times$ compared to general-purpose VLMs, despite operating at orders of magnitude fewer parameters. We introduce the Interpres-Parallel-Corpus (IPC), a novel dataset comprising 1,383 aligned manuscript image lines, transcriptions, and expert translations, to our knowledge the first of its kind for medieval Latin. Our experiments uncover a complexity paradox: the simplest pipeline, a specialized OCR model feeding directly into a VLM, outperforms all multi-component variants. Adding retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or post-OCR correction introduces prompt saturation and error propagation that degrade aggregate translation quality. These findings offer both a new benchmark and practical guidance for deploying translation systems in low-resource historical settings.
evidence_items.title: When Simpler Is Better: Evaluating Translation Pipelines for Medieval Latin Manuscripts

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for multi-step workflows in real-world software environments. However, existing agent benchmarks are limited by trajectory-opaque grading, underspecified safety and robustness evaluation, and narrow coverage of modalities and interaction paradigms. We introduce Claw-Eval, an end-to-end evaluation suite addressing these gaps with 300 human-verified tasks spanning 9 categories across three groups: general service orchestration, multimodal perception and interaction, and multi-turn professional dialogue. To enable trajectory-aware grading, each run is recorded through three independent evidence channels: execution traces, audit logs, and environment snapshots, yielding 2,159 fine-grained rubric items. The scoring protocol evaluates Completion, Safety, and Robustness, with Average Score, Pass@k, and Pass^k across three trials to distinguish genuine capability from lucky outcomes. Experiments on 14 frontier models show that: (1) Trajectory-opaque evaluation is systematically unreliable, missing 44% of safety violations and 13% of robustness failures detected by our framework. (2) Capability does not imply consistency, with Pass@3 remaining stable under error injection while Pass^3 dropping by up to 24 percentage points. (3) Agent capability is strongly multi-dimensional, with model rankings varying across task groups and metrics, indicating that our heterogeneous evaluation coverage is essential. Claw-Eval highlights directions for developing agents that are not only capable but reliably deployable.
evidence_items.title: Claw-Eval: Towards Trustworthy Evaluation of Autonomous Agents

evidence_items.summary: Video summarization creates an abridged version (i.e., a summary) that provides a quick overview of the video while retaining pertinent information. In this work, we focus on summarizing instructional videos and propose a method for breaking down a video into meaningful segments, each corresponding to essential steps in the video. We propose **HierSum**, a hierarchical approach that integrates fine-grained local cues from subtitles with global contextual information provided by video-level instructions. Our approach utilizes the "most replayed" statistic as a supervisory signal to identify critical segments, thereby improving the effectiveness of the summary. We evaluate on benchmark datasets such as TVSum, BLiSS, Mr.HiSum, and the WikiHow test set, and show that HierSum consistently outperforms existing methods in key metrics such as F1-score and rank correlation. We also curate a new multi-modal dataset using WikiHow and EHow videos, and associated articles containing step-by-step instructions. Through extensive ablation studies, we demonstrate that training on this dataset significantly enhances summarization on the target datasets. The code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/ApoorvaBeedu/HierSum.
evidence_items.title: HierSum: A Global and Local Attention Mechanism for Video Summarization

evidence_items.summary: Complex cyber-physical systems (CPSs) combine physical processes, computation, communication, sensing, and actuation across subsystems developed with different tools and assumptions. When a composite model is reduced to implementation code, its component boundaries, interface assumptions, and governing laws can become difficult to recover for reconfiguration, analysis, and assurance. Large language models (LLMs) can generate such implementations rapidly, but their outputs remain difficult to verify and reuse. Applied category theory (ACT) provides mathematical abstractions for describing how scientific systems are organized and composed; categorical CPS models use wiring diagrams to retain subsystem interfaces and compositional structure. Building on this foundation, this paper constructs a compositional abstraction for CPS, enriches it with a reusable domain knowledge base, and makes it accessible to LLM agents through an executable domain-specific language and deterministic validation workflow. Categorical composition is mapped to executable DAEs through a structure-preserving interpretation that retains the typed system schema. The 1R1C example demonstrates how this interpretation commutes with composition, while larger thermal systems and a deterministic mixed-CPS fragment test its application to more complex composites. We then evaluate the ACT-based DSL within an agentic workflow under five different configurations. Across six building-control tasks, access to the ACT-based DSL and engineering skills substantially improves validator pass rates and engineering representation quality relative to direct code generation, although performance remains bounded by primitive-library coverage. The results support reusable and verifiable AI-assisted CPS model development through the combination of formal abstraction, domain knowledge, and agent-oriented tooling.
evidence_items.title: Typed Category-Theoretic Semantic Representations for AI-Assisted Engineering of Cyber-Physical Systems

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents a comprehensive survey of different researchs on large language model text watermarking. This survey reads 29 related works in depth and organises the field by the place where the watermark enters the generation pipeline: the model's weights, the decoding step, or a rewrite of text outside the model, subdividing decoding-time schemes by the mechanism that carries the signal. It argues that the insertion point can be viewed the one of the most important properties, deciding a scheme's detector requirements, its attack surface, and the deployment settings open to it. Additionally, this survey summarizes existing watermark attacks, which are organised by adversarial operation and quantified budget, from paraphrasing and translation to text mixing, key stealing, and model distillation. Because the three benchmarks surveyed are based on mutually incompatible axes, no cross-paper ranking is reported here. Finally, this paper concludes the key open challenges in current research and possible future research directions. This survey intends to provide researchers and engineering practitioners with a concise, systematic and in-depth understanding of the latest progress in LLM watermarking, and further facilitate the development of trustworthy generative artificial intelligence systems.
evidence_items.title: Large language model watermarking: a survey of techniques, attacks, evaluation, and future directions

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit a specific and previously undercharacterised reasoning failure we term symbolic drift hallucination: an intermediate variable within a multi-step computation graph silently receives an incorrect value, which then propagates through all subsequent derivations to yield an output that is linguistically coherent, structurally sound, and numerically wrong. This failure mode is invisible to existing single-signal verifiers because the model’s verbally stated answer and its generated symbolic code both carry the same corrupted value, causing them to agree on an incorrect result. We present HalluciNOT (Hallucination Neutralisation via Obligatory Testing), a three-stage post-hoc framework comprising: a constrained Program-of-Thought equation generator that enforces structural integrity of symbolic outputs; a guarded drift detector that compares sandboxed execution results against the ground truth, closing the detection gap that defeats verifiers restricted to the model’s own outputs; and a targeted Reflexion repair loop that isolates the corrupted variable for re-grounding. Because the repair stage accepts a candidate only when it lies within $$10^{-6}$$ of the ground truth, a strictly tighter bound than the $$10^{-3}$$ tolerance of the evaluation metric, the framework cannot convert a correct result into an incorrect one; the guarantee is unconditional, independent of repair quality, and independent of detector calibration. This framework is scoped to contexts where ground truth is available at inference time, such as automated grading, evaluation pipelines, and educational platforms with known answer keys. Evaluated on 600 samples across three benchmarks (GSM-Hard, SVAMP, and MAWPS, each with $$n = 200),$$ HalluciNOT achieves accuracy of 92.0%, 99.5%, and 100.0% respectively, with gains of +23.0, +4.0, and +5.5 percentage points over the LLM baseline.
evidence_items.title: HalluciNOT: execution grounded detection and targeted repair of symbolic drift hallucinations in large language model reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The increasing global deployment of solar photovoltaic (PV) systems needs robust, scalable, and automated inspection technologies capable of detecting a wide range of panel flaws under a variety of operating situations. The lack of comprehensive, multi-modal, publicly available annotated datasets is a major obstacle preventing advancement in this field. We introduce SolarFCD, a harmonized multi-modal dataset of solar panel defects created by methodically combining and reconciling three publicly accessible datasets covering two imaging modalities. Following near-duplicate removal, the dataset comprises 3,742 unique real images, expanded to 6,651 through targeted augmentation of the three under-represented classes; augmentation was applied to the training and validation partitions, and all test images are unique real observations. The dataset was divided into training, validation, and test splits at an 80:10:10 ratio through methodical label mapping, near-duplicate removal, and targeted augmentation of minority classes. Sixteen classification architectures from five design families were trained and assessed on the dataset to provide repeatable benchmark baselines. With an accuracy of 86.93%, precision of 88.79%, recall of 88.72%, and F1-score of 88.27%, ResNet101V2 performed the best overall. Per-class results showed balanced detection across all four defect categories within a narrow performance band. To promote open and repeatable research in automated PV inspection and solar energy operations and maintenance, the dataset, annotation files, and baseline code are made openly available.
evidence_items.title: SolarFCD: A Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for Solar Fault Classification in Photovoltaic Systems

organizations: University of California
evidence_items.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have drawn more research interest in construction safety inspection recently due to their capacity to integrate visual understanding, language understanding, and reasoning. In this paper, a survey is conducted to review the recent research on MLLMs in construction safety inspection, covering techniques, datasets, evaluation, applications, and limitations. The current studies primarily utilize prompt-based adaptation and in-context learning, domain-specific fine-tuning, and knowledge-augmented reasoning to enhance the performance of MLLMs in the construction domain. Applications of MLLMs in construction safety inspection include hazard detection and localization, safety inspection, visual question answering, assistance, and report generation. From the current studies, it can be found that MLLMs can be used to perform flexible and interpretable analysis for construction safety inspection with the assistance of domain knowledge and prompts. Nevertheless, the limitations of MLLMs in construction safety inspection are still present, such as poor visual grounding and spatial reasoning, lack of domain knowledge, lack of large and balanced datasets, and uncertainty of application in real-world scenarios. For the future work, it is recommended to enhance multimodal grounding, construct a larger and more balanced dataset in the construction domain, integrate safety regulations in a trustworthy manner, and perform human validation systematically. MLLMs have great potential to be applied in construction safety inspection; however, they can be used as decision aids rather than replacements for safety inspectors at present.
evidence_items.title: Multimodal Large Language Models for Construction Safety Inspection

evidence_items.summary: Objective: The Comparative Toxicogenomics Database (CTD) provides expert-curated chemical-gene interactions about environmental exposure effects on human diseases. Existing automated relation extraction systems are typically restricted to 3-10 interaction types and operate on abstracts only. We introduce CLOVER, a systematic benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on full-text chemical-gene interaction extraction using CTD-defined chemical-gene interaction terminology. The framework is designed to support 47 base interactions with directional modifiers (increase, decrease, affects), yielding 136 possible supported interaction classes. Evaluation is restricted to the subset of classes represented in the selected articles. Methods: CLOVER processes 50 full-text PubMed Central articles (1,563 sections) with PubTator and CTD integration. The pipeline consists of four stages: (1) LLM Extraction with one-shot and few-shot prompting; (2) LLM Validation to confirm and revise interactions; (3) Rule-based Refinement of extracted interactions to standardize terminology and eliminate errors; and (4) Human Review for expert oversight. We benchmark four LLMs (GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) and compare against a naive baseline that applies unstructured prompting directly to full-text PDFs. Results: The naive baseline achieves only 13% recall and 36% precision. Refinement significantly enhances performance by eliminating unsupported interactions. Under strict limitations, Claude-Sonnet-4.5 alone achieves 72% recall and 61% precision, and Claude with self-validation achieves 74% recall and 49% precision compared to CTD. Of the 136 supported interaction classes, 17 were represented in our evaluation. Conclusion: To our knowledge, CLOVER establishes the first benchmark for full-text chemical-gene interaction extraction aligned with CTD.
evidence_items.title: CLOVER: Chemical-gene LLM benchmark for obtaining valid entity relationships for the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database (CTD)

organizations: Graduate Program in Systems and Computer Engineering (PESC), COPPE, Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro 21941-914, Brazil

evidence_items.summary: Evaluating lay-facing health guidance from Large Language Models (LLMs) in the Global South requires human-centered explainability (HCXAI) tailored to local health systems and vulnerable populations. We introduce HCXAI-BR, a reproducible evaluation protocol featuring a five-axis, behaviorally anchored rubric—Safety, Accessible Language, Local Contextualization, Contestability, and Transparency—applied to 15 low-risk health scenarios in Brazilian Portuguese. In a pilot model-identity-masked evaluation of six global and national LLMs (90 responses), top-tier global proprietary and adapted commercial models achieved comparable performance (GPT-5.6 Luna 7.33/10, Sabiá-4 BR-SP 7.03/10, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite 6.83/10), outperforming the national open-weight models, even on local contextualization within Brazil’s public health network (SUS/UBS). These pilot-scale comparisons, from fifteen prompts and a single response per model, demonstrate the protocol’s ability to discriminate between models, not a statistically validated ranking. An instrument-diagnostic pass resolved conceptual ambiguities between safety directives and epistemic humility, improving contestability inter-rater agreement (κ = 0.485). Our findings demonstrate that post-training alignment of capable base models offers a more viable path toward human-centered, sovereign AI in resource-constrained health ecosystems than small-scale pre-training from scratch. This single, confounded comparison (parameter count and training budget differ between the two models) should be read as a provisional, exploratory observation rather than a general, statistically established claim. SUS and UBS, used above, abbreviate Brazil’s Unified Health System (Sistema Único de Saúde) and its primary-care clinics (Unidades Básicas de Saúde), respectively.
evidence_items.title: HCXAI-BR: A Reproducible Benchmark for Human-Centered Explainability and Contestability in Brazilian Health Information Guidance

organizations: Fudan University;
The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in imaging-based spatial transcriptomics have enabled high-resolution characterization of gene expression and cellular organization in situ. Resolving within-cell-type heterogeneity is essential for understanding how cellular states relate to tissue function and disease. However, imperfect cell segmentation and RNA spillover can contaminate cell-level expression profiles, obscuring intrinsic expression patterns and generating spurious variation. Existing decontamination methods can struggle to distinguish intrinsic variation from contamination when both are inferred from spatial measurements alone, and may suppress genuine state-associated signals when within-cell-type heterogeneity is not explicitly modeled. Here we present Dancer, a reference-guided probabilistic framework that disentangles within-cell-type heterogeneity from transcript contamination by combining cell-type-specific gene programs learned from single-cell data with explicit modeling of intrinsic expression, neighboring-cell contamination and background RNA. Across multiple human tumor datasets with varying gene compositions and panel sizes, Dancer improves cell-type separation and expression specificity while preserving identity-associated signals, achieving superior overall performance in benchmark comparisons. Inferred gene program activities reveal within-cell-type heterogeneity in the form of distinct cellular states and continuous spatial gradients associated with local tissue environments, while reference-guided panel expansion extends molecular characterization beyond the measured genes. Together, Dancer supports accurate transcript decontamination and more faithful interpretation of cellular heterogeneity within its native tissue context.
evidence_items.title: Disentangling within-cell-type heterogeneity from transcript contamination in imaging-based spatial transcriptomics

organizations: School of Computer, Hubei Polytechnic University

evidence_items.summary: Neuroimaging studies increasingly combine brain measurements with multiple clinical scales, yet prediction remains difficult when a new subject has imaging data but an incomplete clinical profile. Standard PARAFAC is transductive: it learns one subject-factor row for each training subject and has no direct mechanism for a held-out subject without fold-in or model refitting. We introduce SI-PARAFAC, a side-information-guided extension that replaces this lookup table with a learned attribute-to-factor mapping. A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) maps functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) measurements from 108 anatomical brain regions defined by the Automated Anatomical Labeling (AAL) atlas to subject factors, whereas the clinical-variable and AAL-region factors retain the standard PARAFAC form. We evaluated the method on 70 subjects with 108 AAL-region fMRI measurements and 15 clinical variables, several of which had substantial missingness. In the reported 5-fold subject-level analysis, SI-MLP achieved lower cold-start RMSE than a direct MLP regressor (0.6736 versus 1.1503) and lower warm-start RMSE than standard PARAFAC (0.3686 versus 0.3946). A nested rank-selection experiment yielded a cold-start RMSE of 0.6883 ± 0.0534 and selected R = 15 in 50.0% of outer folds. Standard PARAFAC with post-hoc fold-in rules was competitive or better, with ridge fold-in reaching 0.6309. These findings indicate that AAL-region fMRI features can support held-out-subject prediction while preserving the clinical-variable-by-AAL-region tensor structure, although larger multi-site studies are required to assess external generalization.
evidence_items.title: Cold-start prediction of depression clinical profiles from neuroimaging: a systematic benchmark of attribute-guided tensor factorization

evidence_items.summary: As AI agents increasingly assist people across digital and physical settings, evidence about individuals accumulates through digital interactions and observations of physical-world activities. When multiple agents maintain separate personal contexts, knowledge about the same person can become fragmented, making it difficult to maintain continuity and user control. We argue that personal AI should instead be organized around a shared personal representation under the individual's control. We propose Personal Agentic Twin, a three-plane architecture that connects distributed evidence to an evolving private twin of the individual, from which purpose-specific scoped twins draw personal knowledge to provide assistance and act on the individual's behalf. Authorization and execution controls link the personal knowledge available to each scoped twin with the actions it is allowed to take and the updates it can propose. We illustrate the architecture through representative application scenarios and call for research on the methods and evaluations needed to realize this vision. Personal Agentic Twin offers a foundation for personal AI that extends people's capabilities while preserving their authority over how they are represented and how agents act on their behalf.
evidence_items.title: Personal Agentic Twin: User-Controlled Memory and Policy-Scoped Representations for Agentic AI

organizations: SLB, France
SLB, Kazakhstan
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Formation evaluation depends as much on judgement — which minerals are present, which log response has a cause the model does not assume, when the agreement with independent data is good enough — as on equations. We describe how an agentic system encodes that judgement in reusable skills and couples it to server-side petrophysical computation. A skill is a reviewed procedure with structured triggers, input requirements, an ordered evidence hierarchy, a loop with permitted moves, a convergence gate and a stop rule, plus reference documents loaded only when a symptom calls for them. We dissect fe-mineral-inversion, the skill that runs a calibrated multi-mineral inversion, and contrast it with a display skill that renders logs without passing curve data through the language model. The harness runs a generic plan–act–observe–check loop; the skill supplies the thresholds, moves and stop rule; and a wellbore computation service reached through the Model Context Protocol (142 methods in 18 groups) produces every number. On Antelope 1-36-25H, a Madison Group well in the Williston Basin, a carbonate interpretation without halite reported 386.5 ft of pay; an evaporite-masked chain reduced this to 101.5 ft, and Madison Group pay fell from 309.5 to 52.0 ft. The calibration loop reduced the mean reconstruction error from 3.44 to 0.51 in two self-diagnosed steps — adding halite, then using its apparent log density of 2.04 g/cm3 — and brought salt-bed porosity from 0.33 to 0.011 against NMR 0.026. Independent sub-agents applied the same procedure to three further wells chosen from 75 with calibration data. It diagnosed kerogen in the Bakken shales, halite and an unrepresentable potash bed in the Devonian Prairie Evaporite, and an NMR discrepancy that was not a mineral problem in a Madison limestone. In two wells it rejected an iterate that fitted the logs better but contradicted spectroscopy or cuttings.
evidence_items.title: Inside an Agentic Formation-Evaluation Harness: Skills, Skill-Controlled Loops and a Calibrated Mineral Inversion on Antelope 1-36-25H, Williston Basin

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can help cyber-threat-intelligence (CTI) teams interpret unstructured reports, identify potential techniques, and draft response recommendations. The existence of a plausible narrative, however, is not evidence that the threat attribution is warranted or that an automated action is authorised. This conceptual article proposes an evidence-constrained and intervention-ready architecture for LLM-assisted CTI. It develops a bounded critical synthesis of recent research on LLM-assisted CTI and cloud retrieval, established cybersecurity standards, and recent work on action-level accountability. The model passes every interpretation through five gates: source admission, claim extraction, interpretation, decision authorisation, and execution with post-incident review. It specifies a claim-to-evidence ledger, attack-taxonomy version tracking, a calibrated abstention rule, an approval ladder for consequential actions, and a privacy-sensitive audit record. Three hypothetical scenarios (a contaminated threat report, false corroboration across copied sources, and an over-confident automated quarantine) show how a system might fail despite strong benchmark performance. The paper offers evaluation criteria covering support fidelity, mapping accuracy, adversarial robustness, escalation quality, and the time needed to reconstruct and reverse harmful actions. It makes no claim to have trained, deployed, or benchmarked a new CTI model. Its principal contribution is to reframe trustworthy CTI as a question of decision rights: not only whether an AI system recognises a threat, but who may rely on its interpretation, who can authorise an intervention, and who can challenge a damaging classification.
evidence_items.title: From Threat Detection to Decision Rights: Evidence-Constrained Cyber-Threat Intelligence and Accountable Agentic AI

evidence_items.summary: Large language models increasingly serve as judges of other models, shaping benchmark rankings and model development. Yet, a judge whose rationale consistently supports its verdict may still disagree with human preferences. To study this, we introduce PRIMEAPE, a multilingual benchmark for evaluating judge verdicts and rationales. PRIMEAPE provides 2,205 response pairs covering 243 instructions in English, French, Spanish, Urdu, Hindi, Norwegian Bokm{\aa}l, and Yoruba, with 11k human annotations of preferences and rationales across relevance, naturalness, truthfulness, safety, and overall quality. Our evaluation of twelve open- and closed-weight judges reveals that aggregate performance conceals differences across languages and criteria, while requesting rationales does not consistently improve agreement with human preferences. Judges also favor the first position, longer responses, and responses from related models, with effects that vary across criteria and languages. Crucially, judges can justify verdicts that disagree with human preferences while maintaining consistency between their verdicts and rationales. These findings show that consistency with a judge's own verdict does not establish alignment with human judgment. PRIMEAPE enables assessment of both, providing a foundation for more reliable multilingual judges. We release our benchmark and all annotation materials under the CC BY-NC 4.0 license at github.com/Toloka/primeape.
evidence_items.title: PRIMEAPE: A Multilingual Benchmark for Fine-Grained Meta-Evaluation of Judge Models

evidence_items.summary: Visual Entailment (VE) determines whether a textual hypothesis is entailed, contradicted, or unverifiable from an image. However, existing VE benchmarks are largely English-centric and do not capture Vietnamese-specific linguistic distinctions or culturally grounded visual contexts. To address this gap, we introduce OpenViVE, the first large-scale native Vietnamese VE benchmark, containing 62,268 balanced image-hypothesis pairs from 10,378 culturally grounded images. OpenViVE is constructed using an Artifact-Aware Hybrid LLM-Human Pipeline that combines constrained generation, human validation, and PMI-guided refinement. The pipeline substantially reduces hypothesis-only shortcuts, with Contradiction accuracy dropping from 96% to 66% after artifact refinement. We further evaluate a dual-stream PhoBERT-ConvNeXt framework with bidirectional co-attention to align visual evidence with Vietnamese hypotheses. The framework achieves 84.84% accuracy and 84.90% macro-F1 on the test set, while PhoBERT consistently outperforms multilingual XLM-R variants. These results highlight the importance of language-specific encoding and explicit cross-modal interaction for Vietnamese VE.
evidence_items.title: OpenViVE: New Benchmark and Dual-Stream Co-Attention Framework for Vietnamese Visual Entailment

evidence_items.summary: Audio large language models (LLMs) are typically evaluated on song genre, mood, and instrumentation. A more basic skill is telling whether two short clips play the same melody, chord or instrument. We introduce MusicListenBench, a benchmark of paired listening tests for melody, harmony, timbre, and tempo. Each test item comes with two variants. A FLIP variant changes the music, so the answer must change. A STAY variant changes only the sound, such as room echo or hiss, so the answer must stay the same. The two variants have opposite answers, so a model that ignores the audio scores 50%, whatever letter it prefers. The benchmark has a training split and two test sets, one rendered from symbolic music with exact labels and one built from real recordings. On the rendered test, seven of eight open audio LLMs score within 4 points of this floor. Of four commercial models, both GPT-Audio models are at chance, and the best, Gemini 2.5 Pro, reaches 74.2%, 12.8 points below human listeners (87.0%). Post-training with GRPO on 10k rendered clean pairs raises Qwen2.5-Omni from 61.2% to 99.0% on held-out clean pairs, and the gain transfers to a task left out of training. On FLIP/STAY, however, it only reaches the level of our listeners (86.0%). It now misses almost no change (1.9%, against 24.7% for Gemini 2.5 Pro), yet when only the sound changes, it turns a correct answer into a wrong one 25.7\% of the time. More than half of its false flips come from a quiet background hiss. Models learn to hear a difference much faster than they learn which differences matter. On real recordings, open models again stay near chance, and the trained model calls 27 of 42 pairs of two strums of the same chord different. Adding sound-only pairs to training lowers false flips on both test sets, but no training run teaches relative pitch. We release the data, code, and an open leaderboard.
evidence_items.title: MusicListenBench: Can Audio LLMs Hear the Difference Yet?

evidence_items.summary: Recent progress in large language model reasoning has been driven by benchmarks and reinforcement learning environments with automatically verifiable rewards, particularly in mathematics, code, and formal logic. These settings make model accuracy easier to evaluate and optimize, but it remains unclear how far success under fixed problem specifications and stable evaluation criteria transfers to reasoning outside such domains. Real-world reasoning often proceeds under incomplete and revisable information: conclusions may be supported provisionally, defeated by counter-evidence, reinstated by further arguments, or revised when stronger reasons become available. Reasoning of this kind is generally referred to as defeasible reasoning. We introduce ArgGYM, a procedural benchmark and RLVR-compatible training environment for structured defeasible reasoning. ArgGYM decomposes this reasoning into twelve tasks and grounds task-specific scoring in a symbolic argumentation engine that computes the formal states used to evaluate model outputs. It includes a frozen benchmark of 1,440 verified instances across fifteen curriculum configurations, two argument preference orderings, and two set orderings, while the same generators and verifiers can produce fresh instances, reducing dependence on static test sets, for both evaluation and verifiable-reward training. On the frozen benchmark, frontier and open-weight models show sharply different reasoning profiles: they can recover substantial parts of structured answers without solving the complete task, and performance declines in later curriculum configurations with longer dependencies and more interacting structures. Training Qwen3.5-4B with ArgGYM's verifiers as rewards more than doubles complete-task success on held-out instances, with the largest gains on constructive tasks.
evidence_items.title: ArgGYM: A Procedural, Engine-Verified Benchmark for Structured Defeasible Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: We introduce a reusable generator–jury framework for measuring whether synthetic household fi-nancial narratives support financial assessments consistent with their source records, without requiring human-written reference narratives. The framework uses a two-tier large language model (LLM) jury to derive refer-ence assessments from structured household records. These model-derived reference assessments are producedonce and retained when generation instructions or settings change. Each new narrative is assessed separatelyby the same jury under shared criteria, without access to its source record or reference assessment. Comparingnarrative-derived assessments with the fixed references enables generation conditions to be evaluated on thesame households. The framework measures how closely narrative-derived assessments match assessments ofthe source records, how this agreement varies across household groups, and how often jury responses can beused in the comparison. We applied the framework to baseline and candidate conditions that differed in promptinstructions and thinking mode. The candidate reduced the average gap between narrative-derived and refer-ence financial-health scores by 32%, demonstrating how the framework can guide generation choices duringsynthetic data development.
evidence_items.title: Synthetic Household Financial Narratives: A Dataset and Evaluation Study

evidence_items.summary: While vision-language models (VLMs) currently obtain notable results for highly-studied languages, e.g. English, they exhibit significant performance drops in certain low-resource languages, especially due to the lack of annotated datasets. To this end, we propose PaMuk-Bench, a novel parallel multilingual multitask benchmark for vision-language tasks. Our benchmark includes a set of over 10K curated English prompts that are translated into six languages: Arabic, Danish, French, Hindi, Italian, Romanian. Parallel translations, which are obtained via a semi-automatic process, along with accompanying generated and retrieved images enable the comparative development and evaluation of VLMs across a wide range of tasks: text-to-image generation, image captioning, content-based image retrieval, image generation difficulty estimation, image retrieval difficulty estimation. We empirically show that zero-shot English and multilingual pre-trained VLMs compare consistently worse than their fine-tuned counterparts, confirming that PaMuk-Bench is a valuable resource that can drastically reduce the language gap across a variety of VLM architectures and tasks. PaMuk-Bench is available at https://github.com/ghesil/pamuk_bench.
evidence_items.title: PaMuk-Bench: A Parallel Multilingual Multitask Benchmark for Vision-Language Tasks

evidence_items.summary: Long-term memory enables embodied agents to reuse past observations across tasks. However, existing cross-episode vision-and-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks often leave it unclear whether successful navigation relies on historical memory or current exploration. We introduce Mem-X, a benchmark designed to evaluate memory-dependent cross-episode VLN. Mem-X organizes episodes into sessions in which subsequent instructions refer to objects or routes encountered in earlier episodes. Its three levels evaluate historical-object recall, in-memory localization and episodic indexing, and off-memory relocalization and historical-route reproduction. For the latter two levels, agents receive episode-local poses but no transformations between episode frames, requiring them to establish spatial correspondence with historical memory. Mem-X comprises 2,071 episodes across 710 sessions in 34 scenes, including 1,204 memory-dependent episodes. We also provide MemBridge, a modular baseline that combines semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval to support existing VLN agents. Experiments with state-of-the-art VLN methods demonstrate the benefits of MemBridge while revealing substantial room for improvement on memory-dependent navigation. The benchmark and baseline code are available at https://github.com/NJU-R-L-Group-Embodied-Lab/Mem-X.
evidence_items.title: Mem-X: A Memory-Dependent Cross-Episode Benchmark for Vision-and-Language Navigation

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. To uncover these vulnerabilities at scale, automated red-teaming methods often leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to generate attacks that achieve high attack success rates (ASR). Model developers use the attacks discovered during internal red-teaming to harden agents through adversarial training before deployment, a collaborative offensive-defensive process known in cybersecurity as purple-teaming. However, we show that achieving high ASR during red-teaming does not guarantee robustness gains from subsequent adversarial training. Specifically, we find that two state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, suffer from mode collapse, repeatedly discovering similar attack strategies whose additional successes add no additional robustness improvements to adversarial training. To address this gap, we introduce PIPETTE, a unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that effectively converts red-teaming discoveries into defender robustness improvements. PIPETTE employs a dictionary learning-based reward that encourages broader coverage of attack strategies during red-teaming. It also integrates an on-policy adversarial training pipeline tailored to IPI defense, enabling agents to resist attacks while completing legitimate user tasks. Extensive evaluations across agentic benchmarks (AgentDojo and ASB) demonstrate that PIPETTE produces defenders that achieve near-zero attack success rates on static attacks and can withstand strong adaptive attacks, while maintaining benign task utility close to that of the undefended baseline.
evidence_items.title: PIPETTE: Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming for Robust LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: As agents become more capable, they are moving beyond one-off tasks toward sustained assistance across successive user goals. Such assistance requires agents to discover how unfamiliar environments work, reuse what they learn across tasks, and keep that experience current as environments evolve. Existing benchmarks increasingly study experience reuse and adaptation, but provide limited insight into which parts of accumulated experience agents revise, retain, or lose. To address this gap, we introduce ReScopeBench, a benchmark for the experience lifecycle across 18 interactive environments. It distinguishes structural experience about how an environment is organized and accessed from rule experience about reusable principles and constraints that guide decisions across tasks. To study how experience is acquired, reused, and revised, we propose an experience-first construction approach. It builds task streams around shared experience and introduces silent environmental changes. We evaluate task performance and track changes in saved experience throughout each stream. Across 20 models, we find that retained experience improves task performance, but agents struggle to keep it current as environments change. Even when the required experience is correctly recorded, agents do not always complete tasks successfully. These findings identify selective maintenance and effective use as complementary challenges for long-lived agents.
evidence_items.title: Towards Robust Long-Lived Agents: Benchmarking Experience Lifecycles in Evolving Environments

evidence_items.summary: Frequent urban floodwater poses a serious threat to the safety and efficiency of intelligent transportation systems. Existing vision-based methods for floodwater level detection face two main limitations. First, the lack of explicit reasoning leads to poor detection performance and little interpretability. Second, these methods struggle to generalize to the complex and varied real-world road scenes seen from different viewpoints. To address this, we reformulate the task as an explicit visual reasoning problem and propose HydroReasoner, a floodwater level reasoning framework designed for cloud-edge collaboration. HydroReasoner builds on Qwen2.5-VL and is trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization. To address the scarcity of reasoning process annotations, we build a floodwater domain knowledge graph HydroKG and design a novel KG path reward. Through deterministic graph traversal over HydroKG, this reward supervises the model's reasoning process at a fine granularity, which improves both reasoning and generalization. For edge deployment, we apply 4-bit quantization to the model, cutting GPU memory usage by 57% and inference latency by 43% while out-of-domain accuracy drops by only 0.2 percentage points. We also propose a confidence-based cloud-edge routing mechanism, which improves system safety and eases the computational load on the cloud. In addition, we build HydroLevel, a floodwater benchmark dataset of 3,000 images, for training and evaluating the model. Experimental results show that HydroReasoner achieves detection accuracy 4.0 and 13.6 percentage points higher than conventional vision baselines in the in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations respectively, with performance dropping by only 4.4 percentage points out of domain.
evidence_items.title: Knowledge-Guided Floodwater Level Reasoning for Cloud-Edge Collaborative Monitoring

evidence_items.summary: A game ships when a player can launch it, finish it, and return to a saved world, none of which a successful build guarantees, yet game-creation agents are mostly tested on one engine or on one-prompt browser games. We present CEGame-Bench, the first long-horizon benchmark for complete-game creation across five production engines: Defold, Godot, Roblox Studio, Unity, and Unreal Engine. Agents build each game from an empty project and a design document in runs averaging up to 295 steps and 65M tokens; the document doubles as a contract, and a hidden evaluator accepts a game only by real-input play. Under four scaffolds, agents earn most integration points but usually under half the gameplay points, and their games reach the ending in only 16% of runs, while references built by engineers with coding agents score near the maximum, which places this artifact-to-play gap in the agents. No two engines rank configurations alike (Kendall's tau 0.14-0.62), and the same game usually scores higher on Unity and Unreal Engine, which check more before play. We release Game Completion Boost, an agent skill for requirement-driven playtesting and repair that raises the execution-based score of three models by 14.1-24.3 points.
evidence_items.title: From Code to Playable Systems: CEGame-Bench for Long-Horizon Game Creation Agents

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents are increasingly used to optimize code, but existing benchmarks fix one accelerator, programming model, or harness, so they cannot isolate what each component contributes or show whether added skills and tools repay their cost. We present HPCAgent-Bench with 722 kernels in three tracks: loop-level optimization challenges, kernels extracted from HPC codes, and machine-learning models. The framework specifies each kernel once in NumPy, derives C and Fortran references, accepts submissions through a common C ABI or Python interface, and runs them on CPUs or GPUs, on one or multiple nodes. An external judge checks correctness on hidden fuzzed inputs and times each submission, closing the paths agents use to exploit the testing system. We introduce a reporting protocol, intervention efficacy, which reports an intervention, such as adding a tool, through paired runs on speedup, success rate, and cost, and a metric, weighted token cost, which reports input, cached-input, and output tokens under explicit weights. Agents reach up to $5.0\times$ speedup over automatic parallelizers, and their optimizations transfer to another machine: 93--99% of answers without device-specific code remain correct, and per-kernel speedups keep a rank correlation of $r_s \ge 0.84$. Of 48 intervention comparisons, 6 change speed and 9 change token cost significantly, and 5 leave speed equivalent. Because token weighting decides whether a saving is significant, we state the weights and release every token count as a standard for cost reporting. HPCAgent-Bench is a broad, hardened benchmark for the sound evaluation of agentic optimization, with transparent cost metrics.
evidence_items.title: HPCAgent-Bench: A Framework for Sound Benchmarking of Code-Optimizing Agents, Harnesses, and Skills

evidence_items.summary: While AI agents are useful for many tasks, they regularly misbehave in destructive ways, such as deleting important data. While prior work has focused on preventing such misbehavior, we consider how to recover after an agent misbehaves. We propose verifiable agent insurance (VAI), a framework for agent providers to commit financially to promises, a list of programmatically-specified policies that an agent is meant to follow. These promises are embedded in a smart contract on an immutable ledger (e.g., a blockchain) to prevent tampering, along with a monetary escrow. A user who detects a violation of committed promises can prompt a verifier to review agent execution traces, which are logged through the agent harness's shared tool-execution path, without instrumenting each tool separately. Upon verification of the violation, the agent provider's escrow funds are paid to the reporting user. We instantiate VAI as an end-to-end implementation on an Ethereum layer-2 network, and evaluate its coverage on three prominent agent benchmarks, two of which we re-annotated to obtain task-level policy-compliance labels. Currently, many agents do not emit user authorizations and security-relevant information as explicit, structured data objects -- rather, they embed the data needed to verify policy violations in natural language exchanges. Even so, VAI manages to detect violations in 63.6% of runs containing violations across three benchmarks. By augmenting agents to explicitly emit such objects, violation detection rises to 79.8% of runs containing violations. Our findings suggest that for improved auditability, agents should be co-designed with their security policies to emit explicit, structured records of user authorization and security-relevant actions.
evidence_items.title: Holding Agents Accountable with Verifiable Agent Insurance

evidence_items.summary: Lifelong LLM agents increasingly adapt through external learning states that store past interactions as retrievable memories or reusable skills, yet existing benchmarks rarely account for how the path of accumulated experience shapes what agents transfer and retain. In this work, we establish PATH-Bench, a benchmark for path-dependent evaluation of lifelong agents. PATH-Bench estimates directed task relationships via multi-model in-context learning, constructs probe-centered sequences with controlled helpful and interfering histories, and repeatedly evaluates probe tasks to measure average performance, forward transfer, backward transfer, and forgetting. We evaluate eight representative agents on single-turn code generation and multi-turn tool-use tasks under positive- and negative-dominant histories. Benchmark results show that experience utility depends jointly on how experience is represented and on the task's interaction structure, that strong transfer does not ensure retention, and that later experience can reshape gains acquired earlier in the learning path. Based on these findings, we propose Selective Experience Use (SEU), an agent harness that regulates how path-accumulated experience influences each new task, admitting helpful items while filtering out potential interference. SEU consistently reduces forgetting while improving forward transfer in the majority of settings. The PATH-Bench provides both a controlled evaluation framework and actionable guidance for designing more selective and robust lifelong agents. The benchmark data and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/Xidong-Yang/Pathbench.
evidence_items.title: PATH-Bench: Path-Dependent Evaluation of Lifelong Agents

evidence_items.summary: Accurate epidemic forecasting is crucial for public health response, resource allocation, and outbreak intervention, but remains difficult with sparse, noisy, and highly non-stationary data. Because epidemics unfold across interacting regions, spatiotemporal methods are natural candidates for improving forecasts. Despite growing interest in spatial information, no standardized benchmark exists, and current evaluations often use simple chronological train-test splits that do not reflect real-time forecasting practice. We address this gap with SpatialEpiBench, a challenging benchmark for spatiotemporal epidemic forecasting in realistic public-health settings. SpatialEpiBench includes 11 epidemic datasets with standardized rolling evaluations and outbreak-specific metrics. We evaluate adjacency-informed forecasting models with widely used epidemic priors that adapt general models to epidemiology, but find that most methods underperform a simple last-value baseline from 1 day to 1 month ahead, even during outbreaks and with these priors. We identify three major failure modes: (1) poor outbreak anticipation, (2) difficulty handling sparsity and noise, and (3) limited utility of common geographic adjacency for epidemiological spatial information. We release benchmark data, code, and instructions at https://github.com/Rachel-Lyu/SpatialEpiBench to support development of operationally useful epidemic forecasting models.
evidence_items.title: SpatialEpiBench: Benchmarking Spatial Information and Epidemic Priors in Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for ensuring the safety and reliability of vision-language models (VLMs). A central challenge is to identify the source of uncertainty, whether it arises from the image, the text, or their interaction. We introduce VLM-UQBench, a benchmark for modality-specific and cross-modal data uncertainty in VLMs. It combines human-curated VizWiz subsets covering clean, image-, text-, and cross-modal uncertainty with a scalable perturbation pipeline comprising visual, textual, and cross-modal perturbations. We further introduce two metrics to assess how UQ scores respond to these perturbations and how their changes correlate with hallucinations. Using this framework, we systematically benchmark both LLM-based and VLM-specific UQ methods across nine VLMs and three datasets. Empirically, we find that (i) UQ performance varies substantially across uncertainty sources and VLMs; (ii) modality-specific uncertainty frequently co-occurs with hallucinations, yet changes in UQ scores only weakly track these failures; and (iii) we uncover response-length confounding in UQ evaluation, where seemingly effective uncertainty detectors may rely on simple answer-length cues. These findings highlight limitations in both current UQ methods and their evaluation, calling for more robust, modality-aware UQ approaches and more rigorous evaluation protocols that go beyond detection performance to assess the reliability of uncertainty signals.
evidence_items.title: VLM-UQBench: A Benchmark for Modality-Specific and Cross-Modality Uncertainties in Vision Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Web measurements based on top lists of popular websites are a well-established methodology for assessing the security and privacy landscape of the Internet. However, existing top lists are unlabeled and lack semantic information about the nature of the included websites, forcing researchers to rely on custom techniques to focus on specific website classes of interest. This makes targeted web measurements, e.g., over shopping websites, challenging to carry out. In this paper, we investigate the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to enable targeted web measurement studies. Building on prior literature, we identify key website classification tasks relevant to web measurements and highlight limitations in state-of-the-art classification approaches. We thus construct more carefully curated datasets to evaluate different LLMs on these tasks using standard performance measures. Our results show that LLMs can achieve strong performance across multiple classification scenarios, but the choice of the model and its configuration play a significant role in both the quality and the efficiency of the classification process. Finally, we use LLMs to emulate the setup of a targeted web measurement by automatically detecting adult websites in a subset of the Tranco list, without any need for custom techniques for dataset construction. Together, our benchmark evaluation and case study show that LLMs can enable high-quality targeted web measurements at scale directly over the Tranco list.
evidence_items.title: LLM-Based Website Classification for Targeted Web Measurements

evidence_items.summary: We introduce a controlled evaluation setting for image-text fusion in older adult emotion recognition, instantiated in the ERIT benchmark. Many existing video-based emotion datasets rely on frame sampling during evaluation, and differences in how frames are sampled can substantially affect results - yet such details are seldom disclosed, limiting reproducibility and fair comparison. ERIT removes this source of variability by pairing representative annotated frames with corresponding transcribed speech, so that each sample has fixed visual and textual inputs. The dataset covers seven emotions (anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise, and neutral), and is designed primarily as a controlled evaluation resource for the underrepresented population of older adults. We evaluate ERIT in zero-shot settings with LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen2-VL, GPT-4V, and GPT-4o, and also fine-tune LLaVA-NeXT with LoRA, comparing results using strict, multi-label, and balanced accuracies. We show that multimodal fusion improves ambiguity-aware metrics but remains visually dominated under strict evaluation, exposing limitations of current VLMs for older-adult affect recognition. Robustness and label agreement experiments show how age-related facial morphology introduces misclassifications, and how cross-modal label disagreement (e.g., happy text / sad image) influences fusion results.
evidence_items.title: ERIT: A Responsible Multimodal Affective Computing Benchmark for Older-Adult Emotion Recognition in the Wild

organizations: University of Cape Coast
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Missing data are common in clinical datasets, and imputation performance depends on the dataset and downstream classifier. Feature scaling is usually fixed rather than evaluated experimentally. We investigated whether imputation effects on classification performance depend on scaling and classifier. Methods We used the Wisconsin Breast Cancer Diagnostic (WBCD) and Pima Indians Diabetes datasets, simulating missingness under a missing-at-random (MAR) mechanism at a target rate of 20%. Mean, median, and MICE-style iterative single imputation were crossed with three scaling strategies (none, standard, robust) and three classifiers (logistic regression, random forest, radial basis function support vector machine [SVM]). Iterative imputation produced one completed dataset per run without pooling using Rubin’s rules. Imputers and scalers were fitted exclusively on training partitions. Five-fold stratified cross-validation repeated five times, with three missingness masks per split, yielded 75 matched split-mask units and 2,025 evaluations per dataset. ROC-AUC was the primary outcome. Analysis used sum-coded ordinary least-squares models with split-cluster-robust covariance and paired comparisons with cluster-bootstrap intervals. Inference was exploratory. Results In WBCD, scaling and classifier choice dominated ROC-AUC variation. Scaling effects were largest for SVM (none versus standard: −0.0219; 95% CI − 0.0267 to − 0.0175), smaller for logistic regression (− 0.0034), and absent for random forest. Marginal imputation differences were at most 0.0009; the largest conditional paired difference was approximately 0.0017. In Pima, SVM performance depended on the imputation-scaling combination: median imputation with robust scaling yielded mean ROC-AUC of 0.757, compared with 0.799 using standard scaling.
evidence_items.title: Does the Effect of Missing-Data Imputation on Classification Performance Depend on Feature Scaling? A Factorial Study Across Classifiers and Clinical Benchmark Datasets

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Accurate RNA secondary structure prediction is essential for understanding RNA function, molecular interactions, and regulatory mechanisms across diverse biological processes. Reported performance for RNA secondary structure predic-tors is difficult to compare because studies use different datasets, preprocessing pipelines, splits and metrics. We present a unified benchmark for RNA secondary structure prediction and evaluate 16 representative methods spanning end-to-end deep models, hybrid models with thermodynamic or structural constraints, and pretrained RNA foundation models. Across five settings, intra-dataset, cross-dataset, cross-family, length generalization and pseudoknot prediction, performance rankings vary markedly with evaluation protocol, and no single method dominates all settings. Methods incorporating biophysical priors or explicit structural constraints, together with some pretrained models, are generally more robust under distribution shift, whereas long RNAs and pseudoknots remain challenging for most predictors.
evidence_items.title: A unified benchmark of deep learning methods for RNA secondary structure prediction

evidence_items.summary: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts.
evidence_items.title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling <em>What</em> Is Fake

evidence_items.summary: Hybrid quantum-classical models are increasingly explored for medical classification, but their practical benefit over classical baselines remains unclear, especially for small tabular datasets. We present a reproducible hybrid quantum-classical classifier (HQCC) for breast cancer diagnosis and evaluate it on the Wisconsin Breast Cancer dataset (). The pipeline standardizes 30 features, reduces them to eight principal components, passes them through a classical preprocessing network (32 ReLU units), encodes them into an 8-qubit variational quantum circuit with three layers of trainable rotations and fixed circular CNOT entanglement, and classifies the measured expectation value with a classical output network. Training uses Adam, binary cross-entropy, 150 epochs, and an 80/20 train–test split. HQCC achieves test accuracy and an AUC of , comparable to random forest (), XGBoost (), and a matched classical MLP (). A post-hoc single-feature perturbation analysis identifies the first principal component as the most influential feature; in one correctly classified benign case, increasing PC1 by radians reduced the benign probability from to . Ablation shows that the classical preprocessing network contributes accuracy and circular entanglement contributes , while replacing the quantum circuit with a classical linear layer yields , indicating no measurable quantum advantage on this task. We therefore present HQCC as a transparent simulation benchmark for hybrid quantum–classical classification with interpretability-oriented sensitivity analysis, not as evidence of quantum advantage. Limitations include simulation-only evaluation, a small dataset, PCA information loss, and single-feature perturbations. Future work will address noise robustness, multi-feature optimization, and larger multi-omics datasets.
evidence_items.title: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Classifier for Breast Cancer with Post-Hoc Single-Feature Sensitivity Analysis: A Reproducible Simulation Benchmark

organizations: Dr. Mahalingam College of Engineering and Technology
The University of Texas at El Paso
