evidence_items.summary: Abstract Problems with plant diseases put global food supply at risk; they result in many crops not being able to produce as much or in lower quality than would otherwise be produced. Many small-scale farmers have difficulty accurately and in a timely manner diagnosing disease because of the high expense and limited availability of traditional inspection methods. This study suggests using a novel framework based on agentic artificial intelligence (AI), which incorporates deep learning-based visual analysis and the use of relevant context within the environment, to achieve new levels of intelligent crop health evaluation. The proposed solution is a collaborative multi-agent architecture where dedicated agents can independently complete all steps: automated image preprocessing, automated disease classification, environmental risk assessment, and treatment recommendations. The study employs MobileNetV2 as its backbone because of its lightweight design and low computational requirements, making it possible to use within the resource-limited agriculture environment. To further enhance the quality of diagnostic testing over the long term, there is an added adaptive learning component involved that incorporates feedback from the previous learning cycles. The PlantVillage dataset was used for an empirical analysis and showed in the proposed methodology has a total overall accuracy of 95.32% for the classification. The macro-AVG. for precision 0.95, recall 0.95 and F1 Score 0.95 are indicate the ability to predict well, with stable convergence. The system performs computations with less energy than other systems and can be deployed in a real-time manner on small devices. The transition from intelligent decision support systems to disease diagnostics will be an important milestone toward evolving scalable and precise agricultural systems as well as future sustainable crop production.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI Based Plant Disease Detection System

evidence_items.summary: STARLI | Skin and Mucosal Biomimetic Barriers | FAMILY 02 F006-F010 | White Rainbow Era | Research Working Edition v1.0 SCIENTIFIC POSITION This five-flagship research essence is a concise account of proposed physical questions rather than a record of completed laboratory trials. The original source roadmap establishes the official bilingual topics, while the 819-page visual and scientific mother establishes a durable system of dimensional formulas, reconstructable three-dimensional mathematical diagrams, strong comparators, research gates and independently stoppable future prototypes. The resulting Family 02 turns toward distinctly different epithelial materials: the skin stratum corneum, airway mucus, intestinal mucus and junctions, the ocular tear film, and the difficult question of transferring models across dissimilar organs. We treat their differences as scientific information. A physical endpoint must retain its unit, reference geometry, complete denominator, calibration chain and uncertainty. An attractive surface or a unified algorithm never counts as independent biological evidence. The reasoning framework uses five stages: physical origin, mathematical evolution, counterfactual branching, extreme extrapolation and convergence of evidence. These are stages of disciplined scientific thought; they do not control physical time or compress real experimental duration. Each new hypothesis is prospective, falsifiable and explicitly nonclinical. This booklet does not report measured tissue benefit or establish human efficacy. FLAGSHIP F006 | Stratum Corneum Biomimetics and Water Retention | 角質層仿生材料與水分保持極限  The core proposition is that corneocyte water binding, intercellular lipid lamellae and humidity-dependent sorption might have a measurable causal relationship with water retention fraction [%]. The smallest bounded demonstration is layered synthetic lipid-corneocyte coupon inside a sealed humidity-gradient diffusion cell. The strongest ordinary reference is matched nonresponsive lipid-polymer laminate and an inert permeation coupon of equal thickness; it should receive the same material mass, observation time, geometry and calibration budget. The experiment does not begin by promising improvement. It begins by asking whether an independent witness can tell the proposed mechanism from edge-seal leakage, uncontrolled specimen mass, hygroscopic contamination or a humidity calibration shift. The main independent evidence is paired gravimetric sorption, calibrated water-vapor flux and independent infrared hydration readout. The stopping condition is mass balance cannot be closed within a preregistered tolerance, or lower water loss coincides with impaired selective transport.   RESEARCH LENS 01: Molecular water-binding versus visual swelling.  Begin with the question of molecular water-binding versus visual swelling. The physically relevant state is not the image of an intact surface but corneocyte water binding, intercellular lipid lamellae and humidity-dependent sorption. In F006, describe the tissue or synthetic analogue, the open transport route, and the conserved quantity before proposing a controller. A plausible rival is already visible: bound-water signal can rise without the same decrease in evaporation. The model must identify which boundary can be measured without reusing the algorithm being tested. Define the operational numerator, denominator, exposed area, time base and unit before choosing samples. For F006, measure water retention fraction [%] with paired gravimetric sorption, calibrated water-vapor flux and independent infrared hydration readout, paired against matched nonresponsive lipid-polymer laminate and an inert permeation coupon of equal thickness. Record an unmodified blank, a empty chamber, repeated instrument zero and span, and every initiated specimen including failed and operator-rescued cases. Preregister the acceptance of missing data; a single photogenic image or internal simulation cannot serve as the endpoint witness. An immediate refutation is that edge-seal leakage, uncontrolled specimen mass, hygroscopic contamination or a humidity calibration shift explains the candidate signal. Expose the empty chamber to the same perturbation, and retire the causal claim if the independent physical reference cannot distinguish it. The precommitted stop is: mass balance cannot be closed within a preregistered tolerance, or lower water loss coincides with impaired selective transport. Do not substitute a correlated proxy for water retention fraction; no result in this prospective volume demonstrates performance on real human tissue.   RESEARCH LENS 08: Repeated desorption and rehydration loops.  Repeated desorption and rehydration loops becomes a mathematical problem only after its unit contract is fixed. Let the perturbations be relative humidity [% RH] and ceramide analogue fraction [fraction], and keep water retention fraction [%] distinct from the illustrative synthetic water retention [%]. Explore an interior stationary point, a cliff near the allowed upper bound, and a nonmonotonic ridge. If several parameter pairs fit one sensor trace, that ambiguity is evidence about identifiability, not a discovery of a universal law. Execute a calibrated factorial grid over relative humidity [% RH] and ceramide analogue fraction [fraction], including center, corners, repeated boundaries and one untouched region. Independently reconstruct water retention fraction [%] at the same sampling times as the reference instrument. Fit both a simple no-interaction surface and an interaction model; release their residual maps, uncertainty intervals and spatial registration errors. The equal-thickness passive polymer follows the identical schedule to reveal an apparatus-only response. Challenge the dimensional model by reversing one gradient, changing the acquisition frequency or exchanging a calibrated area while holding the sample constant. If the model surface changes in the reference channel alone, the purported corneocyte water binding, intercellular lipid lamellae and humidity-dependent sorption is unsupported. A robust mathematical fit is insufficient when edge-seal leakage, uncontrolled specimen mass, hygroscopic contamination or a humidity calibration shift survives. Set aside the fitted relation when the held-out residual or the independent safety witness exceeds its preregistered band.   MATHEMATICAL SIGNATURES FOR F006  1. Gravimetric water-vapor flux: J_w = Delta_m / (A * Delta_t). Units and constraints: J_w [g m^-2 h^-1]; mass [g]; area [m2]; time [h]; mass conserved through sealed cell. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Plot effective area and mass loss at fixed elapsed time; discriminate leakage from tissue transfer. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  2. Hydration retention percentage: R_w = 100 * (m_t - m_dry)/(m_0 - m_dry). Units and constraints: R_w [%]; all m [g]; m_0 > m_dry; same dry baseline. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Sweep retained mass and dry reference; reject percentage gains from shifted tare. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  3. Tortuosity-adjusted water diffusivity: D_eff = D_0/(1 + alpha*phi). Units and constraints: D_eff,D_0 [m2 s^-1]; alpha,phi [1]; alpha >= 0; bounded accessible porosity. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Inspect diffusivity against porosity and tortuosity; test whether a leak bypasses serial resistance. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  4. Lamellar water permeance: P_w = K_w*D_eff/L. Units and constraints: P_w [m s^-1]; K_w [1]; D_eff [m2 s^-1]; L [m]; L > 0; fixed activity and partition model. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Separate K, D and L; identify parameter manifolds with indistinguishable permeance. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  5. Bound-water depletion time: tau_b = m_bound/(J_w*A). Units and constraints: tau_b [h]; m_bound [g]; J_w [g m^-2 h^-1]; A [m2]; positive flux; fixed area and reservoir definition. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Map reservoir mass against evaporative flux and identify nonstationary boundaries. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  6. Flux uncertainty propagation: u_J = sqrt((u_m/(A*t))^2 + (J_w*u_A/A)^2 + (J_w*u_t/t)^2). Units and constraints: u_J [g m^-2 h^-1]; u_m [g]; u_A [m2]; u_t [h]; first-order independent errors; positive A,t. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Reveal error ridges created by uncertain active area and time calibration. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.   FLAGSHIP F007 | Airway Mucus Barriers and Particle Exclusion | 呼吸道黏液屏障與微粒阻隔極限  The core proposition is that mucin mesh size, particle surface chemistry and periciliary clearance coupling might have a measurable causal relationship with particle passage fraction [1]. The smallest bounded demonstration is nonclinical airway-mucus-on-chip phantom with replaceable gel and fluorescent inert particles. The strongest ordinary reference is unmodified mucin gel with matched viscosity and a particle-free passive clearance chamber; it should receive the same material mass, observation time, geometry and calibration budget. The experiment does not begin by promising improvement. It begins by asking whether an independent witness can tell the proposed mechanism from particle aggregation, fluorophore quenching, irreversible adsorption to polymer walls or hidden convective bypass. The main independent evidence is independent upstream/downstream particle counts, rheometry and fluorescent-tracer mass closure. The stopping condition is particle mass-count ledger fails or the favorable exclusion suppresses the independently measured clearance pathway.   RESEARCH LENS 01: Mesh-geometry threshold for neutral tracer passage.  Mesh-geometry threshold for neutral tracer passage becomes a mathematical problem only after its unit contract is fixed. Let the perturbations be mucin-network pore diameter [nm] and test particle hydrodynamic diameter [nm], and keep particle passage fraction [1] distinct from the illustrative synthetic particle passage [fraction]. Explore an interior stationary point, a cliff near the allowed upper bound, and a nonmonotonic ridge. If several parameter pairs fit one sensor trace, that ambiguity is evidence about identifiability, not a discovery of a universal law. Execute a calibrated factorial grid over mucin-network pore diameter [nm] and test particle hydrodynamic diameter [nm], including center, corners, repeated boundaries and one untouched region. Independently reconstruct particle passage fraction [1] at the same sampling times as the reference instrument. Fit both a simple no-interaction surface and an interaction model; release their residual maps, uncertainty intervals and spatial registration errors. The no-mucin channel follows the identical schedule to reveal an apparatus-only response. Challenge the dimensional model by reversing one gradient, changing the acquisition frequency or exchanging a calibrated area while holding the sample constant. If the model surface changes in the reference channel alone, the purported mucin mesh size, particle surface chemistry and periciliary clearance coupling is unsupported. A robust mathematical fit is insufficient when particle aggregation, fluorophore quenching, irreversible adsorption to polymer walls or hidden convective bypass survives. Set aside the fitted relation when the held-out residual or the independent safety witness exceeds its preregistered band.   RESEARCH LENS 08: Inlet mixing and shear localization.  Construct a second world in which the headline observation is real but the proposed cause is absent. In that world particle aggregation, fluorophore quenching, irreversible adsorption to polymer walls or hidden convective bypass produces the same direction of change. The counterfactual must receive a real physical arm, not a dismissive paragraph; the nonmoving ciliary phantom is therefore a predeclared antagonist. Explain whether the apparent coupling survives when the device, geometry and observation budget remain unchanged but the active material pathway is disabled. Implement the strongest falsification arm by holding the reference sample unchanged while manipulating particle aggregation, fluorophore quenching, irreversible adsorption to polymer walls or hidden convective bypass. Ask observers blinded to labels to reconstruct the endpoint from raw files. Quantify agreement separately for independent independent upstream/downstream particle counts, rheometry and fluorescent-tracer mass closure; two transformations of the same raw image count as one witness. Reweight all attempted trials, including runs with incomplete extraction. Record an explicit estimate of how much of the nominal difference the engineered rival can explain. If the nonmoving ciliary phantom reproduces the supposed intervention gain, the branch is false even when its statistical fit is excellent. If retention can masquerade as successful exclusion if clearance is lost, discard the tempting story and publish the counterfactual. The critical stop is independent of software: particle mass-count ledger fails or the favorable exclusion suppresses the independently measured clearance pathway. A rival may remain unresolved; mark the mechanism as non-identifiable rather than inventing certainty from two coupled readouts.   MATHEMATICAL SIGNATURES FOR F007  1. Particle passage fraction: f_pass = N_out/N_in. Units and constraints: f_pass [1]; N counts particles; N_in>0; count efficiency independently calibrated. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Sweep particle size and mesh spacing; detect spurious passage caused by optical loss. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  2. Particle number flux: J_p = N_out/(A*Delta_t). Units and constraints: J_p [particles m^-2 s^-1]; A [m2]; t [s]; fixed observation window and exposed area. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Map passage-rate hotspots as boundary channels open at a corner. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  3. Stokes-Einstein Brownian diffusion: D_B = k_B*T/(6*pi*eta*r). Units and constraints: D_B [m2 s^-1]; k_B [J K^-1]; T [K]; eta [Pa s]; r [m]; dilute spherical passive particles, Newtonian approximation. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Vary viscosity and radius; mark failure when mucus rheology is non-Newtonian. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  4. Particle Peclet number: Pe_p = U*L/D_B. Units and constraints: Pe_p [1]; U [m s^-1]; L [m]; D_B [m2 s^-1]; positive D_B; declared advective axis. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Map diffusion-dominated and clearance-dominated regimes without equating the two. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  5. Residence-time estimate: tau_r = L/U. Units and constraints: tau_r [s]; L [m]; U [m s^-1]; U>0; steady one-dimensional surrogate. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Plot velocity against path length; challenge plug-flow assumptions. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  6. Absolute exclusion probability: E_p = 1 - f_pass. Units and constraints: E_p [1]; paired counting; bounded f_pass 0..1. Falsifiable 3D geometry: A false-high exclusion ridge appears if the detector selectively misses bound tracers. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.   FLAGSHIP F008 | Intestinal Mucosal Transport and Repair | 腸道黏膜選擇性運輸與修復極限  The core proposition is that mucus turnover, epithelial tight-junction selectivity and transport under microfluidic shear might have a measurable causal relationship with apparent solute permeability [m s^-1]. The smallest bounded demonstration is two-channel intestinal epithelium chip with removable mucus analog and gravimetric tracer recovery. The strongest ordinary reference is matched transwell reference epithelia and acellular microfluidic inserts with equal adsorption budget; it should receive the same material mass, observation time, geometry and calibration budget. The experiment does not begin by promising improvement. It begins by asking whether an independent witness can tell the proposed mechanism from tracer sorption to the chip, flow-induced exposed-area change, epithelial shedding or an electrical-only improvement. The main independent evidence is mass-recovered solute flux, blank-corrected four-electrode TEER and blinded epithelial imaging. The stopping condition is solute mass is unrecoverable, viable reference tissue deteriorates, or TEER rises while independent neutral-tracer flux worsens.   RESEARCH LENS 01: Selective transport after mucus removal.  Construct a second world in which the headline observation is real but the proposed cause is absent. In that world tracer sorption to the chip, flow-induced exposed-area change, epithelial shedding or an electrical-only improvement produces the same direction of change. The counterfactual must receive a real physical arm, not a dismissive paragraph; the recognized intestinal epithelial monolayer is therefore a predeclared antagonist. Explain whether the apparent coupling survives when the device, geometry and observation budget remain unchanged but the active material pathway is disabled. Implement the strongest falsification arm by holding the reference sample unchanged while manipulating tracer sorption to the chip, flow-induced exposed-area change, epithelial shedding or an electrical-only improvement. Ask observers blinded to labels to reconstruct the endpoint from raw files. Quantify agreement separately for independent mass-recovered solute flux, blank-corrected four-electrode TEER and blinded epithelial imaging; two transformations of the same raw image count as one witness. Reweight all attempted trials, including runs with incomplete extraction. Record an explicit estimate of how much of the nominal difference the engineered rival can explain. If the recognized intestinal epithelial monolayer reproduces the supposed intervention gain, the branch is false even when its statistical fit is excellent. If a repair claim needs functional recovery after the perturbation is removed, discard the tempting story and publish the counterfactual. The critical stop is independent of software: solute mass is unrecoverable, viable reference tissue deteriorates, or TEER rises while independent neutral-tracer flux worsens. A rival may remain unresolved; mark the mechanism as non-identifiable rather than inventing certainty from two coupled readouts.   RESEARCH LENS 08: Reversible opening and recovery interval.  Push reversible opening and recovery interval to a deliberately uncomfortable physical limit. Stress the corner that combines high apical flow rate and extreme mucus analog thickness; then repeat after cyclic exposure rather than selecting the first clean trace. The governing approximation solute advection-diffusion coupled to a bounded reversible junctional-state model may fail because a hidden path activates or a local threshold is crossed. A favorable domain average does not excuse a catastrophic local leak, an unmeasured exposure, or an unexplained sensor disagreement. Use boundary tests that cannot be rescued by an operator adjusting a threshold. Apply repeated stress, an intentional instrument drift and a tracer-only no-chip well under matching mass, energy and observation budgets. Report upper-tail failures, not just group means. The most defensible readout is the preregistered apparent solute permeability [m s^-1], jointly checked against blank-corrected TEER [ohm cm2]; if these disagree, preserve both curves and the physical sample provenance. At the extreme corner, explicitly inspect how the denominator and unobserved boundary might reverse the conclusion. A claim of resilience is withdrawn if the sample is functionally degraded despite improved apparent solute permeability [m s^-1]. Stop immediately when solute mass is unrecoverable, viable reference tissue deteriorates, or TEER rises while independent neutral-tracer flux worsens; otherwise let an independent reviewer compare the entire distribution with matched transwell reference epithelia and acellular microfluidic inserts with equal adsorption budget. An extrapolation past the witnessed domain has no empirical authority.   MATHEMATICAL SIGNATURES FOR F008  1. Area-normalized apparent permeability: P_app = (dM_dt)/(A*C_0). Units and constraints: P_app [m s^-1]; dM_dt [mol s^-1]; A [m2]; C_0 [mol m^-3]; sink or corrected donor depletion; A > 0. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Plot loading and active area; detect false advantage from exposure normalization. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  2. Blank-corrected electrical resistance: TEER = (R_t-R_blank)*A. Units and constraints: TEER [ohm cm2]; R [ohm]; A [cm2]; matched electrode frequency; positive area. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Separate electrode polarization from tight-junction change. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  3. One-dimensional advective-diffusive flux: J_s = -D_eff*dC_dx + v*C. Units and constraints: J_s [mol m^-2 s^-1]; D_eff [m2 s^-1]; dC_dx [mol m^-4]; v [m s^-1]; one-dimensional mass-conserving transport. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Vary flow and concentration profile; require mass conservation. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  4. Junction response Damkohler number: Da_j = k_j*L^2/D_eff. Units and constraints: Da_j [1]; k_j [s^-1]; L [m]; D_eff [m2 s^-1]; first-order effective process; positive D. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Map relaxation and diffusion timescales; expose model non-identifiability. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  5. Mass-recovery ratio: r_m = (M_out+M_bound)/M_dosed. Units and constraints: r_m [1]; all M [mol]; separately measured bound reservoir. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Test the discrepancy between tracer disappearance and true transfer. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  6. Exponential return-time estimate: tau_j = -Delta_t/ln((P_t-P_inf)/(P_0-P_inf)). Units and constraints: tau_j [s]; P in [m s^-1]; Delta_t [s]; 00; endpoint identity matched. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Map baseline signal and model mismatch; expose instability near zero reference. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  2. Organ-specific permeability definition: P_i = J_i/DeltaC_i. Units and constraints: P_i [m s^-1]; J_i [mol m^-2 s^-1]; DeltaC_i [mol m^-3]; identical solute and time convention. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Compare organ-specific fluxes without falsely transferring raw resistance. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  3. Normalized domain distance: D_ij = sqrt(sum_k (z_ik-z_jk)^2). Units and constraints: D_ij [1]; each z standardized [1]; frozen standardization; paired features. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Reveal whether omitted physics is hidden inside identical normalized scores. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  4. Independent prediction uncertainty: u_pred = sqrt(u_ref^2 + u_model^2). Units and constraints: u_pred has units of Y; u_ref,u_model same units; independent error components; covariance otherwise included. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Plot calibration and model variance; reject overconfident pooled estimates. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  5. Shared variance contribution: G_shared = V_shared/V_total. Units and constraints: G_shared [1]; both V same units squared; V_total>0; variance components nonnegative. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Contrast partial pooling with completely independent organism-specific fits. The diagram remains an illustration unless a reference measurement reconstructs the physical relation.  6. Transferred residual drift: DeltaE = E_site2 - E_site1. Units and constraints: DeltaE [%]; E_site2,E_site1 [%]; same frozen error definition across sites. Falsifiable 3D geometry: Use held-out domain corners to expose failed generalization. evidence_items.summary: We present a dataset and evaluation setup for a problem in creative machine translation: translating culturally loaded passages that carry much of a text's meaning and humor that may depend on subtle or implicit discourse. We study Soviet comedy quotations that function as memes in Russian-language communication. Off-the-shelf difficulty estimators do not find these passages; current models searching the web find most but not all of them, but their own analyses of the difficulty do not help translation as well as a human-validated one. Given a brief human-validated analysis of why each passage is difficult, older models improve modestly; the strongest current translators (GPT-6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5) improve more, and in human evaluation GPT-6 Sol comes close to the approved references on most films. Newer models have thus become much better at using such an analysis while still not reliably producing it themselves. We release (1) a dataset of five films' Russian subtitles with their audience-selected culturally salient passages, human-validated analyses, and reference translations (into English, Galician, and Spanish), together with every full-film LLM translation and evaluation produced in this study; and (2) an item-level MQM-style evaluation protocol that measures translator and evaluator noise to set the number of runs the evaluation needs, and whose automatic version tracks human judgment of these passages, which reference-free neural metrics do not, whether they score the whole text or the passages alone.
evidence_items.title: Hard to Translate, Harder to Detect: Human Analysis Remains Essential in AI Meme Translation

evidence_items.summary: Identifying subtle errors in generated videos is an important step toward automated video generation, where errors must be detected to assess and refine generated clips. Recent work shows that pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) can localise such errors, but their effectiveness depends strongly on the workflow used: choices about which frames to inspect, which tools and model calls to make, and how to combine predictions can lead to substantially different results. We study VLM harnesses for video error localisation. Instead of relying on manually designed harnesses, we propose Harness Search and Merge (HSM), an algorithm that automatically constructs them by searching over executable evaluation programs. An LLM orchestrator refines candidate harnesses independently on random training subsets, records findings in a memory, and constructively merges complementary candidates. We evaluate HSM on Spotlight, a recently proposed benchmark for localising errors in generated videos. HSM achieves 0.234 +- 0.012 F1, exceeding the strongest benchmark strategy (0.173 +- 0.016), and retains its lead on an unseen video generator (0.213 +- 0.008 versus 0.140 +- 0.003). On IPV-Bench, it achieves strong localisation performance with lower false-alarm rates than existing optimisation baselines. Together, these results show that searching over complete VLM harnesses can outperform existing evaluation strategies, transfer to an unseen video generator, and reduce false alarms on real videos.
evidence_items.title: Optimising VLM Harnesses to Localise Errors in Generated Videos

evidence_items.summary: Coordinating vessels through the shared waterways of busy ports grows more challenging as vessel traffic increases. Port authorities need realistic simulations to assess how arrival schedules, anchorage assignments, and routes affect vessel throughput and navigation safety. Existing AIS-based trajectory models predict a vessel's track from its past trajectory in an open-loop fashion. They do not simulate step-by-step responses to other ships or test whether a vessel collides or reaches its goal. To address this problem, we introduce JaxNaviSim, a data-driven simulator and learning benchmark coupling Automatic Identification System (AIS) data with fast, controllable traffic simulation, in which learned models steer vessels through recorded traffic. First, we release a dataset of ~141 million AIS records from over 30K vessels across eight high-density regions of the Singapore Strait, among the world's busiest waterways, with ~6.7 million vessel-hours. Unlike several existing AIS datasets which mostly cover open seas, ours captures close-quarters vessel traffic in the narrow strait. Second, we define a navigation task for each recorded vessel trajectory. A model steers that vessel every 10 s from its recorded state to its anchoring point or region exit, while surrounding ships follow their recorded tracks or are steered by the model. We implement a JAX simulator that runs these tasks in large batches on a GPU. We also incorporate multiple vessel dynamics models and sea surface currents. Finally, we benchmark imitation learning (IL), offline and online RL, and include Predictive Action Refinement (PAR) as a safety baseline that cuts collision rates to 1-3%. The comparison shows that low tracking error does not ensure arrival, and learned policies can reach most destinations yet collide in 20-45% of episodes.
evidence_items.title: JaxNaviSim: A GPU-Accelerated, Data-Driven Simulator and Learning Benchmark for Maritime Navigation

evidence_items.summary: Decision models, which output probability distributions over candidate labels instead of generating text, are increasingly used as classifiers and evaluators for inputs associated with real-world locations. However, it remains unclear whether they can leverage spatial context and whether their predictions are geographically biased. We introduce GeoDecisions, a multimodal benchmark for evaluating the spatial awareness and geographic bias of decision models. GeoDecisions comprises two tasks: (1) geo-aware image classification, and (2) location rating on objective and subjective topics. Evaluating six decision models against supervised task-specific models, we find that spatial awareness requires vision: textual coordinates alone provide insufficient context for classifying everyday photos and satellite images. We also find substantial geographic bias. On everyday photos, despite achieving higher accuracy, open-weight decision models exhibit more spatially clustered errors than supervised models. Moreover, across all five subjective topics, every decision model gives lower ratings to locations with lower socioeconomic conditions. Finally, we propose a training-free method that combines decision models with a location prior to improve their spatial awareness without substantially increasing performance bias. Our code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/GeoDecisions.
evidence_items.title: Seeing Is Locating: Spatial Awareness and Geographic Bias in Decision Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Proactive streaming video understanding requires models to interpret unfolding events, respond timely, and retrieve relevant historical evidence. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, we introduce SVUBench, a comprehensive proactive streaming video benchmark comprising 12,131 questions and 62,881 answer points across ten proactive tasks spanning Perception, Understanding, and Reasoning. Constructed through model-assisted annotation and human verification, SVUBench introduces two complementary interaction modes. Basic evaluates sustained proactive responses from video onset, while Trajectory requires historical recovery and continuous response updates following task activation during streaming. A Duration-Scaled Challenge further evaluates these capabilities across four video duration tiers. We develop the Proactive Response Score (PRS) with task-adaptive answer windows to jointly assess answer correctness, response timeliness, historical consistency, and content quality. Extensive experiments and analysis reveal the strengths and limitations of existing models, highlighting directions for advancing proactive streaming video understanding.
evidence_items.title: SVUBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Proactive Streaming Video Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Degree certificates play a critical role in high-stakes decisions such as university admission, immigration, and hiring. The issuing institution vouches for the holder, so a forged certificate may let its bearer pass these checks. Degree certificate forgery is increasingly prevalent. Yet, many assume that it is easy to spot. Reported cases show otherwise: in 2024, the business school of the University of Hong Kong found that about 30 master's students had enrolled with forged academic credentials. Few studies have looked at how to detect forged degree certificates, partly because public benchmarks are scarce. We present TamperCert, a benchmark built from 400 real degree certificates issued by 38 universities. Each certificate was subjected to 11 publicly available tampering methods to alter the holder's name and further processed with four additional post-processing techniques, resulting in over 20,000 forged images. We evaluate 13 detectors, a commercial multimodal large language model (MLLM), and detectors trained on TamperCert.Our findings reveal that no detector is reliable for every tampering method. Consequently, a determined forger may still evade detection. Moreover, the commercial MLLM misses most forgeries made by general-purpose generative models, and post-processing, such as resizing an image or photographing it with a camera, severely degrades detection.
evidence_items.title: TamperCert: A Benchmark for Detecting Text Tampering in Degree Certificates

evidence_items.summary: A Large Language Model (LLM), its harness, and the test-time compute budget jointly determine its behavior. Consequently, the same underlying model, embedded in different agentic workflows or allocated different amounts of test-time compute, can exhibit markedly different performance. Psychologists face an analogous challenge when evaluating human performance: the same person may behave differently under different incentives and levels of deliberation. Psychological tasks therefore provide an ideal testbed for studying such behavioral variation. However, when adapted to LLMs, these tasks are typically text-transcribed, replaying fixed, language-rendered experiments as static prompts. This format is ill-suited to agent evaluation, where actions can alter future observations and task states. Conversely, although dynamic environments are prevalent in the evaluation of LLM agents, they rarely ask whether the resulting behavior is human-like. Here, we bridge this gap by transforming psychological tasks into dynamic environments in which agents can interact and by using a learned human-policy model to evaluate how compatible the resulting behavioral trajectories are with human behavior. Across these environments, we find that this compatibility varies with an LLM's agentic configuration and the psychological task, and that memory raises it mainly by making choices more predictable rather than more human-like. These findings motivate a more holistic evaluation of LLM agents in psychology-inspired environments, accounting for both the backbone model and its agentic scaffold.
evidence_items.title: mini-psych-agent: Evaluating Human-Like Behavior in LLM Agents through Interactive Psychological Environments

evidence_items.summary: Lean verifies that a proof establishes its formal proposition, but whether that proposition preserves the mathematical content of an informal source requires separate review. In project-scale formalizations, this correspondence can depend on definitions and constraints distributed across many declarations. We introduce LeanReviewBench, a benchmark for project-level semantic alignment review containing 197 versioned inputs collected from 18 real Lean projects, with 87 aligned and 110 misaligned reference judgments. Each input binds an informal mathematical target to selected formal declarations and an extracted dependency context. Construction combines development-history discovery, independent target binding, reconstruction under a common Lean environment, and Astra annotation with human review of uncertain cases. The collection spans diverse mathematical domains and includes 69 historical pairs. We evaluate six language models with Direct and ReForm prompts on all 197 inputs against final human-reviewed reference labels. GPT-6.1 Sol with Direct prompting achieves the highest reported accuracy of 0.827 and misalignment-detection F1 of 0.844; the effects of prompting vary across models. LeanReviewBench provides a testbed for reviewing semantic correspondence in existing mathematical formalization projects. LeanReviewBench is available at https://github.com/MechMath/LeanReviewBench.
evidence_items.title: LeanReviewBench: Semantic Alignment Review in Mathematical Lean Projects

evidence_items.summary: Earth-observation labels from maps, older products or hurried annotation arrive misaligned, coarse, loosely outlined or incomplete. Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) are nevertheless benchmarked with labels taken as correct. A practitioner therefore cannot tell which encoder to choose when the labels are imperfect. We present a benchmark protocol for fine-tuning under such labels. Four spatially structured error types are calibrated to equal label mIoU and applied identically to every model and seed. Every contrast is paired and read against an equivalence margin of $\pm 3$ points and a minimum detectable effect. We apply it to nine encoders, six decoder heads and ten datasets. In an exploratory reading at a matched learning rate the satellite-pretrained and web-pretrained DINOv3 encoders are equivalent within the margin on 8 of 9 datasets. Multispectral GFMs and an ImageNet ResNet-50 are equivalent within the margin on about half of them. Labels with random offsets cost the least at equal label quality. Under other decoder heads the verdicts mostly hold on FLAIR-2 and are decoder dependent on HLS Burn Scars. On four of five real label pairs the real label costs more than its matched simulated type. No choice of pretraining data makes an encoder consistently more robust, so the encoder is better chosen by its accuracy under imperfect labels.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Geospatial Foundation Models under Calibrated Label Errors

evidence_items.summary: Success-rate gains guide the development of web agents. Yet knowing which agent ranks first does not tell us how much confidence to place in its reported advantage. We study the comparison itself: how success is defined, what evidence supports the judgments, and how the difference between agents is estimated. On fixed web-agent executions, changing a judge from predicting likely completion to requiring recorded support can remove most of a reported lead without changing the ranking. This effect persists when unresolved completion is distinguished from supported failure. Controlled source additions explain how missing relations between task requirements, objects and observations can conceal a difference or create an apparent advantage. We also find that making both agents' score estimates more accurate can make their difference less accurate, because their original errors partly canceled. To estimate a chosen outcome difference, we combine judge predictions with reference labels for sampled task pairs. Across four released execution systems, regression fitted on the same 50 labeled pairs reduces estimation error relative to direct paired sampling. The results give agent researchers a practical basis for assessing claimed improvements: make the comparison target explicit, retain the evidence needed to check it, and use paired labels to estimate the difference directly.
evidence_items.title: Same Executions, Different Gaps: Judgment Rules in Web-Agent Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Diffusion models have shown strong potential in medical image segmentation due to their generative capabilities and robustness. However, existing methods often struggle to preserve fine anatomical boundaries and to retain multi-scale structural information due to the loss of spatial and frequency details during feature encoding, particularly in complex clinical imaging conditions. This work presents WaDiS, a wavelet-powered conditional latent diffusion framework for medical image segmentation that addresses these limitations through multi-scale wavelet conditioning and frequency-aware information filtering for boundary preservation. The model adopts a multi-scale wavelet conditioning encoder to retain rich structural features, leveraging its lossless nature to better preserve semantic priors critical to the diffusion process. In addition, a Frequency-Aware Gating Block (FAGB) is introduced into the skip connections of the diffusion U-Net, enabling adaptive spectral filtering and residual fusion to better emphasize boundary structures while reducing irrelevant content. To improve generalization across clinical domains, we adopt a structure-preserving color augmentation strategy during training. Specifically, global color statistics are transferred between samples in the LAB color space, allowing the model to decouple appearance from structure and focus more on anatomical shape rather than color bias. Experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that WaDiS consistently outperforms existing diffusion-based and conventional segmentation methods, with notable improvements in boundary accuracy, robustness to noise, and generalization under color variation. The code for this work will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
evidence_items.title: WaDiS: Boundary-Preserving Diffusion Segmentation via Multi-Scale Wavelet Conditioning and Frequency-Aware Gating

evidence_items.summary: Calendar arithmetic is non-linear. When 1:59 AM + 1 minute occurs during daylight saving spring-forward, the result is 3:00 AM, not 2:00 AM, as the hour is skipped. We introduce CivilTime-Bench, a benchmark for civil-time reasoning covering daylight saving transitions, non-hour offsets, date-line crossings, and ISO week boundaries. With 60,011 training and 10,500 evaluation examples under strict output-contract evaluation, we benchmark seven LLMs (six instruction-tuned models and Llama-3.1-8B base) and find: zero-shot exact match varies substantially across models, contract-aware prompting often improves format compliance but yields inconsistent accuracy gains, few-shot in-context learning provides model-dependent improvements, and fine-tuning achieves 74.6--86.6% EM on synthetic evaluation but only 36.6--45.2% on HumanTime-500 for models with valid results on both splits, highlighting substantial limitations in generalization. We release the benchmark and code.
evidence_items.title: When 1+1 $\neq$ 2: Benchmarking Civil-Time Reasoning in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Static call graph tools cannot soundly model every dynamic language feature, yet rarely reveal when, where, or why their results are unsound. We present CGRizz, an agentic framework that diagnoses unsoundness for developers and warns users about it. During training, CGRizz compares static and dynamic call graphs to identify boundary edges: calls observed at runtime but missing from the static graph. For each edge, an LLM agent proposes a root cause, including the unmodeled program pattern and responsible tool location. CGRizz validates each proposal using three independent forms of evidence: runtime instrumentation detecting the pattern, a test case reproducing the missing edge, and a warning inserted at the implicated tool location. Validated reports help developers diagnose limitations, while the warnings form an instrumented build that flags potential unsoundness in new programs without dynamic analysis. We evaluate CGRizz on three benchmark suites using WALA, OPAL, and Soot. Of 1,459 boundary edges, CGRizz reasons about 10.3% directly, all confirmed by manual audit, and resolves another 84.1% by grouping edges with validated root causes. Tool maintainers confirmed several limitations, some of which have been fixed. The warnings flag 74%-92% of unsoundness in held-out programs. Guided by CGRizz reports, a coding agent refactored programs to remove 64% of targeted root-cause patterns while preserving functionality.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Root Cause Reasoning and Localization of Unsoundness in Static Call Graph Analysis

evidence_items.summary: As medical VLMs are increasingly evaluated for clinical decision-support scenarios, knowing when to trust their predictions is critical. Closed-ended medical VQA has become a common benchmark format because it enables automated scoring. Yet, systematic investigation into whether this format changes the reliability problem remains scarce. We identify a failure mode that we call stable wrongness: models can produce incorrect yes/no answers that remain confident and repeatable even when patient-specific visual evidence is removed or mismatched. This failure violates the premise behind sampling-stability uncertainty methods, including recent hallucination-aware calibration (HAC) variants: disagreement is informative only when errors are unstable. When shortcut-driven errors are themselves stable, sampling agreement can remain deceptively high. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity (CAS), which shifts reliability estimation from answer stability to evidence sensitivity. CAS uses cross-modal counterfactual interventions, such as text-only, black, and corrupted images, to audit whether a committed yes/no answer remains supported when visual evidence is invalidated. Across 7 VLMs and 3 benchmarks, CAS outperforms the best HAC-family scores across all evaluated settings, achieving a macro-averaged AUROC gain of +0.150 for error detection. Mechanistic analysis further shows that CAS recovers hidden errors in the HAC-confident region and that its strongest standalone signal is counterfactual decision-boundary shift rather than hard prediction stability. Our findings suggest that closed-ended evaluation should test visual dependence, not only answer stability, in safety-critical medical contexts.
evidence_items.title: Rethinking Closed-Ended Medical VLM Evaluation: From Stable Wrongness to Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity

evidence_items.summary: LLM coding agents authorize shell commands by parsing a command string against a policy and passing the raw string to a system shell, so the gate adjudicates one reading while the shell executes another. We present ParseGap, a differential testing framework that runs each command through an unmodified vendor checker and GNU Bash 5.2 in an isolated container, flagging a violation whenever an approved command produces policy-violating runtime effects. Across eight production coding agents, ParseGap identifies 17 root causes across three divergence boundaries: at the parse, where an upstream tree-sitter-bash defect hides a second command from Mistral Vibe and Gemini CLI; at the utility, where every checker permits read-only binaries whose arguments write files or launch programs (9-47 of 55 cases); and at confinement, where an allow rule in OpenAI Codex CLI disables its read-only OS sandbox. Live trials across two frontier models triggered policy violations in all 16 agent-model pairs (14 under configured restrictions). To eliminate the second reading, we design ShellPlan, which compiles a strict Bash subset once into a typed execution plan, validates utility arguments against positive capability specifications, and dispatches approved plans directly via execve without a shell. Over a formal operational model, we prove single-interpretation dispatch and bound touched programs and files under audited assumptions. ShellPlan admitted 0/4,174 active attacks across six static suites and 0/90 hits in a ten-model agent benchmark (62/90 unguarded) at 1.28 ms median gate latency, preserving 36/36 (100%) frontier standard-dev completion (74/100 overall) and 0/348 external over-allows outside modeled exceptions.
evidence_items.title: ParseGap: Testing What Coding Agents Authorize and What Shells Execute

evidence_items.summary: Sequential recommender systems aim to predict a user's next interaction by modeling temporal dependencies in historical behavior sequences. To capture such dependencies, recent approaches increasingly rely on attention-based architectures, particularly transformers. While effective at modeling long-range sequential patterns, these models apply a fixed computation depth to all interaction items, treating them as equally complex. However, user behavior is inherently heterogeneous, with many interactions following simple repetitive patterns, whereas others require modeling higher-order dependencies. This mismatch leads to inefficient utilization of model capacity and unnecessary computational overhead, particularly in deep transformer-based architectures. To address this issue, we propose MoR4Rec, a sequential recommendation framework based on a Mixture-of-Recursion paradigm, which enables item-wise adaptive computation through a shared transformer backbone. A learned routing mechanism dynamically assigns each item to an appropriate recursion depth, allocating deeper computation to complex interactions while processing simpler patterns more efficiently. To improve computational efficiency, we develop a cascade-based strategy with key-value sharing across recursion steps. We further introduce a gated attention mechanism that adaptively regulates contextual information during recursive sequence modeling. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets show that MoR4Rec consistently outperforms strong transformer-based baselines, achieving average gains of 2.28% in Recall@5, 2.50% in NDCG@5, and 2.0% in MRR@5 over the strongest baseline. The improvements remain consistent across top-10 and top-20 recommendation cutoffs, while comparisons with vanilla transformers demonstrate the computational efficiency of adaptive recursive processing.
evidence_items.title: MoR4Rec: Mixture-of-Recursion for Sequential Recommendation

evidence_items.summary: Text-to-video (T2V) models can now generate visually plausible short clips, but multi-shot generation requires a different set of skills: composing multiple shots with intended cut timing, transition style, camera language, and cross-shot continuity. How far this multi-shot output can be controlled from text remains unmeasured: existing benchmarks either evaluate single shots or, when they provide shot-level scripts, typically check whether the requested shots appear but not when they change or how they are joined. We introduce MSBench, a benchmark for controllable text-driven multi-shot video generation built around structured Scene-Entity-Shot mini-scripts that specify each shot's time span, camera state, content, and outgoing transition. MSBench defines a four-dimensional hybrid evaluation framework spanning Visual Quality, Dynamic Quality, Semantic Alignment, and Cross-Shot Consistency with 11 sub-metrics. Experiments on 14 commercial and open-source systems show that visual quality does little to separate the systems, whereas multi-shot control does: many models cut mainly on scene changes and render requested gradual transitions as hard cuts. Human evaluations further validate MSBench, with its system ranking reaching a Spearman correlation of 0.87 with human preferences. The project page is available at https://totalhuang.github.io/MSBench-page/.
evidence_items.title: MSBench: Benchmarking Script-Controlled Multi-Shot Text-to-Video Generation

evidence_items.summary: Standard dense visual prediction architectures scale representation capacity by stacking deep feedforward decoders (6-16 transformer layers with 50M-200M parameters). This explicit layer stacking brings substantial activation memory overhead during backpropagation, requires high off-chip memory bandwidth for non-tied weights, and uses static computational allocation that cannot adapt to spatial image complexity. We propose loopxDINO, which replaces physical decoder depth with iterative latent reasoning. It has two decoupled components: (1) a frozen DINOv2-Base backbone extracting spatial features in one forward pass and caching static Key-Value representations in GPU memory; (2) a compact weight-tied Looped Cross-Attention Decoder (7.96M core, 14.85M total trainable parameters) that recurrently updates queries across T iterations. Recurrence is stabilized by step-conditioned adaLN, LayerNorm-based hyper-ellipsoid manifold regularization, and learnable residual contraction damping. Intermediate mask predictions are fed back as spatial attention biases to guide queries toward ambiguous contours with no extra parameters. On Pascal VOC 2012 semantic segmentation with a single RTX 5060 Ti 16GB GPU, loopxDINO (T=2) achieves 85.66% mIoU and 65.01% Boundary IoU. It outperforms 6-layer DINO-Trans6L (54.06M params) by +1.09% mIoU and +7.41% Boundary IoU with 72.5% fewer parameters. Compared to 4-layer DINO-FCN4L probe (2.43M params, 83.82% mIoU), loopxDINO improves boundary delineation by +6.43% bIoU and occlusion resilience by +6.76% mIoU (60% patch masking). With Adaptive Computation Time (ACT), it reaches 87.3 FPS and retains 29.64% mIoU under 60% occlusion (+5.83% over DINO-Trans6L). Source code, pre-trained weights and evaluation suites are open-sourced under Apache 2.0 at https://github.com/loopxDINO/loopxDINO
evidence_items.title: loopxDINO: Dense Visual Prediction via Iterative Latent Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Civil infrastructure is designed, built, and maintained through engineering drawing sets, yet preparing and revising them remains labour-intensive and calls for automation. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are promising candidates, but assessing them requires a benchmark grounded in real engineering practice. We introduce CivilCADBench, a benchmark for understanding, reconstructing, and designing civil engineering drawing sets, built from real infrastructure drawings and source CAD files containing over 250,000 CAD entities. Unlike parametric 3D CAD models, these drawings are dense, layered, and multi-sheet; and since prints are lossy projections with no pixel trace of layers, a file can print correctly yet remain wrongly organised. CivilCADBench comprises three task families of increasing difficulty: understanding tasks are evaluated with 2,183 expert-reviewed questions ranging from single sheets to whole sets, while reconstruction and design tasks are agentic, requiring models to rebuild printed pages as editable CAD files, either as single pages or entire drawing sets, and to produce new designs. These tasks are performed across 232 pages, 28 sets, and 19 design tasks, and evaluated by a deterministic scorer that compares model outputs with the designers' source files on geometry, layers, text, and dimensions. We evaluate seven frontier MLLMs on CivilCADBench, and find that they read and redraw printed content accurately but recover the file structure poorly: the best model scores above 90% in understanding and single-page reconstruction, yet only 60% on layer assignment and 48% on design. Grounded in real engineering practice, CivilCADBench exposes both the capabilities and the limitations of frontier models in professional civil engineering, laying a foundation for next-generation models and agentic systems for intelligent civil engineering.
evidence_items.title: CivilCADBench: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs for Understanding, Reconstructing, and Designing Civil Engineering Drawing Sets

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal emotion recognition remains challenging due to the intrinsic heterogeneity of different modalities. Effectively leveraging both cross-modal consensus (consistency) and conflict (inconsistency) is essential, as they jointly provide complementary cues that enhance emotion understanding from diverse perspectives. Traditional multimodal methods often suffer from semantic ambiguity and rarely explicitly model the interplay between cross-modal consensus and conflict. Moreover, existing approaches struggle to capture and exploit the dynamic interactions between these two complementary factors. To overcome these limitations, we propose DynFlux, a model guided by a temporal heterogeneous graph that encodes both consensus and conflict relationships across modalities. DynFlux introduces a dedicated graph branch that explicitly captures cross-modal dependencies through sparse temporal graphs, and modulates the conventional multimodal emotion recognition pipeline at three hierarchical stages: adaptive feature modulation during feature extraction, guided aggregation modulation during feature integration, and fusion strategy modulation at the multimodal fusion stage. Through this design, DynFlux dynamically balances cross-modal consensus and conflict, enabling richer and more robust emotion understanding. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets confirm that DynFlux consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, and its generality is further validated on multimodal intent recognition and multimodal sarcasm detection tasks.
evidence_items.title: DynFlux: Learning to Dynamically Balance Consensus and Conflict in Multimodal Emotion Recognition

evidence_items.summary: Depth super-resolution with color guidance is a fundamental problem in geometric scene understanding that aims to reconstruct high-resolution depth using structural cues from color images. In practical RGB-D systems, the resolution gap between depth and color images often varies, requiring flexible upsampling factors. However, many existing methods are designed for predefined integer scales. Although implicit methods support arbitrary-scale reconstruction, they typically rely on computationally demanding per-pixel neural decoding and may struggle to recover sharp depth boundaries and fine structures. To this end, we propose a cross-modal Gaussian rendering framework that learns continuous depth representations for arbitrary-scale depth super-resolution. Specifically, we first construct hierarchical Gaussian representations for progressive depth reconstruction, with explicit spatial support defined by learnable Gaussian primitives. Building on this representation, we design a Structure-Aware Gaussian Aggregation module that combines spatial weights with cross-modal feature affinities to reduce aggregation across depth discontinuities. We then develop a Scale-Adaptive Gaussian Rendering module that adapts Gaussian spatial kernels to the target pixel footprint. To further facilitate cross-modal learning, we propose a training strategy that gradually introduces higher-frequency guidance information during training. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method at both in-distribution and out-of-distribution upsampling scales.
evidence_items.title: Learning Continuous Scene Depth Representations via Cross-Modal Gaussian Rendering

evidence_items.summary: In NAVSIMv1, the standard benchmark for end-to-end driving, $89.6\%$ of the test scenes lie within 4m of a training scene. We show that this geographic overlap inflates the reported scores. We propose a geographically disjoint split of NAVSIMv1 and an evaluation that compares models trained on either split on the same scenes, which neither has seen in training. All sensor-based models we test, DiffusionDrive, Latent TransFuser, and DrivoR, lose 3.4 to 6.1 PDMS points on these scenes, mainly by leaving the road and coming close to other objects, against 1.5 points for a baseline without sensors. The loss concentrates where a training drive of the original split passed the same place. At all other places, models trained on the original split are no better than those trained on the geographic split. Models trained on the original split predict road geometry that no camera can see. The gap persists when the auxiliary map loss is removed, so the models memorize locations even without being supervised to. On nuScenes, the geographic split cuts SparseDrive's mapping accuracy by $59\%$ and also degrades its planning. Driving scores on logged scenes thus partly measure how well a model remembers the test locations. We release the split to evaluate generalization to new places.
evidence_items.title: Don't Test Where You Trained: Geographic Overlap Inflates End-to-End Driving Scores

evidence_items.summary: Anticipating the future behavior of surrounding objects is key for the safe and efficient navigation of autonomous vehicles. State-of-the-art Transformer-based interaction-aware trajectory prediction models are typically trained and evaluated on large-scale, highly curated datasets obtained by filtering any object detection and tracking noise through extensive offline post-processing. However, in real-world deployments, the detected objects' state (position, heading, and speed) estimates are inherently affected by sensing and localization uncertainties. These uncertainties can be even higher for connected and automated vehicles receiving information from other road users through Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communications. In this paper, we first investigate the sensitivity of five state-of-the-art Transformer-based interaction-aware trajectory prediction models to realistic noisy object state estimates. Numerical results show that prediction accuracy degrades by up to a 6x factor as the noise level increases, highlighting the models' sensitivity to the mismatch between the noise conditions encountered during training and those experienced at deployment. We then show that retraining models on a more realistic noise-augmented dataset is a more effective strategy to mitigate the impact of noisy object state estimates on trajectory prediction accuracy than using denoising modules at the input. Retrained models limit the prediction accuracy degradation below a 1.5x factor. The noise-augmented dataset is openly released to support further research.
evidence_items.title: Robust Trajectory Prediction Under Sensing and V2X Noise: Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies

evidence_items.summary: Associative Recall (AR) is the cognitive ability to learn and retrieve links between items in memory. In NLP, AR is used as a benchmark for evaluating the in-context memory capacity of architectures such as Mamba, and has been found to strongly correlate with language modeling performance. This paper explores AR from the perspective of mechanistic interpretability, aiming to reverse-engineer the exact internal algorithm used by Mamba to perform recall. Our key insight is that Mamba performs recall by implicitly learning linear hash functions, and we identify the low-level circuit that enables this behavior. Building on these findings and inspired by theoretical tools in similarity-preserving hashing, such as the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma, we develop a theoretical framework for analyzing AR, which we term Recall Scaling Laws. Given the vocabulary size and the number of facts in context, this framework allows us to (1) predict the embedding and state dimensions required for Mamba to achieve perfect recall, (2) predict recall success probability given the model dimensions, and (3) analyze multi-layer models and multi-head SSM patterns. Empirical results show that our theoretical findings are accurate and predictive, offering insights into how AR capacity scales with vocabulary, state, embedding size, and architecture.
evidence_items.title: On the Recall Scaling Laws in Mamba: A Theoretical and Mechanistic Study via Hashing

evidence_items.summary: We present HierSVA, an integrated suite that combines a pipeline, dataset, and benchmark for LLM-driven hierarchical hardware formal verification. HierSVA-SP pairs an RTL preprocessing toolchain with an LLM-in-the-loop formal verification flow to produce reference SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) on hierarchical RTL. Applying it to BaseJump STL yields HierSVA-DS, a dataset of 342 modules, with hierarchy metadata and depths 0--9, accompanied by a deep subset of 28 module-bug pairs with natural-language specifications and bug variants. HierSVA-B decomposes assertion quality into six metric axes: syntax correctness, assertion proof success rate, vacuity, specification faithfulness, mutation coverage, and formal core coverage. Applying HierSVA-B to twelve recent LLMs reveals three findings. First, the module-level compile rate is 67.1\%; among generated assertions in evaluable runs, 82.1\% prove non-vacuously, but the corresponding assertion sets detect only 70.2\% of eligible injected faults and cover 36.2\% of the formal core. Second, on 211 evaluable model--module entries in the deep subset, assertion sets flag buggy RTL with 0.87 recall, but 40\% of predicted-buggy outcomes are false positives on correct RTL, limiting precision to 0.60. Third, agentic mode improves S1-style provability and strength metrics, but gains plateau and oscillate. Codes and artifacts are available at \href{https://github.com/HierSVAAnon/HierSVACodeAndArtifacts}{https://github.com/HierSVAAnon/HierSVACodeAndArtifacts}. Dataset is available at \href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/AnonymousHierSVA/HierSVA}{https://huggingface.co/datasets/AnonymousHierSVA/HierSVA}.
evidence_items.title: HierSVA: A Data Synthesis Pipeline, Dataset, and Benchmark for LLM-Driven Hierarchical Hardware Formal Verification

evidence_items.summary: Web-enabled LLM agents are changing how online information influences search outcomes. Existing Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) studies mainly focus on individual webpages. However, agentic web search is not a single-document setting: an agent may issue queries, crawl pages, follow links, reformulate searches, and synthesize evidence across multiple browsing steps. Influence therefore depends not only on page content, but also on how pages are organized, connected, and encountered along the agent's browsing trajectory. We study this shift through Ecosystem Generative Engine Optimization (EcoGEO), which treats GEO as an environment-level influence problem for web-enabled LLM agents. To instantiate this perspective, we propose TRACE, a Trajectory-Aware Coordinated Evidence Ecosystem. Given a recommendation query and a fictional target product, our method builds a controlled evidence environment that coordinates an agent-facing navigation entry page with heterogeneous support pages. These pages use shared terminology, internal links, and consistent product attributes to introduce, verify, and reinforce the target product. We evaluate our method on OPR-Bench, a benchmark for open-ended product recommendation. Experiments show that it consistently outperforms page-level GEO baselines in Recommendation. Trajectory-level metrics show improved initial target access and additional internal-link browsing, while follow-up-search effects vary across backbones and comparison methods. Together with the multi-page baseline and ablations, these findings support the role of evidence organization in shaping the agent's evidence-acquisition process. Overall, our findings support an ecosystem research paradigm for GEO, where web-enabled LLM agents are studied in relation to the broader evidence environments that guide search, browsing, and answer synthesis.
evidence_items.title: EcoGEO: Trajectory-Aware Evidence Ecosystems for Web-Enabled LLM Search Agents

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled time series forecasting to move beyond numerical observations and incorporate external information in multimodal settings. Such information can improve forecasting performance, but accuracy alone may not reveal whether models appropriately respond to it: a model may ignore relevant information, fail to distinguish scenarios with different implications, or overreact to irrelevant or weak signals. We introduce What If TSF (WIT), a benchmark for evaluating whether models effectively respond to future scenarios. WIT constructs controlled scenario sets by fixing the forecasting state while systematically varying future scenarios, enabling three complementary evaluations: Factual Comparison, which measures the predictive utility of factual scenario information; Relational Comparison, which evaluates whether forecasts satisfy expected direction, contrast, intensity, and restraint relations across scenarios; and Grounded Comparison, which provides a complementary empirical assessment of scenario-induced revision trajectories where comparable real cases are available. Experiments show that factual accuracy gains do not consistently translate into appropriate responses to alternative scenarios, demonstrating the need to evaluate multimodal forecasting beyond predictive accuracy.
evidence_items.title: What If TSF: Evaluating Scenario-Guided Multimodal Time Series Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: This repository provides the complete Python implementation and verified experimental results associated with the research article entitled “AI-Based Bearing Fault Classification Using Vibration Sensor Data: Effects of Signal Representations and Decision Thresholds.” The study investigates the effects of dimensionless vibration features, signal representations, physical-time dynamics, and source-derived decision thresholds on artificial intelligence-based bearing fault classification. Experiments were conducted using 59 source recordings from the MCC5–THU three-phase asynchronous motor dataset and 32 target recordings from the University of Ottawa Electric Motor Dataset. Five predefined feature and temporal configurations, 11 classification models, and four decision rules were evaluated. The models include physical-time spiking neural networks, a memoryless SNN counterpart, conventional machine learning classifiers, and ensemble methods. Model training, calibration, and decision threshold selection were performed exclusively on source data using nested stratified group cross-validation with three outer folds and two inner folds. The trained models were evaluated on the Ottawa recordings without target-side parameter updates. The Ottawa analyses include exploratory comparisons at the recording level. The archive contains: The complete Python source code and software dependencies. Publication Figures 5–10 in PNG and SVG formats. Publication Tables 5–8 in CSV format. Source cross-validation results and record-level predictions. Ottawa classification scores, calibration results, and decision thresholds. Group-based bootstrap results and supporting feature statistics. Experimental protocol, raw-data checksums, software environment information, and reproducibility verification reports. Numerical results were checked against the manuscript at the reported precision.
evidence_items.title: Reproducible Python Code and Experimental Results for AI-Based Bearing Fault Classification Using Vibration Sensor Data: Effects of Signal Representations and Decision Thresholds

evidence_items.summary: Version: 1.0.0 Author: Phan Thanh TrungAffiliation: Operatorology Research, VietnamORCID: 0009-0000-7520-6781 Description This dataset presents Prime Excalibur, a computational framework for open-vocabulary prime-factor relational learning and zero-shot generalization across previously unseen prime-factor channels. The framework employs a shared-weight neural relational operator with 261 trainable parameters. By learning local prime-factor interactions and aggregating them through a permutation-invariant representation, the model transfers its learned decision rule to unseen prime-factor channels without retraining or expanding its learned parameter set. Across 12 independently seeded experiments, the neural model achieved 100% balanced accuracy on two strictly held-out prime-factor domains (101–199 and 1009–1093), correctly classifying all 19,200 evaluation examples. The release includes 72,000 labeled training pairs, 48,000 evaluation records across the original experimental streams, sample-level predictions, factor-token representations, trained model weights, benchmark comparisons, permutation-invariance tests, source code, scientific figures, and detailed reproducibility reports. The benchmark provides computational evidence of learned structural transfer under numerical distribution shift. Its controlled synthetic arithmetic setting enables exact evaluation and independent reproduction of the reported results. This dataset accompanies the development of Prime Excalibur as a relational representation framework for scientific machine-learning research. Keywords: Prime Excalibur; Operatorology; Prime-Factor Representation; Zero-Shot Learning; Relational Learning; Out-of-Distribution Generalization; Permutation Invariance; Scientific Machine Learning; Reproducible Benchmark.
evidence_items.title: Prime Excalibur: Open-Vocabulary Prime-Factor Relational Learning — Strict Zero-Shot Benchmark and Reproducibility Dataset

evidence_items.summary: This deliverable presents the final version of the Stakeholder Needs Analysis and KPI Framework developed within the EVOLVE2CARE project, building upon the initial framework introduced in Deliverable D1.2. The framework was designed to support the evaluation of HealthTech innovation processes in the field of transitional care, with a particular focus on the collaboration between Living Labs, innovators, end-users, and broader healthcare ecosystems. The main objective of this deliverable is to provide a comprehensive analysis of the process applied to the framework during the project’s implementation phase. The revision was primarily driven by evidence gathered through the EVOLVE2CARE Open Calls and the experimentation activities carried out between Living Labs and innovators. By analysing the KPIs proposed during both the application and contract phases, this deliverable establishes the degree of alignment between the theoretical framework and the practical needs emerging from real-world experimentation settings. The methodological approach relied on an alignment scoring system based on keyword matching and weighted coverage rates, allowing for the systematic identification of areas with strong, partial, and weak correspondence across the different KPI repositories. The analysis confirms that real-life testing and experimentation, business and scale-up support, and technical usability are the most consistently represented dimensions across projects. At the same time, important gaps were identified in areas such as environmental sustainability, cost-effectiveness, patient digital literacy, and gender-responsive evaluation practices, which served as an update for the refinement of the framework. Furthermore, the deliverable outlines the strategic activities undertaken to promote the framework across European and international health innovation networks, ensuring its wider adoption and long-term sustainability beyond the project lifecycle.
evidence_items.title: EVOLVE2CARE – KPI Framework
