evidence_items.summary: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both interactive worlds and the tasks agents must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation (WD). World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. Explicit states and tool-call traces support task validation and agent evaluation. We evaluate 22 models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 88.8% mean Pass@1. Construction experiments demonstrate token efficiency and expansion of task coverage. At the richest knowledge level, WD fully covers 22/23 properties, 19/29 functionalities, and 30/39 event requirements specified in a real RobotVacuum protocol. Furthermore, the 1,000 sampled tasks semantically cover 81.6% of the 854 reference instructions in the real-world corpus. SynthDCB connects an expanding space of real-to-sim executable capabilities to verifiable agent evaluation.
evidence_items.title: SynthDCB: World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking

evidence_items.summary: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. Finally, we validate our critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B, whose failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%, enabling low-cost action-level analysis.
evidence_items.title: AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control

evidence_items.summary: Persistent spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents to operate reliably in environments they repeatedly encounter. It requires recognizing revisited places despite viewpoint changes, distinguishing them from similar-looking rooms, and updating memories as environments change. Yet existing evaluations often leave physical place identity across separated visits implicit. We introduce ReSpaceBench, a benchmark comprising 3,244 questions across 590 synthetic and real-home scenes, organized into 9 tasks spanning room association, persistent state tracking, and downstream reasoning. Controlled walkthroughs define visits by physical room entry and deliberately include same-type room distractors and cross-session object changes. Our evaluation of 32 models and 3 agentic video-understanding frameworks reveals substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated zero-shot model achieves 50.5% overall accuracy and 52.2% on a 450-question subset, compared with 90.1% for human annotators. The evaluated agentic frameworks offer no overall improvement over direct inference with the same base model. Analysis of agent execution traces reveals evidence omissions and incorrect cross-visit room associations as major failure modes, suggesting that iterative evidence seeking alone does not ensure consistent spatial memory. Further analyses expose a gap between recognizing familiar rooms and identifying the correct visited room, while annotation-guided sampling highlights the importance of preserving intervening visits and transitions. We also provide RS-30K, a separate training dataset from synthetic sources with no template, scene, route, or video overlap with the benchmark. Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B raises overall accuracy from 35.5% to 60.4%, with the largest gains in association and improvements extending to real-life scenes.
evidence_items.title: Lost in the Hallway: Benchmarking Persistent Spatial Memory Across Revisits

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence increasingly connects business forecasts, clinical information, cloud services, and security operations, yet a prediction becomes useful only when an organization can act on it safely. The corpus is organized into seven primary themes covering business operations, governance, cybersecurity, privacy, healthcare, representation learning, and sustainable infrastructure. Bibliographic coding is distinguished from selectively inspected publisher content; the study is neither a systematic review nor a quantitative comparison of model performance. The synthesis identifies a common design problem: predictive components, privacy mechanisms, and operational controls are often discussed through different objectives, leaving their joint decision consequences difficult to assess. We propose a layered architecture that connects data provenance, calibrated inference, constrained action, independent verification, and monitored feedback. Its evaluation protocol combines temporal and organizational holdouts, budget-matched baselines, adversarial testing, cryptographic cost accounting, and prospective assessment of operational outcomes. Four falsifiable propositions specify when additional verification, privacy protection, simulation, and bounded adaptation could improve deployment. Original figures visualize corpus composition, architectural dependencies, and evidence requirements without presenting simulated values as observations. The principal contribution is an auditable research design for studying trustworthy decision systems across heterogeneous applications. Empirical superiority, clinical effectiveness, and economic benefit remain questions for subsequent evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence for Enterprise Decision Systems

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents can now turn a well-specified ticket into a patch that passes its tests. Experienced engineers also notice risks the request never mentioned, question flawed premises, reuse what already exists and say plainly what they did and did not check. We present sudo L7, a benchmark of 60 software-engineering tasks written by staff-level engineers, mostly in private production codebases and each built around a place where a frontier model failed. A task pairs a realistic, underspecified request with a hidden, expert-authored rubric of atomic criteria (1,287 in all), tagged with eight behavioral dimensions from functional correctness to truthful reporting. An agentic grader reads the agent's transcript, inspects and runs its code, and treats test output as evidence. An attempt passes only if it meets every criterion of the two highest severities, and more than half of these gating criteria test something other than functional correctness. On the public leaderboard as of November 2026 (19 models, each in its developer's harness or in OpenCode, three attempts per task), Claude Fable 5.2 passes 52.2% of attempts, Claude Sonnet 5.5 50.6% and Claude Opus 5.5 46.1%. GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra pass 31-34%, and the other 13 models at most 18.9%. In a human-label study, three candidate model graders each agreed with a software engineer on 85-86% of criterion verdicts, about as often as two engineers agreed with each other. Cases from the benchmark show how one unsupported claim can fail an otherwise strong attempt and illustrate two sides of engineering judgment: flagging hidden hazards and avoiding needless work.
evidence_items.title: sudo L7: Can Coding Agents Act Like Staff Engineers?

evidence_items.summary: Agricultural management is heterogeneous along two axes. The first is distributional shift within a fixed task interface: weather, crops, and prices vary across years and locations while sensors, actions, and objective stay fixed. The second is structural shift across interfaces: different farms expose different observed variables, available actions, and management objectives. We formalize the second axis as schema shift: variation in the policy-facing schema $Σ= (Σ O, Σ A, Σ R)$ between training and deployment. We test whether LLM-RL generalizes across both axes with AgriManager, to our knowledge the first framework that trains LLM policies with RL across multiple process-based crop simulators, unifying DSSAT, WOFOST, and Cycles. We design a three-tier generalization ladder: Tier 1 within-schema distributional shift, Tier 2 single-axis schema shift along $Σ O / Σ A / Σ R$, Tier 3 compositional schema shift across simulators, all scored on a frozen held-out test suite with three training seeds per method. Within fixed schemas, Qwen3-4B trained by RL with explicit reasoning exceeds neural-network PPO trained with the same interaction budget; without reasoning, training stalls near no-action where the reward penalizes input use. Under single-axis schema shift, $Σ O$ transfer needs decision-critical state, $Σ A$ results are consistent with joint action-menu coverage, and with reasoning a policy trained on yield alone transfers to unseen objectives. Under compositional schema shift, single-source training mostly hurts zero-shot transfer across simulators, and a unified policy trained only on other combinations of the same components recovers about 86% of the gain of a specialist trained on the target combination on DSSAT and stays below the specialists on the WOFOST and Cycles profit targets. Project page: https://agrimanager-framework.github.io
evidence_items.title: AgriManager: A Framework and Benchmark for LLM-RL Generalization in Agricultural Management

evidence_items.summary: Typhoon OCR 1.5 focused on reading Thai documents. However, in real-world workflows, users often need to extract specific information or preserve the structure of an entire page for further processing. Typhoon OCR 2 handles both tasks in a single model, with prompt-driven extraction and structured full-page parsing. Full-page parsing covers Thai, English, and Chinese. We release compact 2B and 0.8B models adapted from open document parsers through supervised fine-tuning on curated Thai and public multilingual data, followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with task rewards and a rule penalizing unfinished responses. Among evaluated open models, Typhoon OCR 2 2B scores highest on Thai MDPBench (80.7 versus 68.9 for Typhoon OCR 1.5) and on ThaiOCRBench (59.91 versus 40.45), which covers recognition, extraction, and document understanding. The 2B model remains close to its base on English olmOCR-bench (84.7 versus 84.4) and on OmniDocBench, which evaluates English and Chinese together (90.97 versus 91.03). On MDPBench, GRPO reduces the mean share of pages with repetition loops for the 2B model from 3.2% to 0.7%, with a smaller and statistically uncertain score gain for the 0.8B model. We release the model weights, Python package, and evaluation suite.

evidence_items.summary: This repository contains the source code for the article "A Spatial–Frequency Dual-Branch Network with Learnable Gabor Filters for Iris Recognition" by Nushrat Praveen, Danish Ali Khan, Tapan Kumar Dey, Alekha Kumar Mishra and Rashmi Panda. SFG-IrisNet is a compact iris recognition network with about 1.2 million parameters. It processes the normalised iris image through two branches: a MobileNetV3-Small trunk that captures local spatial structure, and a bank of 32 complex Gabor filters whose orientation, wavelength, bandwidth, aspect ratio and phase are learned during training. A spatial–frequency attentive gating module fuses the two branches, and a shift-equivariant spatial-grid embedding keeps the angular and radial layout of the iris features. The network is trained with an additive angular margin (ArcFace) loss. The package provides the complete experimental pipeline used in the article: iris localisation with an integro-differential operator and rubber-sheet normalisation to 64 × 512 pixels; the proposed SFG-IrisNet model and seven ablation variants; four CNN baselines (ResNet-18, MobileNetV3-Large, EfficientNet-B0 and ShuffleNetV2) and a classical log-Gabor IrisCode baseline; a subject-disjoint evaluation protocol with three random seeds, cross-dataset tests, and subject-level bootstrap confidence intervals and significance tests; scripts that produce all result tables and figures (300 dpi TIFF); the result tables reported in the article. The experiments use the CASIA-Iris-Interval (CASIA-IrisV4) and IIT Delhi iris databases. These datasets are not included and must be obtained from their owners. Instructions for installation and for reproducing all experiments are given in README.md. The code is written in Python with PyTorch and is released under the MIT licence.
evidence_items.title: SFG-IrisNet: Source code for "A Spatial–Frequency Dual-Branch Network with Learnable Gabor Filters for Iris Recognition"

evidence_items.summary: Robust in-situ monitoring can expedite the development and tuning of reactive extrusion (REX) processes, especially for the synthesis of polymers requiring insight into the reaction course, such as specialty polyurethanes (PUs). In order to advance the feasibility of such analysis, our research concentrated on a spectroscopic protocol that combines at-line mid-infrared (MIR) and on-line near-infrared (NIR) measurements in a laboratory extruder, assessing both their qualitative and quantitative capabilities. To mimic the depletion of the reactive species during polymerisation, a series of premixes were formulated and characterised under non-reactive conditions using a benchmark pair of a polyol and a diisocyanate. By this means, we identified suitable spectral features for quantifying isocyanate content via multivariate regression models. This approach achieved good calibration metrics for both MIR and NIR models and enabled a robust assessment of their predictive performance through cross-validation, using only a moderate number of spectral datasets. Our work is therefore the first step towards establishing a method for in-process NIR analysis with streamlined at-line MIR verification. It provides a shortcut for designing monitored REX syntheses of PUs and other material systems amenable to quantitative calibration based on spectroscopic data from raw reagents.
evidence_items.title: Mid- and near-infrared spectroscopies for quantitative tracking of isocyanate content: Streamlined development of monitoring tools for reactive extrusion synthesis of specialty polyurethanes

evidence_items.summary: VegVault is an open database that brings together vegetation plots, fossil pollen records and plant traits with the climate and soil conditions of their place and time ( data paper ; website ). It is part of the BIODYNAMICS project . This repository prepares VegVault's plant trait data: about 10.9 million measurements of six traits, as defined by Díaz et al. (2016) : plant height; leaf area; leaf mass per area; leaf nitrogen content per leaf dry mass; seed (diaspore) mass; stem specific density (wood density). They come from two public trait databases, the TRY Plant Trait Database and the Botanical Information and Ecology Network (BIEN) . Every measurement is converted to one standard unit per trait, and each conversion is recorded. Measurements that cannot be converted reliably, or that appear in both databases, are not published; the audit tables count them. Who would use these files Most users get these data through VegVault itself, which links the traits to the vegetation and climate data. The files of this release show how each trait value was obtained, serve to rebuild VegVault, or can be used on their own. Format: the records are R data frames in the qs2 format, although the extension is .qs . Read them with qs2::qs read() . The rule and audit tables are CSV files. evidence_items.summary: Understanding a system that can be run but not inspected is a core engineering skill: one designs experiments, forms hypotheses about hidden state and timing, discards those that observations refute, and finally builds a replacement that works and is efficient. To evaluate this capability of LLM agents in the hardware domain, we present ChiProgramBench, 18 tasks derived from open-source processors, accelerators, codecs, transforms, interconnects, and control circuits. Agents can only drive and read the pins of a hidden, stateful simulated reference, then submit a gate-level netlist made of public library cells. Agents work in two settings: black-box discovery gives only anonymized functional pins and the interfaces of fixed memories, while function-guided reconstruction adds the circuit's purpose and each pin's role. Hidden test cases compare outputs with the reference cycle by cycle; power, delay, and area earn credit relative to the reference only when every case passes. Across 432 trials of 6 LLM agent configurations, successful agents recover algorithms and numerical conventions, yet only 12.0% of black-box and 14.8% of function-guided trials pass every case. Function-guided reconstruction raises the mean functional score, the cycle-weighted share of passed cases, from 24.6% to 30.9%. Of the 58 fully passing designs, only three improve on the reference's combined power, area, and delay, so behavioral recovery and efficient implementation remain distinct challenges.
evidence_items.title: ChiProgramBench: Can LLM Agents Rebuild Efficient Circuits from Pin-Level Experiments?

evidence_items.summary: Continual learning (CL) seeks to enable Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) to acquire knowledge sequentially across tasks without catastrophically forgetting previously learned task information. Existing regularization-based approaches mitigate forgetting by penalizing changes to DNN parameters deemed important for a past task, based on gradient sensitivity measures, without explicitly accounting for what the DNN has actually learned. Inspired by the selectivity of human memory consolidation, where the importance of a synapse is determined by the memory it encodes rather than by its raw sensitivity to stimulation, we propose Quantifying DNN Knowledge for Continual Learning (QKCL), a regularization-based CL method that grounds parameter importance directly on DNN-encoded knowledge. Upon completing DNN training on each task, QKCL identifies DNN knowledge as the input units whose information is retained through the DNN layers, its knowledge points. It uses gradient analysis to determine which DNN parameters are most responsible for preserving it. These parameters are assigned high importance and protected during subsequent task training. Extensive experiments across six standard CL benchmarks using three architecture families and a real-world Natural Disaster Management (NDM) benchmark demonstrate that QKCL achieves competitive performance, outperforming existing regularization-based methods in the majority of evaluated settings and showing particular effectiveness in fine-grained benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: Quantifying DNN Knowledge via Knowledge Points for Continual Learning

evidence_items.summary: VegVault is an open database that brings together vegetation plots, fossil pollen records and plant traits with the climate and soil conditions of their place and time ( data paper ; website ). It is part of the BIODYNAMICS project . This repository prepares VegVault's fossil pollen data: pollen records from the Neotoma Paleoecology Database , processed with the FOSSILPOL workflow into a global dataset of the last 20,000 years. For each record it gives the location and the depositional environment, the levels (samples) with their ages from new age-depth models, the age uncertainty of every level, and the pollen counts harmonised to a common taxonomy. This release is a complete rerun of the workflow on a fresh download from Neotoma (19 November 2026). It holds 1,551 fossil pollen datasets with 100,341 levels, against 1,393 datasets and 88,423 levels in 1.0.0. Who would use these files Most users get these data through VegVault itself. The files of a release serve to rebuild VegVault, or to reuse the processed pollen records directly. Format: R objects in the qs2 format, although the extension is .qs . Read them with qs2::qs read() . The files of 1.0.0 were written with the older qs package, which qs2 cannot read. Light assembly ( data assembly light .qs ): one row per dataset. The columns that VegVault relies on are: dataset id : the Neotoma dataset identifier; source of data : Neotoma ; doi : the DOI of the Neotoma dataset (the site table has one for all 1,551 datasets); long and lat : the site location in decimal degrees (WGS84); depositionalenvironment : the Neotoma depositional environment; levels : one table per dataset with one row per level, with the level identifier sample id and its age , the median modelled age in calibrated years before 1950 CE (negative for levels younger than 1950); counts harmonised : one table per dataset with one row per level, the column sample id and one column per harmonised pollen type holding the pollen count.

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Tasklets, a benchmark of small synthetic tasks for evaluating the computational capabilities of language model sequence-mixing layers. These tasks probe foundational capabilities such as recall, sequence manipulation, and state tracking. Such tasks are widely used in architecture research, but differences in task selection, formulation, and evaluation make comparisons across studies difficult. Tasklets brings these tasks together, organizing them by the capabilities they test and providing a shared setup for evaluating how different architectural layer types learn fundamental computations. We compare a broad range of layer types through controlled experiments with small models. Our task implementations and evaluation code support reproducible, low-cost testing of new architectural proposals: https://github.com/zaydzuhri/flame/tree/tasklets.
evidence_items.title: Tasklets: A Unit-Test Benchmark for Language Model Architectures

evidence_items.summary: Hy-MT3 is the third generation of the Hunyuan multilingual translation model family, including \textbf{Hy-MT3-1.8B}, \textbf{Hy-MT3-7B} and \textbf{Hy-MT3-30B-A3B (MoE)}. Compared with Hy-MT2, Hy-MT3 translates \textbf{more accurately, more completely and more faithfully to user constraints}: on real-world scenario data, the share of samples with mistranslations is reduced by \textbf{43\%}, omissions or additions by \textbf{74\%}, and instruction-following errors by \textbf{40\%}, while language coverage is expanded from \textbf{38 to 102} languages. With only 3B activated parameters, \textbf{Hy-MT3-30B-A3B achieves the best overall performance among all evaluated models in non-thinking mode}, including flagship models such as Qwen3.8-Max, Kimi-K3.1-Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and approaches the strongest closed-source thinking models such as GPT-6.1-Sol and Gemini-4-Argon, while surpassing models that consume \textbf{more than 30$\times$} its inference compute. Beyond general translation, Hy-MT3 is optimized for two industrial scenarios. For \textbf{game localization}, built with high-quality game-domain data and a professional evaluation system from the Honor of Kings team, Hy-MT3-30B-A3B matches or outperforms strong closed-source models such as Gemini 3.1 Pro on all core metrics, and can be plugged into game development pipelines through an open-source toolchain. For \textbf{image translation}, Hy-MT3 improves context understanding and error correction to better tolerate OCR errors, achieving the best result among models of comparable size. Finally, we open-source \textbf{TransRubric}, a rubric-based automatic evaluation suite for translation, which outperforms other evaluation schemes on the WMT26 metrics shared task test set and is more stable with respect to human evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and Practical Multilingual Translation Models in the Wild

evidence_items.summary: The robust safety of Vision-Language Large Models (VLLMs) against joint multilingual and multimodal threats remains severely underexplored. Current benchmarks typically isolate these dimensions, being either multilingual but text-only, or multimodal but monolingual. While recent red-teaming efforts attempt to bridge this gap by rendering harmful prompts as images, their overreliance on typography-style visuals and lack of semantically grounded image-text pairs fail to capture realistic cross-modal interactions under multilingual and multimodal conditions. To address this, we introduce Lingua-SafetyBench, a comprehensive benchmark of 100,440 harmful image-text pairs spanning 10 languages. Crucially, Lingua-SafetyBench explicitly partitions data into Image-Dominant and Text-Dominant subsets to precisely disentangle sources of risk. Extensive evaluations reveal that current VLLMs retain non-negligible vulnerabilities under these joint inputs. Furthermore, analyzing modality-language interactions uncovers a striking asymmetry: on average, Image-Dominant Risk poses greater threats in High-Resource Languages (HRLs), whereas models are more vulnerable in Non-High-Resource Languages (Non-HRLs) under Text-Dominant Risk. Finally, a controlled study on the Qwen series demonstrates that while model scaling and iterative upgrades improve overall safety, they disproportionately benefit HRLs. This exacerbates the safety disparity between HRLs and Non-HRLs under Text-Dominant Risk, highlighting that achieving robust safety requires dedicated language- and modality-aware alignment strategies beyond mere scaling. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/zsxr15/Lingua-SafetyBench. Warning: This paper contains examples with unsafe content.
evidence_items.title: Lingua-SafetyBench: A Benchmark for Safety Evaluation of Multilingual Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly used to extract records, generate SQL, summarize reports, answer policy questions, and route operational work. At these software boundaries, parseable output is necessary but does not establish task correctness. We present a reproducible benchmark protocol, a public executable artifact, and a confirmatory live API evaluation that separate structural validity from task-specific correctness across five business workflow tasks and six Python implementation conditions: PydanticAI, LangGraph, DSPy, CrewAI, Agno, and a framework-free SDK reference. We hypothesize that (H1) schema validity and task quality are separable, (H2) structured-output binding paths are heterogeneous under a shared model and lowest-common-denominator contract, and (H3) condition-by-task interactions concentrate failures rather than shifting all tasks equally. Confirmatory analysis uses distinct task instances (100 extraction and 50 per other task, with three nested replicates) under a frozen analysis plan, yielding a 5400-row primary matrix with equivalence margins and Holm-adjusted contrasts against the SDK reference. In the eligible confirmatory run, overall schema validity was 0.684 and mean automated quality was 0.638. PydanticAI, LangGraph, and DSPy retained near-ceiling schema validity with mean quality 0.91-0.94, while the plain SDK, Agno, and CrewAI conditions were substantially lower in this package and model configuration. Schema-valid rows still produced many task-score flags, especially in extraction and compliance QA, and quality residuals show strong condition-by-task interactions (including a workflow collapse for CrewAI). Labelled ablations address retry budgets and feature-using mechanisms; primary contrasts remain system-configuration findings, not causal attributions to marketed library features.
evidence_items.title: Schema-Validated LLM Workflows: A Benchmark Protocol and Comparative Evaluation Across Six Python Implementations

evidence_items.summary: Overview: This dataset provides asset-level estimates of gross value added (GVA), employment and net capital stock for four sectors of the Spanish economy: power generation, mining and quarrying, manufacturing, and agriculture (crops, forestry, and intensive pig and poultry rearing). Values are allocated from national or provincial sector totals down to individual power plants, mining facilities, manufacturing zones, crop-province combinations, and livestock facilities, giving spatially explicit economic exposure data at a resolution not available from standard national accounts. Coverage: The database covers 3,169 power generation assets, 113 active mining and quarrying facilities, 11,953 industrial manufacturing zones, 5,984 crop and forestry records, and 3,996 intensive pig and poultry facilities, all located and classified to official Spanish province and autonomous-community boundaries (INE administrative codes). Economic figures reflect 2023 (GVA, employment) and 2022 (net capital stock, the most recent year available at provincial level). Methodology: For each sector, sector-level economic totals (from INE national accounts and, for agriculture, a value-added decomposition of Eurostat's Economic Accounts for Agriculture) are distributed to individual assets using a weighting variable appropriate to that sector: installed capacity share for power, national activity-class production share split evenly across comparable facilities for mining, manufacturing land area for industrial zones, crop value share for agriculture, and live-animal output share for intensive livestock. Net capital stock is sourced from the Fundación BBVA-Ivie capital stock database and allocated on the same basis as the corresponding GVA figure.
evidence_items.title: Asset-Level Economic Exposure Dataset for Spain's Power, Mining, Manufacturing and Agriculture Sectors

evidence_items.summary: Researchers submitting deep learning jobs to shared GPU clusters need runtime estimates to request time limits, choose hardware, and budget compute. Large language models (LLMs) offer a tempting shortcut: describe the job and ask. We introduce PreRun, a benchmark for predicting deep learning training and inference runtime from information available before execution. PreRun contains 801 training and 1,884 inference records of language and vision models collected on a GPU cluster, paired with workload configurations and explicitly defined timing targets. It also includes 64 text-generation configurations measured under standardized conditions, each in three separate program launches. We compare three LLMs (Qwen3.5-9B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Claude Opus 5.5) with regression baselines and evaluate analytical estimates on a supported forward-pass subset. On 16 held-out generation configurations, the open-weight LLMs underestimate latency by 90-99% on average without examples. Claude's zero-shot mean absolute error is 4.5 times that of a Random Forest fit on 32 configurations. Five labeled examples substantially reduce Claude's generation error, but their benefit varies across timing targets. We will open-source our data and evaluation pipeline upon acceptance.
evidence_items.title: How Long Will My Language Model Run? A Benchmark for Pre-Execution Runtime Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Optimization benchmarks play a fundamental role in assessing algorithm performance; however, existing artificial benchmarks often fail to capture the diversity and irregularity of real-world problem structures, while benchmarks derived from real-world problems are costly and difficult to construct. To address these challenges, we propose an evolutionary automatic benchmark generation framework that leverages a large language model (LLM) as a generative operator, termed the LLM-driven evolutionary benchmark generator (LLM-EBG). In this framework, the LLM serves as an evolutionary operator that generates and evolves benchmark problems within a flexible, expressive representation space. As a case study, we generate unconstrained single-objective continuous minimization problems represented as mathematical expressions designed to induce significant performance differences between a genetic algorithm (GA) and differential evolution (DE). Experimental results show that LLM-EBG successfully produces benchmark problems in which the designated target algorithm consistently outperforms the comparative algorithm in more than 80% of trials. Furthermore, exploratory landscape analysis reveals that benchmarks favoring GA are highly sensitive to variable scaling, demonstrating that the proposed framework can generate problems with distinct geometric characteristics that reflect the intrinsic search behaviors of different optimization algorithms.
evidence_items.title: An evolutionary framework for automatic optimization benchmark generation via large language models

evidence_items.summary: We investigate whether pairwise attention features improve coreference readout beyond pooled span representations in frozen language models with up to 7B parameters. We train mention-ranking probes on hidden states, attention features, or both. Across 15 decoders from 7 families and 3 encoders, combining the two gives the highest OntoNotes scores with gold mentions; decoder gains over hidden states range from +1.5 to +2.5 CoNLL F1, and most of the gain is lost when attention features are shuffled across pairs. Without target-domain threshold calibration, attention-only probes transfer best to the pronoun benchmarks GAP and WinoBias, although calibration changes their ranking against combined probes. In three models, mean-ablating the heads that the attention probe ranks highest lowers the hidden-state readout even after the probe is retrained, with much smaller effects for heads sampled outside the top 64. A frozen 0.5B model comes within 1.1 F1 of our LoRA baseline.

evidence_items.summary: Background After discharge, caregivers must distinguish expected swelling or discomfort from cast damage, skin change, altered circulation, and other complications that require urgent reassessment. Large language models (LLMs) can provide immediate bilingual advice, yet fluent answers may omit safety-critical context or remain difficult to act on. We compared six LLMs’ English and Chinese responses to pediatric fracture cast care questions. Methods In total, 36 question concepts across six clinical domains were expressed in English and Chinese. GPT 5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Fable 5, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Qwen 3.8 Max, and Doubao Seed 2.1 Pro generated 432 responses. Two topic-relevant clinical specialists independently evaluated global quality, treatment information quality, artificial intelligence–specific quality, completeness, actionability, clinical accuracy, safety, and hallucination; a senior specialist adjudicated unresolved differences. English and Chinese responses underwent language-specific readability assessment. Comparisons were paired by question concept; relationships among dimensions were examined by language. Results Within-model English–Chinese differences varied by endpoint, with no consistent language advantage. Exploratory contrasts between the two selected model sets were attenuated or imprecisely estimated after adjustment for response length. Quality Analysis of Medical Artificial Intelligence and Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials scores were concentrated at 26/30 and 60%, respectively. For English, every model missed the prespecified median readability targets. For Chinese, all median Chinese Language Difficulty Coefficient values exceeded the teaching material reference value of 30. Five of 432 responses (1.2%) received safety score 2, none received score 3, and 11 (2.5%) contained an unsupported or fabricated claim under the study rubric.
evidence_items.title: Does language change the answer? A bilingual evaluation of large language models for cast care in pediatric fractures

evidence_items.summary: Smart public spaces combine sensing infrastructures, digital services, responsive facilities, and physical spatial elements, producing experience evidence that cannot be adequately represented by questionnaires or isolated environmental indicators. This study develops a multimodal artificial intelligence model that evaluates comfort, perceived safety, spatial engagement, accessibility, and an integrated experience score from synchronized behavioral video, UWB trajectories, environmental sensing, and textual feedback. Data are collected from 120 participants completing four eight-minute spatial conditions in an instrumented campus plaza. Modality-specific encoders generate 128-dimensional representations, which are temporally aligned and integrated by a four-layer cross-modal Transformer with hierarchical regression heads. On participant-independent testing, the proposed model achieved an overall MAE of 0.044 ± 0.004, RMSE of 0.061 ± 0.005, R² of 0.905 ± 0.012, and Spearman ρ of 0.951 ± 0.008, significantly outperforming early-fusion and single-modality baselines (p < .001). Removing trajectory or textual information increased overall MAE to 0.061 ± 0.006 and 0.059 ± 0.005, respectively. The model also retained stable performance across crowd-density and lighting conditions, while SHAP analysis identified distinct modality contributions to each experience dimension.

evidence_items.summary: AI transforms financial reporting via predictive anomaly detection, semantic analysis, and continuous auditing. The fractured literature between computer science and accounting lacks a unified framework. To correct this, a scoping review mapped global scholarship. Evaluating 562 Scopus records published before April 2026 exposed exponential growth between 2020 and 2025. Reflexive Thematic Analysis yielded four themes: algorithmic classification predicting distress; semantic quantification decoding narratives; continuous audits using robotic workflows; and ethical hurdles from transparency barriers. Bridging this gap demands grounding machine learning in accounting theories. Future operations must implement explainable AI, align with sustainable development goals, and obey regulatory standards.

evidence_items.summary: Natural products (NPs) remain a valuable source of chemical diversity for pharmacological research and drug development. Their complex structures and biological activities have contributed to the discovery of medicines and inspired new therapeutic strategies. Nevertheless, conventional natural-product discovery can be slow and resource-intensive because researchers must address source selection, extraction, isolation, dereplication, structural elucidation, biological testing and subsequent optimization. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), natural-language processing, computer vision and graph-based methods, offers computational approaches to help manage these tasks. This review discusses the role of AI across the natural-product discovery pipeline, with emphasis on data integration, plant and microbial source exploration, biosynthetic gene-cluster analysis, metabolomics and spectral interpretation, activity and target prediction, virtual screening, network pharmacology, toxicity and ADMET estimation, and molecular design. It also describes commonly used databases and computational resources, outlines a practical AI-supported workflow, and considers opportunities for integrating experimental evidence with computational predictions. The benefits of AI include prioritization of candidate compounds, improved analysis of large and heterogeneous datasets, hypothesis generation and more systematic exploration of chemical and biological relationships. Important limitations remain, including dataset bias, inconsistent annotation, small sample sizes, overfitting, poor external validation, limited interpretability, reproducibility concerns and the need for experimental confirmation. Ethical, regulatory and biodiversity considerations are also discussed. AI is best regarded as a decision-support layer that complementsnot replacesphytochemistry, pharmacology, analytical chemistry and biological experimentation.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Natural Products Discovery

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) holds great promise in radiotherapy. However, prospective evaluation and robust assessment frameworks for AI contouring and planning tools are lacking, casting doubt on the quality and cost-effectiveness of some AI radiotherapy solutions and hindering wider clinical deployment. ARCHERY, an international, prospective multi-cancer basket trial, seeks to undertake a large-scale evaluation of AI-assisted contouring and planning for cancers of the head and neck, prostate and cervix for patients in diverse country settings. We describe the evaluation approach led by the UK Radiotherapy Trials Quality Assurance (RTTQA) Group which, through literature appraisal, established protocol-defined reference standard contour and planning parameters and, following a scoping review and consensus discussion, developed evaluation definitions to enable robust and consistent assessment. This approach demonstrates a strong example of AI radiotherapy study methodology and tool assessment, and serves as a foundation for adoption, adaptation and development in future AI radiotherapy studies.
evidence_items.title: Defining an evaluation framework for radiotherapy trials which use artificial intelligence- lessons from the ARCHERY trial

evidence_items.summary: This chapter explores how artificial intelligence reshapes assessment design in higher education, using Cantonese as a second language as a distinctive lens. Cantonese's tonal and sociolinguistic complexity provides a rigorous case for evaluating AI's role in oral proficiency testing. The discussion highlights the shift toward adaptive, learner-centred formats that move beyond standardised methods. Drawing on Hong Kong's higher education practices, it demonstrates how integrating Automatic Speech Recognition, Large Language Models, and Text-to-Speech enables contextualized tasks, real-time feedback, and alignment with ACTFL and CEFR frameworks. It also addresses challenges of transparency, cultural sensitivity, and human-in-the-loop mediation. Ultimately, AI-driven assessment design fosters flexible, inclusive, and pedagogically robust approaches across multilingual higher education.

evidence_items.summary: This chapter examines how immersive technologies and artificial intelligence can enhance accessible tourism experiences for people with disabilities. Building on literature on tourism constraints and the tourism value chain, it first discusses physical, informational, communicative, cognitive, attitudinal, and psychological barriers that shape travel participation. It then evaluates the accessibility roles of virtual reality, augmented reality, extended reality, metaverse environments, robot-supported systems, and AI-based smart tourism platforms across pre-travel planning, on-site experience, remote participation, and post-travel feedback. The chapter argues that these technologies can support destination preview, real-time guidance, multimodal communication, personalization, remote access, and service improvement. evidence_items.summary: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into prosthodontics, with potential applications in prosthesis design, treatment planning, fabrication, implant placement, esthetic assessment, and prediction of prosthodontic outcomes. However, the available evidence is heterogeneous, and the clinical applicability of these technologies remains incompletely established. Objective: This systematic review aimed to evaluate the current evidence regarding the application and performance of artificial intelligence in prosthodontics and to summarize its potential clinical applications, performance characteristics, and limitations. Methods: A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, ScienceDirect, the Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar. Studies evaluating AI-based methods, including machine learning, deep learning, artificial neural networks, convolutional neural networks, generative models, case-based reasoning, and large language models, in a prosthodontic context were eligible. Clinical, experimental, and computational studies with a direct prosthodontic application were considered. Study selection and reporting followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Methodological quality was assessed using study-design–appropriate appraisal approaches. Results: The search identified 3,279 records, of which 475 duplicates were removed. After title and abstract screening, 114 reports were sought for retrieval and 71 were assessed for eligibility. Ultimately, 14 studies published between 2015 and 2026 were included. AI applications encompassed removable partial denture design, complete denture fabrication and treatment planning, crown design and outcome prediction, occlusal surface reconstruction, implant planning and guided surgery, tooth-shade and prosthetic color assessment, and maxillofacial prosthesis coloration.
evidence_items.title: The Effects Artificial Intelligence Applications in Prosthodontics Treatment: A Systematic Review

evidence_items.summary: Abstract A new gyrokinetic code, TEK , was benchmarked in simulating energetic particle (EP) driven toroidal Alfvén eigenmodes (TAEs) in the simple tokamak configuration chosen by the ITPA-EP group for code benchmarking purposes. Linear benchmark has been well established by other codes, whereas nonlinear benchmark for this case is lacking. This paper presents, besides the linear benchmark, nonlinear results for both single- n and multiple- n simulations ( n is the toroidal mode number). The nonlinear results are in good agreement with an analytical theory on zonal field beat-driven by Alfvén eigenmodes, partially verifying the correctness of the nonlinear simulations. The saturation level and the resulting EP transport are examined. This provides data for future inter-code nonlinear benchmarking. In TEK , all species (electrons, thermal ions, EPs) are treated on the same footing using the gyrokinetic model (with electrons in the zero Larmor radius limit). The electromagnetic cancellation problem is mitigated by using the mixed-variable pullback method. Numerical details related to electromagnetic gyrokinetic simulation are discussed.
evidence_items.title: Linear and nonlinear benchmark of gyrokinetic simulation of energetic particle driven toroidal Alfvén eigenmodes in ITPA TAE benchmark case

evidence_items.summary: Background Unsupervised multi-omics workflows can yield stable partitions within one analytical framework while assigning patients differently across frameworks. We benchmarked this distinction in gastric cancer under shared feature identities and matched patient perturbations. Results Five protocol-frozen primary integration tracks were benchmarked in 352 TCGA-STAD primary gastric cancers with matched mRNA, microRNA, copy-number variation, non-silent mutation, and DNA methylation data; a second Cancer Integration via Multikernel Learning (CIMLR) preprocessing scheme was examined post hoc . Patient-dependent scaling, integration, and clustering were refitted in the same 100 prespecified 80% patient perturbations at K = 2–6. K = 2 was the only resolution without a cluster containing &lt;10% of patients in any primary track or perturbation. Mean within-track pairwise adjusted Rand indices ranged from 0.078 to 0.955, whereas mean agreement among primary tracks within the same perturbation was 0.175. K = 3 increased mean cross-track agreement to 0.263 but produced two small-cluster perturbations in primary CIMLR. Thus, no tested K yielded a universally stable discrete patient partition. Reference microsatellite instability (MSI) status was associated with four of five K = 2 primary partitions and all five primary partitions at K = 3. MLH1 promoter methylation and cytolytic activity were associated with four of five K = 2 partitions, whereas six-gene interferon-gamma and 18-gene T-cell-inflamed scores were associated with all five. Within-perturbation feature reselection and related-modality exclusion for principal component analysis (PCA), similarity network fusion (SNF), and non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) retained method dependence and most biological associations, with method-specific exceptions.
evidence_items.title: A fixed-feature perturbation benchmark of unsupervised multi-omics integration in gastric cancer

evidence_items.summary: Shallow groundwater contamination remains a major environmental challenge in urban–agricultural environments, where multiple sources of pollution and natural hydrogeochemical processes contribute to pronounced spatial variability in groundwater quality. This study aimed to characterize the hydrochemical properties, spatial patterns of contamination, and potential pollution sources of shallow groundwater in Kisújszállás, Hungary. Groundwater levels and physicochemical parameters were investigated in 24 residential dug wells in autumn 2026, with complete hydrochemical datasets available for 22 wells. Field and laboratory measurements were assessed using correlation analysis, hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA), principal component analysis (PCA), and GIS-based spatial interpolation and land use assessment. Groundwater elevations ranged from 80.14 to 84.57 m a.s.l., while groundwater depths varied between 0.46 and 5.72 m. Considerable hydrochemical variability was observed, with EC ranging from 367 to 8460 µS/cm, NO3− from 0.131 to 1233.28 mg/L, and Cl− from 22.73 to 2236.39 mg/L. Spatial analysis revealed localized areas of elevated concentrations, particularly in the northeastern and central-southern areas. HCA identified three distinct groundwater groups characterized by contrasting salinity, nutrient enrichment, and redox conditions. The spatial distribution of the HCA-derived clusters showed possible association with land-use categories, with differences between the built-up area, enclosed garden areas, and agricultural surroundings. PCA revealed that the first three components explained 82.38% of the total variance, supporting the identification of distinct hydrochemical patterns. The NO3−/Cl− relationships suggested overlapping influences of domestic wastewater, household gardening, agricultural activities, and natural salinization.
evidence_items.title: Hydrochemical Characteristics and Spatial Patterns of Shallow Groundwater Contamination in a Lowland Settlement in Hungary

evidence_items.summary: Superfund sites are an important public health concern in Texas and may disproportionately affect underserved communities. This exploratory ecological study examined whether county-level Superfund site presence was associated with having a publicly reportable early-onset colorectal cancer (EOCRC) incidence estimate across all 254 Texas counties. Superfund site data were obtained from the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, demographic data from the U.S. Census Bureau, and cancer incidence data from the Texas Cancer Registry for 2018–2022. Because county estimates based on small numbers were suppressed, the outcome distinguished counties with a non-zero, non-suppressed EOCRC estimate from counties with a zero or suppressed estimate; it should not be interpreted as a clinical threshold for elevated incidence. Exposure was represented by the presence and number of Superfund sites in a county. Logistic regression evaluated county-level associations with adjustment for median age, median household income, rurality, and percentage of Black residents. Sixty-eight counties contained at least one Superfund site. A reportable estimate was available for 38 of 68 counties with a site (55.9%) and 25 of 186 counties without a site (13.4%). In the primary adjusted models, site presence (OR = 4.19, 95% CI: 1.66–10.60) and each additional site (OR = 2.76, 95% CI: 1.51–5.04) were associated with higher odds of a reportable estimate. However, after additional adjustment for log-transformed county population, the associations attenuated to the null for site presence (OR = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.02–3.19) and site count (OR = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.31–2.14), and residual spatial autocorrelation was no longer detected. The primary associations therefore appear largely attributable to the concentration of both Superfund sites and reportable cancer counts in populous urban counties.
evidence_items.title: Environmental Contamination and Early-Onset Colorectal Cancer: A Statewide Ecological Analysis of Superfund Sites in Texas

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Students miss deadlines because the information about tasks is spread out across email, the learning management system (LMS) and the institutional ERP and there is no tool that checks the information against the time a student actually has. This paper introduces CollegeOS, an agentic planning framework that senses academic tasks, ranks them with a four-signal priority score, packs a day-by-day study schedule into a capacity model reduced by the student’s real class timetable, and repairs the plan when conditions change. The framework is by construction constraint-safe: a deterministic scheduler enforces deadlines and daily capacity as hard constraints, while an optional large language model (LLM) can only provide bounded priority boosts and can never change feasibility. The connector for the NorthCap University ERP provides the attendance and timetables, which feed the capacity model and attendance-aware boosts. We evaluate the system against an earliest-deadline-first (EDF) baseline over 40 simulated semesters. Repair-mode replanning reduces mean plan churn from 0.899 to 0.813 (the 95% confidence intervals do not overlap), while on-time completion (50.2% vs. 51.0%) is indistinguishable from the baseline in the saturated workload regime tested. We report these results openly, along with a weight ablation and the known limitations, and identify a feasibility-aware scheduler as the next step.
evidence_items.title: A Constraint-Safe Agentic Framework for Academic Task Planning Using ERP-Aware Capacity Modelling

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents an agentic artificial intelligence framework that detects, diagnoses and resolves hold transactions, which are stuck or failed transactions, in integrated hospital pharmacy environments. Large health systems often run order entry, medication processing, billing, stock and inventory, laboratory, blood bank and automated dispensing software from different vendors, and holds arise at the interfaces where no single vendor sees the whole transaction. Analysts resolve holds manually today, so backlogs build up and stock records drift from physical reality. The research problem is how to automate the repetitive part of this work without weakening audit, inventory accuracy or patient safety. Using a design science approach, the paper develops a taxonomy of five hold causes, a five agent architecture based on a monitor, analyze, plan, execute and knowledge control loop, a tiered autonomy policy with approval gated reprocessing, and an artificial intelligence governance model. A 30 day simulation with 20 replications and a sensitivity analysis evaluate the design. Under stated assumptions, about 82 percent of holds are resolved automatically and mean handling time falls from about 43 to 11 minutes, but the human escalation queue stays bounded only above a break even of about 80 percent automatic resolution. The work indicates that governed agentic automation is a promising option for multivendor hospital pharmacy operations, provided that automatic resolution and false fix rates are confirmed through the staged pilot protocol proposed here.
evidence_items.title: Agentic AI for Autonomous Detection and Resolution of Hold Transactions in Integrated Multi-Vendor Hospital Pharmacy Systems

evidence_items.summary: We release DictaRashi, a Tesseract OCR model for scanned Hebrew books printed in the so-called "Rashi" font. We trained DictaRashi on over one million manually corrected lines of text from over 100 different books of Rabbinic and post-Rabbinic literature. On a held-out set of 1,120 manually transcribed lines from scanned Rashi-script pages, DictaRashi reaches a character error rate (CER) of 0.86% and a word error rate (WER) of 3.38%, setting a new state-of-the-art for publicly-available Tesseract models. We provide a full comparison of our results to those of the 31 other publicly available Hebrew Tesseract models; the best of those models achieves a 2.98% CER and 11.86% WER. We further demonstrate that DictaRashi outperforms the current frontier LLMs on this OCR task. We release the test set of Rashi-script documents so that it may be used as a benchmark for future work in this area. We are pleased to release the model and test set to the community under a CC BY NC 4.0 license.
evidence_items.title: DictaRashi: A State-of-the-Art OCR Model For Rashi Script

evidence_items.summary: Decision models score candidate answers in a single forward pass, but the intermediate reasoning that improves decision quality adds latency. We introduce GLiDE, a family of decision models from 0.4B to 27B parameters that distills reasoning into single-pass inference. Building on Qwen's hybrid architecture, GLiDE removes causal masking from full-attention layers so that context, question and candidate answers interact bidirectionally. It is trained with soft-target distillation from multiple teachers, including a reasoning model, and progressive post-training on diverse decision tasks. On the Hugging Face Decision Index, each of the five GLiDE models outscores every alternative of equal or smaller size. GLiDE V1.2 (27B) ranks first on edition 0.4.1 (22 October 2026) with a hidden-set score of 71.52, 2.0% calibration error and 92.9 ms median latency on one GPU, and shares first place on all three versions of the Artificial Analysis Decision Index. Both leaderboards are run by their maintainers on closed test sets. With checkpoint averaging and recurrent depth, GLiDE 27B reaches 73.37.
evidence_items.title: GLiDE: A Fast, Calibrated Decision Model Distilled from Reasoning Teachers

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a robot-control interface, while the Reflector converts execution evidence into reusable operational guidance. Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution context and long-term experiential knowledge to support execution and reflection. Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement refines operational guidance across successive attempts. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness in generalization under environmental variations, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation. Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks, respectively. Real-world evaluation further yields an average success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks. These results highlight the potential of Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation through experience-driven harness self-improvement.
evidence_items.title: Embodied-Harness: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Robotic Manipulation
