evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in world models are opening new possibilities for fine-grained embodied tasks, with hand-object interaction offering a particularly demanding setting. Modeling these interactions involves capturing how hand actions change objects and how the resulting states persist over time. Yet systematic evaluation tailored to these hand-centric capabilities remains underdeveloped. To address this gap, we introduce HandWorldBench, a unified benchmark that systematically evaluates hand-centric world models across human hands, simulated dexterous hands, and real dexterous hands along six dimensions: visual quality, hand fidelity, appearance consistency, instruction following, physical consistency, and temporal coherence. To construct the benchmark, we develop a data curation pipeline that extracts hand-object interaction clips and screens them for quality, yielding 20,500 high-quality egocentric clips from over 600 hours of footage. We then manually select 500 clips covering seven task families for evaluation. Benchmarking eleven models under a unified protocol reveals that stronger hand-pose control does not consistently translate into coherent object-state evolution and persistence or robust cross-embodiment performance, with several specialized hand-control models underperforming general-purpose text/image-to-video generators on dexterous-hand tasks.
evidence_items.title: HandWorldBench: A Unified Benchmark for Hand-Centric World Models

evidence_items.summary: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems in Persian law remains challenging because benchmarks lack realism, grounding, and coverage of legal reasoning. Existing resources are either synthetically generated from statutory texts, lacking natural information needs, or derived from informal legal question--answer sources without explicit linkage to authoritative legal documents, making them unsuitable for rigorous evaluation of grounded legal reasoning. To address this gap, we introduce TUSI-Bench, a structured Persian legal benchmark designed for the evaluation of RAG-based systems. TUSI-Bench is built upon a multi-layered legal knowledge framework containing 7,261 legal articles and integrating codified statutes, legal commentaries, doctrinal writings, and Supreme Court unification rulings. We also construct a legal knowledge graph linking articles and concepts for structure-aware retrieval. Based on this foundation, TUSI-Bench provides two complementary evaluation tasks: (i) TUSI-QA, an open-ended question answering benchmark containing 1,999 questions that requires grounded responses with explicit legal citations, and (ii) TUSI-Bar, a multiple-choice benchmark containing approximately 500 four-option questions derived from Iranian Bar examination questions. Furthermore, we propose a graph-based retrieval baseline that leverages relational structure within the legal knowledge graph. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating graph-based relations improves retrieval recall by up to 8 percentage points compared to standard baselines, highlighting the importance of structured legal representations for RAG systems. The proposed benchmark provides a standardized resource for evaluating grounded legal reasoning in Persian and enables future research on structured legal intelligence.
evidence_items.title: TUSI: A Citation-Grounded Graph-Based Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Persian Legal Question Answering

evidence_items.summary: Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) adapts a model trained on a labelled source domain to an unlabelled target domain without access to the source data. Almost the entire SFDA literature assumes mutually exclusive classes, yet many deployed settings are multi-label. This paper formulates SFDA for multi-label classification and establishes the first benchmark for it: five adaptation tasks over six datasets spanning remote sensing, natural, clipart-style and driving imagery, with four single-label SFDA methods extended to provide the first baselines and a published multi-label method run alongside them, over three seeds. The benchmark shows that extending a single-label method is unreliable rather than merely suboptimal: half of the extended baselines fail to improve on the unadapted source model at all, and on two of the five tasks none of them does. The failures are not incidental. Nearest-centroid pseudo-labelling, softmax-based confidence, the diversity term of information maximization and confidence-weighted prototype construction each rely on mutual exclusivity, and each fails differently without it, so replacing the softmax with per-class sigmoids is a valid but insufficient extension. Multi-label Prototype Alignment with Contrastive Teaching (MPACT) is proposed in response, a mean-teacher framework whose objective, prototype construction and alignment term are each reconsidered for overlapping label sets. It attains the best average on every reported metric and is the only method that improves on the unadapted source model on all five tasks. The analysis further introduces a prototype-agreement diagnostic separating feature-space alignment from self-reinforcing agreement with the classifier, and reports a negative result for confidence-based pseudo-label filtering.
evidence_items.title: Source-Free Domain Adaptation for Multi-Label Image Classification: A Framework, Baselines, and Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: 3D visual grounding (3DVG) localizes language-referred objects in 3D scenes, with broad applicability in both indoor and outdoor environments. However, existing 3DVG research focuses on static indoor objects, limiting its use in dynamic outdoor autonomous driving. Motion descriptions, which capture the temporal dynamics of moving objects, offer a promising way to address this challenge. We therefore introduce MoT3DVG, a large-scale dataset for dynamic-aware outdoor 3DVG with temporally evolving motion descriptions. It contains 850 scenarios with 31,128 frames from nuScenes dataset, and provides 144,568 language prompts with motion-aware descriptions for dynamic objects across time. We further propose DynaVG, a novel framework that effectively leverages temporal cues for outdoor 3DVG. In addition to the standard modality-specific encoders, DynaVG introduces a Short-Long Integrated Dynamic Encoding (SLIDE) module before the language-point cloud alignment. SLIDE models both local motion cues and global temporal context via short-term window encoding and long-term window shifting. Extensive experiments demonstrate its state-of-the-art performance on MoT3DVG, validating the effectiveness of motion-aware encoding. Our work reveals open challenges and promising directions for future research in outdoor 3DVG.
evidence_items.title: MoT3DVG: A Benchmark for Outdoor 3D Visual Grounding with Motion-Aware Descriptions and Temporal Cues

evidence_items.summary: Deploying generative world models for end-to-end closed-loop evaluation and policy learning requires precise scenario control, consistent observations, and sustained generation quality during extended interactions. This report presents X-World 1.6, advancing X-World 1.0 toward a more reliable and versatile driving simulator. The upgraded base model offers finer-grained control over traffic semantics, including traffic lights and road markings, together with improved spatial consistency across cameras. Virtual City capabilities broaden scenario construction through a family of models conditioned on diverse 2D and 3D references, including support for generating multi-camera future videos from a single image. An enhanced post-training framework enables efficient causal, few-step generation with stronger temporal coherence, better quality retention over longer rollouts, and improved alignment with human preferences. We also introduce a dedicated evaluation suite to support systematic assessment and guide model iteration. Together, these upgrades expand the scenarios X-World can simulate and improve the efficiency and reliability of its generated observations, supporting broader use in autonomous-driving development.
evidence_items.title: X-World 1.6: Building Controllable Virtual Cities with World Models

evidence_items.summary: Counterfactual reasoning requires models to reason beyond the observed world and explain how altered conditions propagate through downstream consequences. Existing benchmarks largely target bounded settings with fixed variables or single gold outcomes, overlooking open-domain scenarios requiring causal-process evaluation. To this end, we present $\textbf{WhatIfBench}$, a diagnostic benchmark for open-domain, open-form, long-horizon counterfactual causal reasoning, containing 220 what-if questions across STEM, HSS, and Hybrid scenarios. To evaluate free-form responses, we further propose $\textbf{PRISM}$, which first converts each natural-language explanation into a Response-Derived Semantic Causal Graph of events, states, and mechanisms. On top of this graph, PRISM then jointly applies a Process Metric assessing graph-level causal validity and a Rubric Metric assessing answer-level explanatory adequacy. Evaluating six frontier LLMs with this framework, we find that WhatIfBench remains far from saturated: even the strongest model reaches only a 64.62% final score. Further analysis reveals persistent causal gaps, premise drift, and topology fragmentation, suggesting that fluent counterfactual narratives often mask fragile causal processes. The benchmark, code, and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/zju-gt/WhatIfBench.
evidence_items.title: The Illusion of What If: Evaluating the Breakdown of Counterfactual Reasoning in LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Audiovisual arts encompass diverse creative disciplines, including cinema, visual arts, stage performance, and game design, where artistic meaning arises from deliberate combinations of visual, auditory, and narrative elements (e.g., fear amplified through claustrophobic framing, or grief conveyed through silence and lingering close-ups). Artistic understanding extends beyond recognizing what is depicted to reasoning about why it is expressed through particular creative choices. Despite progress in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), reasoning about artistic intent remains underexplored, as existing benchmarks largely measure perceptual recognition. To address this gap, we introduce MuseBench, a benchmark for evaluating intent-level artistic understanding in MLLMs. It comprises 4,016 questions derived from video essays spanning cinematic arts, static visual arts, stage performing arts, and game arts. To capture the open-ended nature of artistic analysis at scale, the benchmark combines single-select and variable-option multi-select questions. All questions are generated and refined through a four-phase iterative pipeline combining shortcut filtering, adversarial distractors, and expert validation. We evaluate 34 MLLM versions using either video and audio transcripts (V+T) or video, native audio, and text (V+A+T). The highest observed accuracy is 64.62% (V+A+T), trailing the 87.18% human expert baseline. Further analysis reveals that native-audio models score lowest on game arts, models often recover partial interpretations but struggle to identify complete correct option sets on multi-select items, and adaptive frame-selection models trail the strongest video-specific model. These results identify artistic knowledge and complete interpretation as challenges for audiovisual models.
evidence_items.title: MuseBench: Benchmarking Intent-Level Audiovisual Arts Understanding in MLLMs

evidence_items.summary: Code RL rewards a policy for passing a task's tests, so a test suite that accepts a wrong patch trains the wrong behavior. We measure how often open code RL environments accept wrong patches and how reliably hackable tasks can be detected and repaired, checking each claim by execution against the task's gold patch. First, 22.4% of 49 SWE-bench Verified tasks accept a Docker-verified patch that behaves differently from the gold patch, and 57.8% against a stronger attacker. The gold-patch check is necessary: an attacker not shown the gold patch returns it for 31% of its passing "exploits". Second, across 134 public SWE-bench submissions, models pass hackable tasks 28.6 pp more often than tasks of the same difficulty, mostly because those tasks are passable at all; pooled over three attacker runs, hackable tasks still exceed matched passable ones (p=0.014). Third, repair is harder to verify than detection: 61.9% of LLM-written repair tests fail on the gold patch, and even behind a gate an LLM judge is wrong on 38% of the verdicts execution can check. Finally, of 873 training trajectories behind an open coding agent run beside the gold fix, 19.4% answer differently on a case the issue describes; an LLM review that can only demote these executed differences judges 6.9% to be wrong fixes the tests rewarded (6.4-10.5% across three model reviews), and 5.4% in a second public training set (R2E-Gym). End to end, the gated repair yields verified tests for 290 of 324 wrong fixes in that agent's data and all 9 in 384 rewarded Open-SWE-Traces rollouts (2.3%). One-shot attacks hack 23 of 100 SWE-bench Pro V2 and 9 of 112 DeepSWE tasks; 12 of 1,344 passing DeepSWE leaderboard patches are model-judged wrong. Science graders mostly hold: an agentic red team passes 0 of 61 Terminal-Bench-Science tasks. Audits and repairs of code RL environments should be decided by execution wherever execution can decide.
evidence_items.title: Auditing Reward Hackability in Code RL Training Environments

evidence_items.summary: Personalized image generation should compose several people, each with the right objects and outfits, in a specified scene, yet current generators collapse as references are added and existing benchmarks do not capture this degradation. We introduce CogCanvas, a benchmark of 1,361 compositional prompts with 2--5 subjects, 1,952 curated references (100 people, 115 objects and fashion items, 29 scenes), and graphs specifying interactions and spatial relations. It adds two metrics: BG-Sim for background fidelity outside foreground regions, and Attr-VQA for person--item binding, with 76.5% agreement with human majority judgments. We also propose Context2Canvas, a training-free multi-agent framework built on a verify-then-route principle: agents verify a layout against a hierarchical scene graph, and its masks then route each reference to its own region in a two-phase renderer that grounds references independently before refining them jointly. Context2Canvas achieves 2.5x the attribute-binding score of the strongest published baseline, with larger gains as the subject count increases. Project page: https://longbaocoder2.github.io/cogcanvas
evidence_items.title: From Context to Canvas: Benchmark Dataset and Verify-then-Route Framework for Multi-Subject Reference-Based Image Generation

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as self-study assistants in technical disciplines, yet their reliability as mathematical reasoning assistants remains poorly understood. We introduce GTBench, a curriculum-grounded benchmark for evaluating LLMs as mathematical research assistants in graph theory, comprising 63 problems organized into three groups of increasing difficulty: undergraduate definitions and basic properties (Group 1), algorithm tracing and structural reasoning (Group 2), and graduate-level proof construction (Group 3). Problems are sourced from verified academic materials including Diestel's Graph Theory. We evaluate five frontier models -- GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, Llama 3.3 70B, and Mistral Large 3 -- under zero-shot and chain-of-thought prompting, using exact-match and LLM-as-judge evaluation for Groups 1 and 2, and a hybrid human expert and LLM-as-judge protocol for Group 3. Our results reveal a pronounced performance hierarchy: GPT-5 approaches ceiling on Group 1 (95.8% zero-shot) and maintains meaningful accuracy on graduate proofs (82%), while all other models degrade substantially with difficulty, with Llama achieving 0% under human evaluation on Group 3 zero-shot. Failure mode analysis shows that correct algorithm, wrong execution errors dominate Groups 1 and 2, while Group 3 additionally surfaces incomplete reasoning failures and reveals systematic disagreement between human evaluators and the automated judge, particularly on verbose or near-complete proofs (kappa = 0.48-0.83 across human pairs). GTBench provides the first curriculum-grounded evaluation framework for graph-theoretic reasoning in LLMs, with direct implications for the governance of AI tools in mathematical education and scientific research.
evidence_items.title: GTBench: A Curriculum-Grounded Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs as Mathematical Research Assistants in Graph Theory

evidence_items.summary: With the rapid proliferation of image generative models, the authenticity of digital images has become a significant concern. While existing studies have proposed various methods for detecting AI-generated content, current benchmarks are limited in their coverage of diverse generative models and image categories, often overlooking end-to-end image editing and artistic images. To address these limitations, we introduce UniAIDet, a unified and comprehensive benchmark that includes both photographic and artistic images. UniAIDet covers a wide range of generative models, including text-to-image, image-to-image, image inpainting, image editing, and deepfake models. Using UniAIDet, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of various detection methods and answer three key research questions regarding generalization capability and the relation between detection and localization. Our benchmark and analysis provide a robust foundation for future research.
evidence_items.title: UniAIDet: A Unified and Universal Benchmark for AI-Generated Image Content Detection and Localization

evidence_items.summary: Logical reasoning is a critical component of Large Language Models (LLMs), and substantial research efforts in recent years have aimed to enhance their deductive reasoning abilities. However, existing deductive reasoning benchmarks suffer from significant constraints that restrict their utility, i.e., the lack of task complexity, the presence of prior knowledge as a confounder, and superficial error analysis. To address these deficiencies, we introduce JustLogic, a synthetically generated benchmark for evaluating deduction in propositional logic. Within this fragment, JustLogic is (i) complex, capable of generating a diverse range of linguistic patterns, vocabulary, and argument structures, (ii) prior knowledge independent, substantially reducing the advantage of models possessing prior knowledge so that questions are answerable from the given premises alone, and (iii) capable of in-depth error analysis on the heterogeneous effects of proof size and argument form on model accuracy. Our experimental results on JustLogic reveal that (i) several state-of-the-art (SOTA) reasoning LLMs score above the human average on JustLogic, although only DeepSeek R1's margin is significant on the matched items after correction for multiple comparisons, and (ii) the evaluated non-reasoning models score below the human average. Given the small human study (18 participants, seven questions each), these comparisons are indicative. All code and data are available at https://github.com/michaelchen-lab/JustLogic
evidence_items.title: JustLogic: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Deductive Reasoning in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains the phenotypic, pedigree and genotypic data used in the genome-wide association study "Multi-model genome-wide association analysis identifies drought-responsive QTL for spike traits in bread wheat" (BMC Genomics). Phenotypic data: Best linear unbiased estimates (BLUEs) of 13 agronomic traits for 181 spring bread wheat ( Triticum aestivum L.) genotypes, obtained from field trials at Bahawalpur, Pakistan, over three seasons (2021–22 to 2023–24) in a split-split-plot design. For each trait, BLUEs are given under well-watered (WW) and water-limited (WL) conditions, together with a drought-tolerance index (DT), so each trait has three columns. Pedigree data: Pedigree, cultivar type and release year for each genotype, with IDs matching the phenotypic data file. Genotypic data: A filtered set of 16,751 SNPs (HapMap format) for the same 181 genotypes that have phenotypic data. It was extracted from the publicly available 16K GBTS fingerprinting dataset of historical wheat cultivars of Pakistan (37,401 SNPs; https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.xwdbrv1kb ). SNPs were filtered for missing data, minor allele frequency and heterozygosity, and only cultivars with phenotypic data were retained. We gratefully acknowledge Awais Rasheed (Department of Plant Sciences, Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad, Pakistan) for providing the germplasm used in this study and the original genotypic data and for making them publicly available.
evidence_items.title: Phenotypic BLUEs, pedigree and filtered SNP genotypes of 181 bread wheat genotypes for GWAS of drought-responsive spike traits (2021–2024)

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Despite the rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) in data-intensive disciplines, archaeology lacks public, large-scale benchmarks, and its spatio-temporally fragmented knowledge resists integration into model parameters. Here we introduce ArchaeoBench, a hierarchically structured benchmark built from 63 official excavation reports across 20 Chinese provinces, comprising over 9.2 million training question-answer pairs and 1,698 evaluation questions spanning multiple cognitive levels. Fine-tuning seven open-source LLMs on this benchmark yields substantial gains, approaching commercial baselines on several question types, whereas chain-of-thought prompting brings only marginal improvements on fact- and text-grounded questions, suggesting that archaeological question answering is constrained primarily by access to reliable domain knowledge rather than reasoning depth. Motivated by this finding, we propose a knowledge-graph-based retrieval-augmented generation framework that injects curated structured evidence to enhance spatio-temporal and cultural-linkage reasoning. ArchaeoBench converts excavation reports into reusable, machine-readable knowledge infrastructure for the discipline.
evidence_items.title: ArchaeoBench: a large-scale archaeological question-answering benchmark for large language models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) attain high accuracy on medical examinations, yet evaluations rely predominantly on single-best-answer multiple-choice questions and report only overall accuracy. Multiple-response items, termed X-type in China, require selecting every correct option and remain understudied. Whether models err by omitting correct options or by commissioning incorrect ones has yet to be assessed within an opportunity-standardized framework. Objective This study aimed to quantify the accuracy penalty of multiple-response (X-type) items relative to single-select items and to determine, after standardizing for the unequal numbers of correct and incorrect options, whether LLMs lean toward omission or commission. Methods We analyzed 1644 text-based items from 10 examination cohorts (2017‐2026) of the Chinese National Postgraduate Entrance Examination in Clinical Medicine, comprising 1344 single-select items of types A1, A2, A3, and B, and 300 X-type items. Five LLMs, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, Doubao Seed-2.1-pro, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Gemini-3.6 Flash, were tested zero-shot bilingually, yielding 16,440 planned responses. Item-type effects were estimated using generalized estimating equations with cluster-robust standard errors, adjusting for model, language, discipline, and cohort. Opportunity-standardized error direction was analyzed 2 ways: an option-level model treating each option as 1 judgment record and the omission-bias index. Results Of 16,440 planned responses, 16,426 (99.91%) were evaluable. X-type accuracy (2527/3000, 84.23%) was markedly below single-select accuracy (12,990/13,426, 96.75%; adjusted odds ratio at GPT-5.6 Sol in Chinese 0.17, 95% CI 0.11‐0.26; P <.001), a gap of 12.52 percentage points observed and 13.55 adjusted, with no statistically significant item type × model or item type × language interaction ( P =.19 and P =.82).
evidence_items.title: Error Direction of Large Language Models on Medical Multiple-Response Questions: Opportunity-Standardized Benchmark Study

evidence_items.summary: Domain ontology construction from unstructured text is a core knowledge-engineering task, and large language models (LLMs) offer a practical route to automating concept and relation extraction. Evidence on how reliably LLMs extract hierarchical and semantic relations under different prompting strategies remains limited for resource-poor, rapidly evolving domains. This study presents a gold-standard benchmark for LLM-based concept and relation extraction and a scripted pipeline that assembles a logically consistent Web Ontology Language (OWL) ontology. Using 19 Chinese university artificial intelligence (AI) course syllabi as a case study, we built a benchmark of 131 concepts and 75 relations of four types through two-author double-blind screening with adjudication (Cohen's κ = 0.707) and an independent blinded audit by two external reviewers (item-level agreement 42/50 and 43/50). Three Chinese LLMs were evaluated under one-shot and decomposed prompting across 114 configurations. On 14 held-out documents, macro concept F1 was 0.42–0.48 (0.51–0.60 on the development set), with a stable Core > Common > Peripheral gradient. Relation extraction was markedly weaker, constrained by concept-granularity mismatch and, among matched predictions, dominated by is-a/prerequisite type confusion. The assembled ontology passes HermiT satisfiability checking and supports downstream knowledge-graph diagnosis. The benchmark, prompts, ontology, and scripts are publicly released.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models for Concept and Relation Extraction in Ontology Construction: A Benchmark on Chinese Domain-Specific Text

organizations: University of Cincinnati College of Medicine

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Diagnostic benchmarks can reward recognition of a disease family without requiring the specificity of the final diagnosis. We evaluated the separation between broad diagnostic concordance and strict diagnostic correctness in a retrieval augmented language model. Methods This retrospective benchmark evaluated MediDx AI, which couples Claude Sonnet 4.6 with retrieval from seven biomedical sources without fine-tuning, on presentation-only text from 100 consecutive published Massachusetts General Hospital Case Records, issued from 26 October 2023 to 11 June 2026. Published expert discussions, final diagnoses, source tables and images were withheld. Five ranked suggestions were adjudicated under broad concordance and strict correct, partial or incorrect scoring. Case-level proportions and Wilson 95% confidence intervals were calculated. A separate evaluation used 1,273 medical multiple-choice questions, counting unanswered questions as incorrect. Results Broad top-ranked concordance was 71% (95% confidence interval 61.5–79.0%), whereas 53% (43.3–62.5%) of top-ranked diagnoses were strictly correct; 19% were partial and 28% incorrect. Within five suggestions, broad concordance was 88% and strict correctness was 63%. The 18 broadly concordant but partial top-ranked diagnoses accounted for the difference between the two top-ranked outcomes. Failures included missed causative organisms, rare neoplasms and structural conditions; partial responses often omitted an underlying mechanism or a component of a multicomponent diagnosis. Medical question-answering accuracy was 86.5% across all submitted questions, compared with 92.0% among parseable responses; response coverage was 94.0%. Conclusions Broad diagnostic concordance and strict diagnostic correctness describe different aspects of performance. Reporting both, alongside ranked inclusion and response completion, exposes information concealed by aggregate accuracy.
evidence_items.title: Diagnostic specificity of a retrieval augmented language model on complex clinical cases: a retrospective benchmark study

evidence_items.summary: Background: Researchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to assess risk of bias in randomized trials, but how task-specific fine-tuned models compare with frontier models remains uncertain. Objective: To develop RoB-BERT, a fine-tuned RoB 2 assessment system, and to compare its agreement with human assessments against that of three frontier LLMs. Methods: RoB 2 rates five bias domains and the trial overall as low risk, some concerns or high risk, based on answers to 22 signalling questions. RoB-BERT answers each question, quotes the supporting sentences from the trial report, and applies the official RoB 2 algorithm. We trained RoB-BERT on 5,304 reviewer-checked assessments, none from a test trial, and compared it with Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Argon, each given identical prompts and text, against 419 published human assessments (ROBoto2, LogiMed-RoB and Cochrane reviews) made without AI assistance. Each reference was the single published judgement for that trial, made by one assessor or agreed by two, rather than an expert reference standard, so we also report agreement between two human assessors of the same trial. Results: In ROBoto2, pairs of human assessors who rated the same trial agreed on 61.2% to 64.7% of domain judgements (κ 0.15 to 0.35) and 46.2% to 50.0% of overall judgements (κ 0.15 to 0.17); across the 185 ROBoto2 trials, RoB-BERT agreed with the human judgement on 67.4% (κ 0.35) and 53.5% (κ 0.20). Across all 419 assessments, domain agreement was 67.9% (κ 0.29) for RoB-BERT, 65.0% (κ 0.24) for Claude Fable 5.1, 52.7% (κ 0.21) for GPT-6 Astra and 66.7% (κ 0.26) for Gemini 4 Argon; overall agreement was 46.1% (κ 0.16), 47.3% (κ 0.17), 31.0% (κ 0.03) and 46.5% (κ 0.14), respectively. For domains the reference rated high risk, sensitivity was 22.2% for RoB-BERT, 23.1% for Claude Fable 5.1, 41.9% for GPT-6 Astra and 24.8% for Gemini 4 Argon, with specificity of 92.5%, 92.8%, 80.0% and 95.0%.
evidence_items.title: Task-specific fine-tuning versus frontier large language models for RoB 2 risk of bias assessment: development and external benchmark evaluation of RoB-BERT

evidence_items.summary: Style words such as delve, intricate and meticulous became several times more frequent in English research abstracts after large language models became public. Publicly named as evidence of machine-assisted writing, they have since turned down as a set. The prevailing explanation, deliberate avoidance, predicts that the words named most widely receded furthest, a prediction tested here on every eligible PubMed abstract entered from January 2018 to June 2026 (N = 10,767,846). Thirty such words were compared by segmented regression against two control sets from the same corpus: comparably frequent words that never rose, and emphatic markers from a published metadiscourse inventory. Lexical density, nominalisation, passive voice and hedging were also measured. How widely each word had been named was scored beforehand across fourteen independent inventories. Twenty-nine of the thirty turned down and neither control set did, ruling out corpus drift and a general cooling of evaluative prose. Public naming did not predict the decline to the extent the awareness account requires: a word&rsquo;s earlier rise predicted its fall, naming added nothing with that rise held constant, and the steepest decliners include words on no inventory. The structural features did not turn back. The test is powered to detect an association of the size that account requires, not a weak one, which cannot be excluded. Model turnover or heavier editing of output fits the pattern better than selective avoidance; these data cannot separate them. The visible lexical signal of machine-assisted writing is weakening; the impersonal texture of the prose is not.
evidence_items.title: Delving into Decline: The Rise and Fall of Large Language Model Vocabulary in Biomedical Abstracts, 2018–2026

evidence_items.summary: Background Wet age-related macular degeneration (AMD) requires long-term, high-frequency management involving multimodal retinal imaging across repeated follow-up visits. Reconstructing disease trajectories from fragmented imaging reports, treatment histories, and clinical notes creates a substantial information integration burden for clinicians in routine chronic disease management. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the preliminary feasibility of a proof-of-concept, multiagent large language model (LLM) framework that integrates longitudinal multimodal imaging findings and treatment records into structured reports to support clinician review during wet AMD follow-up. Methods We developed a 3-layer multiagent LLM framework using GPT-4o and AutoGen. The framework consisted of modality-specific perception agents using a visual grounding prompting strategy, an integration agent, and a tracking report agent. To test technical feasibility, the framework was evaluated on a dense retrospective pilot dataset of 12 patients encompassing 69 long-term follow-up visits. AI-generated outputs were assessed against expert review at the visit level and through report-level quality scoring. Results In this exploratory cohort, the framework achieved a mean visit-level activity classification accuracy of 80.8% (SD 3.4%) across 4 independent runs (range 78.3%-85.5%), with a mean Cohen κ of 0.605 (SD 0.072; range 0.549-0.705). The framework generated structured longitudinal summaries of disease activity, multimodal findings, and treatment histories. The visual grounding prompting strategy reduced the nonimage reference rate from 13.8% (12/87) to 1.1% (1/87), supporting more consistent grounding of image-based outputs in visual evidence. Conclusions This proof-of-concept study supports the preliminary feasibility of using a multiagent LLM framework to organize longitudinal multimodal wet AMD follow-up data and produce structured summaries for clinician review.
evidence_items.title: A Multiagent Large Language Model Framework for Longitudinal Multimodal Tracking of Wet Age-Related Macular Degeneration: Retrospective Feasibility Study

evidence_items.summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the most transformative technologies in modern medicine. Its influence is especially visible in clinical areas that generate high-volume digital data, including imaging, electrocardiography, pathology, patient monitoring, and electronic health records. As these data sources continue to expand, AI is increasingly moving from a theoretical innovation to a practical set of clinical tools that can support diagnosis, triage, documentation, workflow coordination, and patient communication when carefully validated, integrated, and monitored. This chapter examines real-world and emerging applications of machine learning algorithms, deep learning models, and generative AI across hospital medicine, radiology, pathology, oncology, cardiology, nursing, emergency medical services, administrative workflows, and patient portals. Furthermore, we distinguish between AI applications already cleared or deployed in routine clinical settings, applications undergoing prospective or quality-improvement evaluation, and more speculative future use cases. The chapter also addresses critical implementation barriers, including explainability, interoperability, external validation, dataset shift, calibration, fairness across demographic groups, privacy and cybersecurity, hallucination and automation bias in generative AI, and post-deployment monitoring. By evaluating both current deployments and unresolved risks, this chapter outlines a practical “human-in-the-loop” model in which AI serves as a supervised clinical partner rather than a replacement for professional judgment.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Practice

organizations: Guangdong University of Technology
evidence_items.summary: Abstract The concentration of artificial intelligence (AI) firms may accompany local green patent activity without indicating a greener innovation portfolio or providing useful information about subsequent outcomes. This study evaluates these distinctions using a panel of 295 Chinese cities over 2013–2024. Spatial Durbin estimates combine a positive baseline direct effect of 0.139 with an indirect effect of − 5.901; the latter is sensitive to patent definition and spatial weights. Within-city regressions do not establish a positive green-share association or a difference between green and nongreen patent responses. An expanding-window exercise then predicts outcomes one year ahead using only lagged indicators and benchmarks AI against prior patent performance, total patenting and economic conditions. Across 2020–2024, adding AI reduces the pooled RMSE for green invention applications by 1.43%, with a city-block bootstrap interval of 0.33–2.64%, but increases RMSE for all green applications by 2.95%. The green-share improvement is small and its interval includes zero. These results distinguish spatial association from environmental orientation and forward predictive information. They support an outcome-dependent assessment of AI enterprise counts as an innovation indicator, while providing no evidence of a causal policy effect or a general redirection toward green technologies.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Firm Concentration and Urban Green Innovation

organizations: Tongji University
evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has advanced font generation toward greater diversity, personali-zation, and automation. However, assessing generated fonts remains challenging because quality depends on character identity, glyph structure, style, readability, and aesthetic preference. This structured narrative review synthesizes literature on font generation and quality assessment using four categories: traditional image-quality metrics; character correctness and structural assessment; style, readability, and aesthetic assessment; and multimodal or large-model-based evaluation. The review distinguishes direct typogra-phy-related evidence from methods transferred from general image-quality and multimodal research. Across the literature examined, pixel-level and distribution-level metrics remain useful baselines but cannot alone establish character correctness or typographic suitability. Structure-aware methods and hu-man-centred assessment address complementary dimensions, while vision-language and large-model ap-proaches remain promising but require task-specific validation. The review proposes an integrative gener-ation–evaluation–diagnosis–optimization framework and identifies priorities for transparent benchmarks, interpretable sub-scores, multilingual testing, and reproducible human evaluation.
evidence_items.title: From Generation to Evaluation: A Review of Quality Assessment Methods and Development Trends for Artificial Intelligence-Generated Fonts

organizations: Division of Facial Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, Department of Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery, Stanford University School of Medicine, Stanford, California, USA.
evidence_items.summary: Importance: Rhinoplasty requires individualized decisions that balance nasal appearance, airway function, structural support, and patient expectations. This narrative review examines artificial intelligence (AI) applications across the data modalities encountered in rhinoplasty care, emphasizing their potential roles in assessment, counseling, surgical planning, and outcome evaluation. Observations: Relevant modalities include clinical text, structured clinical data, facial photographs, anatomical imaging and three-dimensional surface geometry, and specialized measurements of surgical technique, nasal function, and visual perception. Clinical applications include patient counseling, organization of clinical records, risk and outcome prediction, quantitative nasal assessment, visualization of proposed changes, and postoperative evaluation. Multimodal and agentic systems may integrate these sources and tasks. Limitations include measurement errors, uncertain prediction of surgical outcomes, and limited evidence of improved clinical decisions or patient outcomes. Conclusions and Relevance: Matching clinical questions to available data provides a practical framework for AI research and application in rhinoplasty. Standardized acquisition, secure linkage of longitudinal records, and independent validation are needed to support reproducible assessment and outcomes research. Surgeon oversight remains essential, with clinical value judged by functional and aesthetic outcomes and alignment with patient goals.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Series: Data Modalities and Clinical Applications in Rhinoplasty

organizations: University of Science and Technology Beijing
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Cerebrovascular diseases remain a major cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) provides high-spatiotemporal-resolution visualization of cerebrovascular anatomy and contrast-agent dynamics and plays an important role in diagnosis, interventional treatment planning, and treatment assessment. Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been applied to cerebrovascular DSA, yet the available evidence is distributed across diverse imaging settings, technical tasks, datasets, and validation strategies. This structured topical review provides a DSA-centered overview of AI-assisted cerebrovascular image analysis across 2D DSA, three-dimensional rotational angiography, and four-dimensional DSA. Literature from Web of Science Core Collection and major engineering databases was screened at title, abstract, and full-text levels using predefined eligibility criteria. The literature is organized around six interconnected tasks: image preprocessing, vessel and lesion segmentation, image registration, reconstruction and generation, disease diagnosis and detection, and hemodynamic analysis. Representative conventional and learning-based methods are reviewed together with their datasets, evaluation metrics, validation designs, and available data or code resources, with particular attention to the strength and limitations of the supporting evidence. Recent studies demonstrate increasing use of spatiotemporal modeling, deep learning, and image-generation techniques, but clinical translation remains constrained by small or single-center datasets, heterogeneous acquisition protocols and evaluation practices, limited external and prospective validation, model interpretability, and deployment requirements. Future work should emphasize acquisition-aware and physics-informed modeling, multicenter and privacy-preserving collaboration, clinically meaningful validation, and closer integration with neurointerventional workflows.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence for cerebrovascular digital subtraction angiography: methods, evidence, and challenges

evidence_items.summary: Automated neuroimaging meta-analysis is widely used to generate hypotheses and interpret findings, reducing the time and effort required for manual literature searches and evidence curation. However, how closely these methods recover effortful expert-curated syntheses has not been established. We present NeuroMetaBench, an openly available benchmark linking expert curation records across stages of systematic review, from author-stated eligibility criteria and research-article inclusion decisions to individual analysis selections and meta-analysis-specific reference maps. The resource includes bibliographic records for 1,611 research-article inclusions across 17 quantitative review articles and candidate search pools for three. For nine review articles, it also provides analysis-level selections and coordinate data across 35 meta-analyses, documenting which reported results contributed to each meta-analysis and enabling reproducible construction of standardized reference maps. We demonstrate the benchmark's utility by evaluating three established automated methods: Neurosynth, NeuroQuery, and NeuroVLM. Across the benchmark, automated maps generally showed limited to moderate spatial correspondence with expert-curated reference maps, with substantial variation across meta-analysis topics and characteristics. NeuroMetaBench provides an openly available, community-driven resource for evaluating established automated meta-analysis methods, and is well positioned to evaluate emerging LLM-based approaches to automated neuroimaging synthesis.
evidence_items.title: NeuroMetaBench: Expert-curated benchmark for evaluating automated neuroimaging meta-analysis

organizations: Hasanuddin University
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Published numerical studies of the telegraph equation differ in their coefficients, boundary data and error measures, so their reported errors seldom allow a direct comparison. This article reviews 22 primary journal publications and compares two time integrators on a shared one-dimensional benchmark. Reanalysis of four published constant-coefficient examples gave observed refinement orders of 0.971–1.041 for first-order schemes and 1.995–1.999 for second-order schemes. The new benchmark uses the same centred spatial stencil with backward Euler and the trapezoidal rule under constant and smoothly varying coefficients. The trapezoidal rule showed approximately second-order convergence in both the spatial and temporal sweeps. Backward Euler approached first order in time on the finest temporal refinements. In the variable-coefficient case, it gave a smaller error on the coarsest jointly refined grid because spatial and temporal errors partly cancelled. At the finest joint resolution, its error was about 7.6 times the trapezoidal error. Both integrators dissipated the discrete energy in unforced tests. Separate refinement sweeps and a common evaluation time make these comparisons more informative than errors reported on a single grid.
evidence_items.title: Numerical Methods for Telegraph Equations: A focused review and a variable coefficient benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We present a systematic benchmark of MACE interatomic potentials for iron–nickel alloys, focusing on structural, elastic, and finite-temperature properties of chemically disordered body-centered-cubic (bcc) and face-centered-cubic (fcc) phases. The reference dataset comprises spin-polarized Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof density-functional-theory calculations for special quasirandom structures (SQS) spanning composition, volume, and shear deformation. A system-specific MACE–sqs model trained on this dataset achieves validation errors of 2.0 meV atom − 1 for energies and 24.3 meV Å − 1 for forces. We compare MACE–sqs with several MACE foundation models, including models trained using Hubbard corrections, through equations of state, equilibrium volumes, cubic elastic properties, and thermal lattice expansion. MACE–sqs gives the most consistent overall performance for several zero-temperature structural and elastic benchmarks, although its relative performance depends on property and composition and it does not reproduce all experimental elastic trends. In the finite-temperature comparison, no single model is uniformly superior, and MACE–matpes agrees more closely with experiment for some compositions and comparison metrics. Finite-temperature calculations yield reasonable thermal-expansion coefficients near 300 K, while deviations at elevated temperatures and for magnetovolume sensitive compositions highlight the limitation of representing magnetic effects only implicitly through the spin-polarized reference data. These results define the tested application domain in which targeted SQS-based training improves upon broad foundation models and identify explicit magnetic degrees of freedom and broader configurational sampling as priorities for future development.
evidence_items.title: Capabilities and limitations of MACE interatomic potentials for Fe–Ni alloys: a systematic benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Food-processing expansion does not necessarily translate into greater domestic value capture, particularly in regional production systems that remain strongly dependent on imported intermediate inputs. This study examines food-processing upgrading in Southeast Vietnam as a process of innovative adaptation and reads it against the economic, social and environmental pillars of sustainability. It combines regional evidence on agro-processing development with global value chain (GVC) indicators for the regional manufacturing environment and uses Vietnam's food, beverages and tobacco aggregate (C10T12) as a national sector benchmark. The regional evidence points to improving domestic value capture in agro-processing in Tay Ninh and Binh Phuoc during 2021–2024, within a production structure characterized by high backward participation and predominantly downstream GVC positions. At the national level, two-way fixed-effects estimates for 19 manufacturing sectors over 2018–2022 show that C10T12 increased domestic value-added share and improved GVC position faster than 17 of the 18 other manufacturing sectors. About three-quarters of this gain occurred between 2020 and 2021, the period of most severe pandemic disruption in Southeast Vietnam, and it persisted after reopening. The value-capture gap between primary agriculture and processing narrowed but remained substantial. Set against international agrifood GVC studies, the Vietnamese trajectory is distinctive in combining falling total participation with rising domestic content and a less downstream position. The study contributes an integrative, place-based account in which value capture, chain-wide distribution, adaptive capabilities and production-network position are evaluated jointly.
evidence_items.title: Food Processing and Domestic Value Capture in Southeast Vietnam: Regional Evidence and a National GVC Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Named entity recognition (NER) for extremely low-resource languages is constrained not only by limited labelled data, but also by duplicate-text leakage, annotation inconsistency, severe class imbalance, and uncertain transfer from multilingual pretrained models. This study establishes a leakage-controlled evaluation benchmark for Nya-Həba (Kilba), a Chadic language of Adamawa State, Nigeria, and compares statistical, neural, and transformer-based NER baselines. The strict benchmark contains 1,853 unique, consistently annotated sentences (24,239 tokens; 2,277 entity spans) with fixed train/validation/test partitions and zero exact sentence-text overlap. A feature-based conditional random field (CRF), BiLSTM-CRF, XLM-R, and training-only class-weighted XLM-R were evaluated with exact-span entity metrics. CRF achieved the strongest overall micro-F1 (69.03%), followed by BiLSTM-CRF (63.14 ± 1.75%) and vanilla XLM-R (60.00 ± 1.95%). Class weighting did not improve overall micro-F1 (58.32 ± 1.57%), but increased recall from 53.03% to 67.72% and macro-F1 from 32.04% to 50.74%; TIME F1 rose from 4.60% to 36.80% and ANIM from 0.00% to 42.24%. Error analysis shows that this rare-class recovery is accompanied by substantially more spurious entities. Paired sentence-level bootstrap intervals for weighted-versus-vanilla XLM-R micro-F1 cross zero for all seeds. The results show that model complexity does not guarantee stronger NER performance under extreme resource scarcity, while cost-sensitive training can recover minority categories at a precision cost. The benchmark is publicly available on Zenodo.
evidence_items.title: A Leakage-Controlled Benchmark for Nya-Həba Named Entity Recognition: Statistical, Neural, and Cost-Sensitive Transformer Baselines

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT The Model Context Protocol enables large language model applications to use external resources, but untrusted tool output may be interpreted as instruction rather than data. This study evaluates indirect prompt injection in a controlled, local, read‐only file‐summarization workflow implemented with the official Python MCP SDK and stdio transport. Eight open‐source local models were tested against 18 attack vectors under three defense conditions, with 10 repetitions per model‐vector‐condition cell. Of 4320 attempted executions, 4318 were valid. Target attack success rate was 52.61% (757/1439; Wilson 95% CI 50.02–55.18) without a guardrail, 15.71% (226/1439; 13.92–17.68) with ProtectAI DeBERTa, and 7.92% (114/1440; 6.63–9.43) with zero‐shot XLM‐RoBERTa. In an independent detector audit using 300 benign documents and 18 attack fixtures, DeBERTa achieved 55.56% recall with 33.33% false‐positive rate, whereas XLM‐RoBERTa achieved 77.78% recall with 41.00% false‐positive rate. Across 240 benign summarization attempts, task success was 98.75% without filtering, 66.25% with DeBERTa gating, and 75.42% with XLM‐RoBERTa gating. The results show that guardrails can reduce attack success but may also introduce substantial false alarms and utility loss. The findings apply to the measured local MCP file‐summarization workflow and do not establish security of remote MCP transport, authorization, autonomous tool use, or side‐effecting tools.
evidence_items.title: A Multilingual Security Benchmark for Indirect Prompt Injection in a Local Model Context Protocol File‐Summarization Workflow

evidence_items.summary: Fuel cell hybrid electric vehicle (FCHEV) energy management strategies (EMSs) are commonly evaluated under different vehicle configurations, drive cycles, initial states and modelling assumptions, which complicates direct comparison. This study provides an open-source, reproducible MATLAB/Simulink benchmark for a 50 kW PEMFC and 20 kWh Li-ion battery FCHEV. Nine standard drive cycles are evaluated under fixed vehicle, component, initial-condition and numerical settings using a simple rule-based EMS as the baseline comparator. In the reference simulation, regenerative-braking recovery ranges from 36% on Manhattan to 59% on US06, while fuel-cell conversion losses represent approximately 48%–51% of hydrogen chemical-energy input. Urban cycles spend most of their simulated time at relatively low fuel-cell power, whereas highway operation more frequently occupies the higher-efficiency region. A one-at-a-time and Monte Carlo sensitivity study identifies vehicle mass as the most influential of the investigated parameters on modelled hydrogen consumption. An equivalent consumption minimisation strategy (ECMS) is included only as an illustrative benchmark case, not as a new or state-of-the-art controller. The work does not provide experimental vehicle-level validation; therefore, the numerical results are intended for controlled comparative benchmarking within the defined simulation environment rather than as absolute predictions of a production vehicle. The Simulink model, parameter scripts, selected 1-second outputs and benchmark protocol are documented in the associated repository.
evidence_items.title: A standardised open-source benchmark for cross-cycle evaluation of fuel cell hybrid electric vehicle energy management strategies

evidence_items.summary: As frontier LLMs saturate existing instruction-following benchmarks, measuring further progress requires harder tests that remain faithful to real use. In practice, users often combine several constraints, add them at different turns of a conversation, and expect all of them to hold in the assistant's response. We introduce ComplexIF, a challenging benchmark for this setting, together with the automatic pipeline that generates it. The pipeline expands seed requests into multi-turn conversations, weaves constraints into their turns, and keeps only tasks that a strong model can solve, so difficulty can be raised by adding constraints or turns while every task stays solvable. ComplexIF's two splits test complementary sides of instruction following: a verifiable split of format constraints, checked by programs, and a rubric split of semantic instructions, such as a tone or an audience, checked with an LLM judge. Across 14 proprietary and open-weight models, even the strongest satisfies every constraint on fewer than half of the verifiable tasks, and no model leads on both splits.
evidence_items.title: ComplexIF: A Challenging Multi-Turn, Multi-Constraint Instruction-Following Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: In rateless transmission the transmitter keeps sending until the legitimate receiver (Bob) can decode. Over a wiretap channel this has a useful side effect: the eavesdropper (Eve) sees only as many symbols as Bob needs, although the transmitter knows neither channel. We study the secrecy of rateless lattice codes in this setting. First, using a public dither and privacy amplification, we prove a finite-length secrecy bound, in total variation distance, for every channel realization, even if Eve knows all codes and seeds and combines all packets. Second, stopping when Bob acknowledges successful decoding, as in hybrid ARQ, costs at most the logarithm of the number of possible feedback outcomes in secret bits. Third, for degraded sessions with state-based stopping and without a pre-shared key or other public discussion, the secret-key rate of a session cannot exceed its accumulated Gaussian secrecy capacity, and adaptive key generation with shaped rateless lattice codes comes within any $\epsilon>0$ of this limit when Eve's channel states are revealed after the session. If only their statistics are known, choosing the key length after the session guarantees a prescribed secrecy-outage probability. Finally, over block Rayleigh fading with a CRC-based acknowledgement and joint belief-propagation decoding, and with Eve $20$~dB weaker on average, the scheme reaches $59$--$69\%$ of the outage-weighted throughput of an ideal infinite-length secure hybrid-ARQ benchmark for Bob SNRs of $8$--$20$~dB.
evidence_items.title: Rateless Lattice Codes over Fading Wiretap Channels: Finite-Length Secrecy and the Secret-Key Capacity of Degraded Sessions

evidence_items.summary: Executable code can preserve a world's structural layout, yet video renderers frequently alter the appearance of previously visited places once they leave the camera view. We present Paintress, a code-conditioned world model that couples an executable geometric proxy with an independently parameterized 3D Gaussian appearance memory in a shared metric coordinate frame. While the proxy enforces structural and visibility constraints, 3D Gaussians capture the visual realization synthesized by emitted observations. To balance stable incremental fusion with consistent readout, Paintress separates writing from reading: newly emitted frames update a persistent raw Gaussian map under confidence-gated selection, whereas a cloned reader copy is globally refined against the observation archive and rendered with coverage masks to condition generation. We also introduce Expedition-33, a benchmark for generated-appearance retention across 11 static scenes, five route families, and 15, 30, and 60 s target absences (165 settings per system). Excluded from the opening image, targets are synthesized during a shared prefix and scored against each system's own first visit at matched return cameras. Across ten systems (1,650 videos), Paintress achieves 0.1220 ROI-LPIPS, 0.0613 MAE, and 52.12% detail retention (vs. 0.2731, 0.1401, and 10.91% for CWM), with lower discrepancy at 60 s (0.1630) than CWM, AgentGarten, and Lyra 2.0 achieve at 15 s.
evidence_items.title: Eidetic Code World Model

evidence_items.summary: Automated subject cataloging assigns controlledvocabulary headings to bibliographic records, but LCSH has no standard public benchmark. We introduce LCSHBench: 22,346 books in 15 languages from the openly licensed Harvard, Columbia, and Princeton catalogs. Records enter only when at least two independent cataloging agencies assigned LCSH; we release per-catalog provenance plus union and unanimous answer views. A concordance study of 465,187 works cataloged by all three libraries shows why this design matters: libraries usually agree on the underlying topic (93.3% share a concept-level heading) but often differ in exact expression (39.4% have identical heading sets). LCSHBench therefore scores both exact and concept matches, with set and rank metrics broken down by language and heading type, across open-vocabulary generation and full-vocabulary retrieval. As a first demonstration, a low-rank fine-tune of a 300M on-device embedder improves cross-lingual retrieval and beats a 3,072-dimensional hosted embedder on development exact recall@200 (0.659 vs 0.623). The language panel shows the gain is not uniform, and held-out-test and end-to-end confirmation remain future work.
evidence_items.title: LCSHBench: A Multilingual, Consensus-Grounded Benchmark for Library of Congress Subject Heading Assignment

evidence_items.summary: （＊日本語は英文の後に） Today we are announcing the Sakana AI Applied Research Lab, a research group within Sakana AI that applies the company’s research to large, complex real-world systems, advancing the state of the art in their understanding and delivering it as value to Sakana AI clients. The Lab’s first program is in finance and economics. We expect other programs to emerge in the future. A complex system, such as a market or an economy, is not something one LLM-powered agentic AI can resolve. A complex phenomenon must be modeled as a system: its units, their links, and how changes in one part affect the others. Deciding which questions to ask, what to model, and how to judge the answers has been the work of human experts, and progress has run at the speed of human effort. Agentic AI can now implement, test, and refine models at scale; its weakness is knowing which questions matter. Combining the two, the potential of AI on top of a foundation of human knowledge, will be the focus of the Lab. Our First Program Finance has traditionally studied asset prices, and economics the larger system beneath them. AI connects the two at the granularity of firms and transactions, and in near real time: asset prices become the visible reflection of the economy. The Lab’s Computational Finance and Economics (COFE) program is interested in both: the visible portion and the real economy underneath. The Lab’s Foundations at Sakana AI The Lab builds upon research at Sakana AI since its founding in July 2023, including automated scientific discovery, evolutionary search, agent-based simulation, and evaluation. The Lab’s most direct predecessors are Sakana AI’s projects in finance and economics.
evidence_items.title: Introducing the Sakana AI Applied Research Lab

evidence_items.summary: Contextual Adaptation Failure (CAF) is a conceptual framework developed to identify, characterize, and interpret behavioral vulnerabilities in artificial intelligence systems arising from inadequate recognition, integration, prioritization, persistence, or revision of contextual information during human–AI interactions. Situated within the broader research perspective of the Computational Psychopathology of Artificial Intelligence, CAF proposes six partially overlapping behavioral dimensions: • Under-Adaptation • Over-Adaptation • Maladaptive Adaptation • Context Persistence • Contextual Contamination • Stereotyped Adaptation The framework distinguishes four complementary functional and analytical components: Context Detection, Adaptive Response, Adaptation Auditing, and Longitudinal Comparison. A central theoretical contribution is the Principle of Contextual Proportionality, which proposes that contextual information should influence AI behavior in proportion to its relevance, reliability, and significance. CAF integrates perspectives from experimental psychology, behavioral science, context-aware computing, AI alignment, personalization, model robustness, and human–AI interaction. Its prospective applications include behavioral auditing, AI safety evaluation, contextual generalization, and the investigation of unintended behavioral outcomes associated with reinforcement learning and AI post-training. This publication establishes Version 1.0 of the CAF conceptual framework. It does not constitute an empirically validated diagnostic instrument, a computational architecture, or a causal model of AI behavior, nor does it attribute human mental states or psychological disorders to artificial intelligence systems. The framework provides a theoretical foundation for future operationalization, experimental validation, and the development of reproducible methods for evaluating contextual behavioral reliability in AI systems.
evidence_items.title: Contextual Adaptation Failure (CAF): A Conceptual Framework for Behavioral Vulnerabilities in Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Transformation Tracking and Understanding (TTU), extending video object tracking to environments where objects undergo physical assemblies and disassemblies. TTU requires continuously tracking objects through transformations, identifying new entities, maintaining a state graph of their relationships, and assigning semantic labels to transformations. While foundation models (e.g., SAM 2/3) maintain tracklets through appearance changes, they cannot update semantic identities as objects physically evolve. Prior work addresses only disassemblies, relying on expensive searches triggered only when tracking fails. We propose Tracking Instances via Proposals and Overlaps (TIPO), a training-free framework that continuously infers transformations via a generate-evaluate-judge pipeline. TIPO generates split and merge proposals from disjoint mask components, scores them against mask-decoder priors using inner and external overlap, and queries an MLLM on the top proposal for visual verification and semantic labeling. To benchmark TTU, we curate Video Instances, States, and Transformation Annotations (VISTA), a dataset including state graphs with 124 assembly and 132 disassembly events across 50 sequences and over 26,000 frames. TIPO achieves state-of-the-art tracking and state-graph accuracy on VISTA, while operating 6times to 15times faster than prior methods. Project page: https://davidegardenal.github.io/tipo-tracking
evidence_items.title: Taking Apart and Putting Together: Tracking Objects Through Physical Transformations

evidence_items.summary: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) pipelines and vision-language models exhibit high accuracy on standard OCR and document-understanding benchmarks, yet they systematically underperform on document patterns that are operationally critical in financial workflows. These patterns include vertical or rotated text, logo-embedded vendor names, fine-print regulatory clauses, degraded scans, and complex multi-column layouts. While underrepresented in public datasets, they constitute a substantial portion of real-world failure cases. We introduce SAVIOR, a sample-efficient data curation methodology that targets such high-impact failure scenarios to adapt vision-language models for robust financial OCR. We further propose PaIRS, a structure-aware evaluation metric that measures layout fidelity by comparing pairwise spatial relationships between tokens. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-Instruct with SAVIOR-Train achieves a word recall of 0.93. When the resulting layout-aware OCR output is used as context for document question answering, it attains an F1 score of 0.89, outperforming both open- and closed-source models such as GPT-4o, Mistral-OCR, PaddleOCR-VL, and DeepSeek-OCR.
evidence_items.title: SAVIOR: Sample-efficient Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for OCR Representation

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) now help develop many models published as general solutions. Should generality instead reside in the agent that builds a model for each new task? We examine this question in prognostics and health management (PHM), where every model must work on unseen equipment. Our deployment-style benchmark, NextUnit-Bench, covers 24 public datasets split into 58 folds that hold out units or operating conditions; each agent has two hours to deliver an executable predictor, then run on the hidden units. First, frontier agents outperform AutoML, which reaches less than half the best agent's score, and faithful implementations of published methods on four datasets, of which only 6 of 30 beat the strongest agent's own design; published accuracies, where reproducible, rest on the papers' own conventions, and a single convention, capping the remaining life of test engines, can halve the reported error. Second, the agents' advantage is a design made on each machine's data; once made, a plain-text plan of a few hundred words carries most of the gap between two frontier agents, and given a weaker agent's plan, the strongest agent falls to that agent's level, often to identical predictions. Before touching the data, however, it matters little whose plan an agent carries out, and domain toolkits appear to help neither: what sets the strongest apart is how much it learns from the data. Third, such designs reach only implementers that can execute them: given the strongest agent's designs, a locally deployable open-weight model delivers half as often, even when they are lightened, and scores no higher than without them. Generality, we argue, is not disappearing but moving, from the model to the modeler.
evidence_items.title: Moving Generality from Model to Modeler: LLM Agents for PHM on a Deployment-Style Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: These are the satellite images we used in our paper "Can Multimodal LLMs Predict Rapid Intensification? A Leakage-Controlled Zero-Shot Benchmark for Tropical Cyclones" (GeoCV Workshop, WACV 2027). In the paper, we ask multimodal LLMs whether a tropical cyclone will intensify by 30 kt or more in the next 24 hours. The benchmark has 2,485 six-hourly cases from 140 storms in the 2016 to 2025 seasons. The zip contains one folder, images/. The combined/ folder has the picture we gave the models for each case. It shows up to the last eight observations of the storm in a 2 x 4 grid, oldest first, and each image is labelled with the hours since the storm's first observation. These pictures are built from the single images in mid/. Each mid image is a GridSat-B1 infrared crop about 1,170 km across, centred on the storm with north up. White is a cold cloud top (190 K), black is 310 K, and magenta means the satellite has no data there. There are two CSV files. manifest.csv gives the GridSat time and the share of missing data for each image. combined manifest.csv gives the number of images in each picture. Files are named by case ID, for example 2016240N13224 007 (the IBTrACS storm ID plus an observation number). These are the same IDs used in our code. To use the images with the code, unzip the file into model inputs/ in https://github.com/sukhadaghewari/tropicalcyclone-ri-bench The images are made from NOAA's GridSat-B1 data (doi:10.7289/V59P2ZKR), which is in the public domain. If you use them, please cite our paper.

evidence_items.summary: Useful reaction data is spread across many laboratories, and most of it is never shared. Federated learning lets labs train one shared model while each lab keeps its own data. This study tests whether that works for predicting reaction yields. Five simulated labs of very different size were built from two public datasets (Buchwald–Hartwig and Suzuki–Miyaura couplings), either sharing the same chemistry or each working on its own substrates. The outcome, in four points. (1) When labs share the same chemistry, the federated model is almost as good as a model trained on all data pooled in one place (R2 0.93 against 0.96), and the smallest lab halves its prediction error. (2) When each lab works on its own substrates, a model trained by one lab fails on other labs' reactions (R2 below 0), while the federated model works (R2 0.79 and 0.57 with FedProx), although it stays below pooled data (0.95 and 0.82). (3) In that case no lab gets a better model for its own substrates; what it gains is a model that also works on chemistry it has not yet tried. (4) Protecting single reactions with differential privacy (DP-SGD, ε ≈ 3–11 per lab) is affordable when labs hold different chemistry, but hiding a whole lab's participation is not possible with only five labs. Secure aggregation leaves accuracy unchanged and costs about 50 % more communication. Overall, without moving any data, federated learning recovered about 75–90 % of the gain in accuracy that pooling all data would give.
evidence_items.title: Learning reaction yields across laboratories without sharing data: a benchmark of federated learning with secure aggregation and differential privacy

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The increasing complexity of global logistics necessitates resilient, AI-driven decision support. Same time AI Agents implementation is hindered by cognitive overload and the inherent unreliability of numerical reasoning of LLMs. This paper presents a novel approach built upon the Yet Another Agents Memory (YAAM) architecture, which physically separates transient operating memory from a persistent knowledge layer. To ensure computational reliability, we propose a “Walled Garden” ecosystem of deterministic Agentic Skills (based on Python tools). These tools serve as executable instantiations of abstract Cognitive Task Templates (CTTs) derived from professional supply chain literature and protected by strict Pydantic validation. To mitigate performance degradation, a Dynamic Tool Retrieval (DTR) mechanism binds only the most relevant tools to agents at runtime. System performance is rigorously evaluated against the SCM-Cert-Bench, comprising 119 verified tasks. Results demonstrate that while this architecture enables capable models (e.g., 30B+) to achieve expert-level accuracy in Quantitative Multi-Criteria Optimization through autonomous self-correction, smaller models (~8B parameters) exhibit critical vulnerabilities. Specifically, they suffer from cognitive overload and strict schema constraints, frequently falling into fatal, non-convergent recursion loops instead of successfully self-correcting.
evidence_items.title: LLM-Driven Agentic System for Enhanced Decision Support in Multi-Modal Logistics

evidence_items.summary: Regionalized 2013 FABIO v1.1 input-output data for NUTS 2 regions (NUTS 2021), created with piccolo fabio. This modified dataset is not an official FABIO release. Relation to the paper and access This dataset provides the underlying data for Barre, F. I., Gaona, J., Hertwich, E. G., Strømman, A., & Moran, D. D. (2026), From Dry Fields to Empty Plates: Tracing Drought Exposure Across European Agriculture Supply Chains . The paper uses FABIO v2 covering 2018–2023 for its analysis; for licensing reasons, this record makes FABIO-NUTS2 v1 available. To ask about access to more recent FABIO-NUTS2 data for your research, contact Francis Isidore Barre . Method The national FABIO table is spatially disaggregated to NUTS 2 using crop/livestock production and population weights; observed regional trade and gravity estimates inform trade allocation. Data structure and use The uploader provides five Feather tables: Z.feather : intermediate transactions between producing sectors. Rows identify the supplying region-sector and columns the purchasing region-sector; each cell is the flow from the row sector to the column sector. Y.feather : final demand. Rows identify producing region-sectors; columns identify destination regions and final-demand categories. VA.feather : value-added account categories by producing region-sector. x.feather : gross output for each producing region-sector, calculated from intermediate sales and final demand. fabio.feather : the combined input-output system, with the transaction ( T ), final-demand ( FD ), and value-added ( VA ) blocks. The uploader also includes every top-level .npz file present in the results folder. These are SciPy sparse matrices and can be loaded with scipy.sparse.load npz . Common files, when generated, include: mrio.npz : the combined input-output solution, with shape (N + P) × (N + F) , in the same order as fabio.feather .

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains longitudinal fecal calprotectin (fCAL) measurements and related fecal score, body weight, and infection-shedding variables from two experimental pig studies investigating intestinal inflammation and the effect of fecal dry matter on fCAL interpretation. Fecal calprotectin was quantified using an ELISA assay and is provided both as a raw concentration (fCAL ng ml, ng/mL) and after normalisation to fecal dry matter (fCAL DM ng g, ng/g DM). Study 1 includes 16 pigs monitored from 27 to 110 days of age. Study 2 includes 12 piglets experimentally challenged with enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli serotype F4 (ETEC-F4) at weaning and four non-infected controls, monitored until 110 days of age. Fecal samples were collected at days -1, 6, 25, 39, 53, and 82 post-weaning for fCAL analysis. In Study 2, ETEC-F4 shedding was quantified at days -1, 1, 2, 3, 6, and 7 relative to infection. The dataset includes assay and plate information, ELISA replicates, sampling dates and study days, fecal consistency scores, fecal dry matter, body weight, age, sex, experimental group and box, infection status, and ETEC-F4 excretion variables. Each row corresponds to one ELISA replicate/observation. The data support assessment of longitudinal fCAL patterns and comparison of fresh-feces versus fecal-dry-matter-based fCAL expression.

evidence_items.summary: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) is creating new possibilities for language teacher education, particularly in developing critical thinking and communicative competence. This article examines how an AI-integrated coursebook can support these skills among pre-service English teachers. It proposes a pedagogical approach in which learners use AI to question, evaluate, generate, and improve ideas rather than simply obtain ready-made answers. The article introduces a learning cycle of independent thinking, AI interaction, critical evaluation, redesign, communication, and reflection. It illustrates how this approach can be applied through AI verification, decision-making, collaborative problem solving, prototyping, and responsible AI use. Since the coursebook is still under development, the examples are presented as a pedagogical design model rather than evidence of its effectiveness.
evidence_items.title: DEVELOPING CRITICAL THINKING AND COMMUNICATIVE COMPETENCE IN PRE-SERVICE ENGLISH TEACHERS THROUGH AN AI-INTEGRATED COURSEBOOK
