Overview This repository provides the experimental dataset, model outputs, and machine-learning code associated with the study: "From Single Compounds to Ambient Aerosols: A Machine-Learning-Based Estimation of Organic Hygroscopicity" In this study, we developed a laboratory-anchored, machine-learning framework to quantitatively link organic aerosol hygroscopicity, derived from single-compound measurements, to ambient aerosol hygroscopicity (κ). The framework is based on laboratory measurements of 22 atmospherically relevant organic compounds, covering different chemical families, including organic acids, amino acids, sugars, and alcohols. By organising individual organic species into functional family groups with characteristic hygroscopic properties, we establish a physically interpretable basis for representing the organic fraction of atmospheric aerosol. The laboratory-derived information is further incorporated into a machine-learning framework to estimate organic hygroscopicity and investigate its applicability to ambient aerosol measurements. This approach provides a pathway for connecting molecular-level information with atmospheric aerosol observations and improving the representation of organic aerosol hygroscopicity. 2. Repository contents This repository contains the following materials: A. Laboratory experimental dataset The dataset includes experimental measurements and derived hygroscopicity parameters for 22 individual organic compounds investigated in the laboratory. The measurements cover particle mobility diameters of: 100 nm 150 nm 200 nm 250 nm The dataset includes relevant chemical descriptors and experimental hygroscopicity parameters used to investigate relationships between molecular composition and organic hygroscopicity. evidence_items.summary: Imitation learning failing on a robot can have multiple causes, and it is hard to figure out the root cause just by looking at the failure. From the Action Chunking Transformer's training objective — an L1 reconstruction term and a KL term on its style variable — we derive ten offline metrics, each read against a reference value and applied in a fixed diagnostic order. On two datasets from a low-cost arm they expose a policy trained for 2 steps instead of 20,000; policies whose output is driven 98 to 100% by the camera inputs and almost none by the joint-state inputs; and a demonstration-only coverage metric, computed before training, that moves with the post-training error. This record holds the paper. The analysis code, result files and training configurations are on GitHub (https://github.com/sameershah21/physical-ai-observability); the datasets, the two recordings and the six trained policies are on the Hugging Face Hub (see the README). Every number and figure is reproducible from them. Use of AI tools: the analysis code, including the code that draws the figures, was written with an AI assistant (Claude), which also helped draft and edit the text; every number comes from the recorded files.
evidence_items.title: Toward Observability in Physical AI: Offline Diagnostics for Imitation-Learning Policies in Robotics

evidence_items.summary: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed educational practices, creating new opportunities for improving the quality, accessibility, and effectiveness of English language teaching (ELT). The integration of AI-powered technologies into English language classrooms enables teachers to implement personalized learning strategies, provide immediate feedback, develop learners’ communicative competence, and create interactive educational environments. This study explores innovative methods and practical applications of artificial intelligence in English language teaching, with particular attention to the development of listening, speaking, reading, writing, vocabulary, and grammatical competence. The research is based on an analytical review of recent academic literature and an examination of pedagogical applications of AI-supported learning tools. The findings indicate that AI-based chatbots, intelligent tutoring systems, automated writing evaluation platforms, speech recognition technologies, and generative AI applications can facilitate individualized instruction, increase learner engagement, and support autonomous learning. Furthermore, AI technologies provide opportunities for differentiated instruction and continuous formative assessment.
evidence_items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHING: INNOVATIVE METHODS AND PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS

evidence_items.summary: Continuous oscillatory baffled reactors (COBRs) have been utilised in organic synthesis and crystallisation, however, no validation work has yet been conducted to determine if the fluid displacement caused by the oscillation at the start of the COBR is conserved at the end of the COBR. This work reports, for the first time, both experimental measurements and theoretical evaluations of the displacement. The experimental validation in volves physically measuring the fluid displacement using a laser distance sensor located at the end of the COBR. Surprisingly, the measured displacement values at some operating conditions differ from the initial settings. The theoretical evaluation entails the determination of power dissipation across the COBR using the pressure mea surements at four locations along the COBR. The model evaluated displacements agree well with the experi mental measurements at all operational conditions, validating the methodologies used in this work.
evidence_items.title: An investigation of conservation of fluid oscillation in a continuous oscillatory baffled reactor

evidence_items.summary: This archive accompanies the article "The Butterfly Effect in Coding Agents: Testing Micro-Perturbations, Reasoning Effort and Instructions in a Production Agent". The study asks whether small changes in a coding agent's input are amplified beyond the variation between identical runs. It runs Claude Code 2.1.328 (model claude-sonnet-5-5) in isolated containers on eight short Python maintenance tasks with hidden tests, in four studies of 160 runs each: three micro-perturbations (a polite prompt, a reordered README, reversed test-failure order) at low, medium and high reasoning effort, and a ladder of short instructions ("Think carefully before you start", "make a plan before changing any code") at medium effort. The archive contains: (1) the laboratory code (run orchestration, stream parsing, evaluation, metrics and analysis scripts); (2) the eight study tasks and four pilot tasks, with hidden tests and reference solutions; (3) the preregistration of Study 1 and the dated addenda for Studies 2–4; (4) the run manifests; (5) the raw stream-json transcripts, patches and evaluation outputs of all 640 analysed runs and of all excluded attempts; (6) the per-study analysis results, including the exploratory analyses; and (7) the sources of the article. The README describes the layout and how to reproduce the analysis. Credentials and per-run workspaces are not included; the workspaces are regenerated deterministically from the task sources.
evidence_items.title: Replication archive for "The Butterfly Effect in Coding Agents: Testing Micro-Perturbations, Reasoning Effort and Instructions in a Production Agent"

evidence_items.summary: Omni models answer questions about videos by jointly processing sampled frames and audio in one turn, while VLMs have become strong agents that can search a video over many turns. We ask how far a model can go without hearing the audio, and present \method, a simple multi-turn harness built on such a VLM that never hears the audio directly: speech is transcribed into text, and the VLM sleuths the video without a predefined workflow. On four omni benchmarks with videos up to 90 minutes, \method achieves the best average accuracy: \textbf{75.0\%}, 2.6 points above Gemini 3.8 Flash, and it tops the Video-MME-v2 leaderboard with \textbf{77.8\%}; with Qwen3.8-27B, it is comparable to open-source omni models on short videos and better on long ones. We draw three insights: searching outperforms passive observation; agentic ability matters as much as direct audio access; and small agentic models are highly competitive. So we provide a simple but effective starting point for omni video understanding.
evidence_items.title: SleuthVLM: Do We Really Need Audio-in-Video for Omni Video Understanding?

evidence_items.summary: LLM simulations are validated by equivalence with human effects, yet a zero reference passes whenever the human 90 percent interval lies inside the margin, as the human benchmark shows before simulation. When the zero reference fails, planned precision gives independent simulations the margin up to which passing is a 5 percent test of response. In an exploratory 70-experiment reanalysis, 72 percent of GPT-4's $\pm$0.20 SD passes were zero-reference passes; GPT-4 passed 16 contrasts the zero reference failed (1.58 expected without response). In a preregistered audit, Claude Sonnet 5.5 passed three intention targets, all zero-reference passes, and the registered belief-gradient control; norm beliefs changed 0.065 SD against humans' 0.351 (zero-reference check added after unblinding; norm beliefs emphasized after inspection). Registered tests detected no overestimation; average-effect intervals excluded overestimation above 0.08 SD. A group audit's precision floor is 1.33 facts against a 2.9-fact effect. Report the zero-reference threshold beside every equivalence decision.
evidence_items.title: What Does Matching a Human Intervention Effect Establish? Benchmark Checks for LLM Simulations

evidence_items.summary: Recent multimodal search agents use reasoning, vision, and live web search across many turns to answer questions beyond parametric knowledge by orchestrating a small library of hand-crafted search and visual tools. However, the library is laborious to create and maintain, and frozen when new query types, evidence formats, and failure modes are encountered in the wild. Human practitioners, by contrast, cope with insufficient tools by fashioning new ones from familiar parts and reusing them across tasks. Inspired by this, we propose ToolSmith, an automatic tool-generation framework that grows and reuses modules on top of a lean base tool library. We evaluate ToolSmith on three in-domain multimodal search benchmarks and ten out-of-domain benchmarks under a VLM-as-a-Judge protocol. ToolSmith consistently improves over the base library across deployed agents of varying scales, with larger backbones reaping greater gains, demonstrating the scalability of the approach. Our code and data are available at https://threesr.github.io/toolsmith/.
evidence_items.title: ToolSmith: An Automatic Tool-Generation Framework for Multimodal Search Agents

evidence_items.summary: A streaming video system must decide in a single pass what evidence to retain under bounded frame storage, before it knows which details a future question will require. Recent recursive self-improvement methods automate the design of the harness that stores and retrieves this evidence. They revise the harness in response to failures, but the editor must still devise each repair from its prior knowledge and a predefined set of tools. A failure that recurs across videos, however, may point to a problem that prior work has already addressed. We introduce MORSE (Memory Optimization with Recursive Self-Evolvement), an open-world auto-research framework that uses recurring failures to guide an online search for solutions. Its editor groups failures in training traces by cause, then searches papers, model cards, and code for methods it can adapt or pretrained perception models it can use. When the editor introduces a new perceptual capability, it can also revise how the harness stores and retrieves the resulting evidence for a frozen video-language model. On held-out validation streams, MORSE first selects revisions that improve answer quality, then seeks faster revisions that preserve those gains within a specified tolerance. Across three streaming video benchmarks, MORSE consistently achieves the highest answer accuracy within each frozen-backbone comparison. On OVO-Bench, our Qwen3-VL-8B harness answers queries in 0.30 seconds on average while achieving 75.1% accuracy, 3.1 percentage points ahead of the next-best evaluated harness using the same frozen backbone.
evidence_items.title: MORSE: Optimizing Streaming Memory Design via Open-World Auto-Research

evidence_items.summary: We present WeMM-Ecom, a family of multimodal large language models that deliver frontier e-commerce capabilities while achieving state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at their respective scales. The family spans five sizes, from a 0.8B dense model to a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. Our training pipeline begins with two-stage continued pre-training that progressively raises the proportion of e-commerce data within a diverse multimodal data mixture, followed by hybrid-thinking post-training that combines on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning to support both non-thinking and thinking modes. For evaluation, we construct a comprehensive suite of 28 e-commerce benchmarks (23 in-house and five open-source) covering eight business scenarios and complement it with 64 public general-purpose benchmarks. On the e-commerce suite, WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B surpasses substantially larger open-source flagship models, including Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, HY4, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. On the general-purpose suite, every WeMM-Ecom model surpasses its similarly sized Qwen3.5 counterpart, with the lightweight variants (e.g., WeMM-Ecom-2B) showing clear advantages over leading lightweight models such as Qwen3.5-2B, MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B, and LFM3-VL-2B. Beyond benchmarks, WeMM-Ecom now powers hundreds of production use cases in WeChat, including catalog management, multimodal product search, and livestream commerce, serving billion-scale requests per day. We publicly release all model weights and detail our data curation, training recipe, and benchmark construction to facilitate future work on domain-specialized multimodal models. We have released the model weights and code to facilitate future research at https://github.com/Tencent/WeMM-Ecom.
evidence_items.title: WeMM-Ecom: Advancing Multimodal Content Understanding for WeChat E-Commerce

evidence_items.summary: Robot policies must adapt to the speed of moving objects, yet existing benchmarks rarely measure this ability across diverse tasks and speeds. We introduce SWEEP-Bench, a simulation benchmark with 80 conveyor-belt manipulation tasks spanning 16 skill categories, each evaluated at 13 belt speeds (0.10-0.40 m/s). Objects are transported through physical contact with a visibly moving belt. Each task has a static counterpart, and each evaluation episode uses the same randomized scene at all 13 speeds. We fine-tune eight vision-language-action and world-action models on demonstrations spanning the full speed range, comparing observations from the current frame alone with those including two past frames. For six models, the success rate peaks at intermediate speeds, and their failures indicate that they tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed rather than to the actual one. Past frames raise the success rate by 10-40 percentage points for three models, and linear probes show that the belt speed is also most linearly decodable from these three. Adding ground-truth speed input to four of the models improves all of them, and a speed estimated from the images keeps most of this gain. These results show that SWEEP-Bench exposes speed-dependent failures and suggest that past frames help only policies from which the speed is most decodable, such as those pretrained on multiple frames. Project page: https://damin3927.github.io/SWEEP-Bench
evidence_items.title: SWEEP-Bench: Do Embodied Policies Act on the Speed They See?

evidence_items.summary: Animating arbitrary 3D assets from instructions requires both structural inference and motion control, yet existing motion benchmarks mostly cover conventional human or animal skeletons with simple instructions. We introduce DivDynBench, which evaluates rigging and motion generation across six morphology categories, with instructions requiring multi-phase part coordination and explicit timing, angle, repetition, and trajectory constraints. With large language models, we systematically compare three common paradigms: specialized motion generation, video generation followed by motion recovery, and direct agent-driven generation. We analyze their control capabilities, cross-morphology adaptability, and generation costs. Guided by this comparison, we propose an Agentic Motion Framework in which an agent writes compact parametric skeleton and motion programs, and a deterministic executor performs rigging, kinematic solving, and geometric correction. Compact parameter control reduces generation overhead and improves rigging reliability and motion-control accuracy, providing practical guidance for deploying complex 3D motion generation.
evidence_items.title: 3AGameFactory-Motion: Agentic Rigging and Reliable Complex Motion Generation for Diverse 3D Assets

evidence_items.summary: Discovering cooperative behavior in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is challenging due to the combinatorial complexity of joint state-action spaces, which hinders the emergence of coordinated behaviors from trial-and-error alone. Intrinsic rewards are often used to aid discovery, but naively combining them with team objectives can distort the learning signal, compromising task performance. In this paper, we propose EFXPLORER, a constrained exploration framework that maximizes exploration objectives subject to a constraint that preserves established task performance. We solve the resulting problem using an epigraph reformulation that introduces adaptive exploration budgets. This approach separates intrinsic rewards from task objectives and regulates exploration through task feasibility. To further encourage diverse and temporally extended exploration, we incorporate a successor distance-based intrinsic reward that captures long-horizon dependencies. Empirically, our method outperforms strong baselines and induces novel cooperative strategies across SMAX, VMAS, and MPE benchmark suites.
evidence_items.title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Epigraph-Form Guided Exploration

evidence_items.summary: Consider a firm that surveys its competition for a particular agentic task and seeks to offer superior accuracy at every price point. A firm that Pareto-dominated its competitors would leave no rational customer a reason to buy elsewhere. This paper shows a path to this kind of capability by evolving multi-LLM Python agents from training pools of at most 100 examples. Given a priced menu of nine LLM endpoints; brief documentation of the task, objective, and API; a simple seed agent; and an operator-chosen per-problem cost target--usually set at an incumbent's own price--RoboPhD, an evolutionary meta-agent, evolves complete agent programs that attack the public frontiers of two semantically dissimilar tasks point by point: DS-1000 (execution-checked code generation) and PaperFindingBench (LLM-judged scientific document retrieval). On public leaderboards for each task, the evolved agents hold every Pareto-frontier slot on PaperFindingBench and all but one on DS-1000, including Pareto domination of both the top-scoring and the lowest-cost competing points.
evidence_items.title: Competing at Every Price Point with Agentic Evolution over a Menu of LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Multi-object tracking (MOT) is usually split into detection and association, with identity kept as external state: track buffers, motion models, appearance embeddings. We ask whether a video generator can keep that state in pixels. We fine-tune a 22B text-to-video diffusion model (LTX-2.3) with an in-context LoRA to translate an RGB clip into an ID-map clip, where every person is painted a flat, distinct colour that persists over time. Long videos are generated as chained windows, each conditioned on the cleaned tail of the previous one; a brief continuation fine-tune teaches the model to extend a given colouring, after which identity flows through the chain with no separately trained detector, motion model or association module. On the DanceTrack test server the system reaches 40.3 HOTA, to our knowledge the first entry read off a pretrained video generator. This is well below today's specialists (66-76 HOTA), but its association (AssA 44.1) exceeds every tracker of the 2020-22 benchmark suite while detection is the deficit. A 2x2 factorial on validation shows where identity comes from: neither chaining nor continuation training helps alone (16.8 and 15.9 HOTA against 18.2 for independent windows linked post hoc), but together they reach 34.8; re-linking the chain's own windows changes nothing (34.7), and motion- and appearance-based associators on the same boxes reach only 22-24 AssA against 38.3 for the colours, an ordering that holds in three sampling seeds and on SportsMOT. On 383 mined occlusion and exit events the chain re-acquires 42% of the identities it held on both sides of the gap, including gaps longer than its 49-frame context; the pre-gap colour is painted during the gap in every recovery but also in 110 of 119 failures, so carry-over is necessary but not sufficient. We offer the system as a proof of concept, not a competitive tracker. We release code and checkpoints.
evidence_items.title: The generator is the tracker: Multi-object tracking by painting persistent identity colours

evidence_items.summary: Air--ground collaborative perception uses aerial observations to extend vehicle sensing coverage and alleviate occlusion. However, viewpoint differences create a cross-platform representation gap that limits the effective use of aerial information. Existing methods focus on depth estimation, feature interaction, and agent association, with less attention to explicit UAV-to-vehicle feature adaptation. UAV features can be adapted before fusion to bridge this gap, but adapters are typically trained with detection loss alone, which supervises adaptation indirectly through the final predictions. To provide explicit cross-platform supervision, we propose AGuide, a dual-granularity Flow Matching framework that provides explicit cross-platform auxiliary supervision through paired velocity prediction. Object-level Flow Matching captures foreground semantics, while token-level Flow Matching accommodates local cross-view differences. Both branches learn to predict UAV-to-vehicle feature displacements along interpolation paths, providing directional guidance for UAV adaptation alongside detection supervision. We further introduce OPV2V-Air, a camera-based benchmark for air--ground collaborative perception. AGuide improves AP@0.7 by 2.5 percentage points on OPV2V-Air and 4.0 percentage points on V2U4Real, demonstrating more accurate detection in both camera-based simulation and real-world LiDAR-based collaboration.
evidence_items.title: AGuide: Guiding Air-Ground Feature Adaptation with Flow Matching

evidence_items.summary: Large-scale single-cell transcriptomic data provide a new avenue for precision medicine by uncovering cellular heterogeneity. However, systematic comparison of remodeling patterns across various biological states remains unavailable. Here, we first developed a computational framework based on a foundation model of single cell biology, Universal Cell Embedding (UCE), to harmonize annotations comprising 36 cell types. Based on an integrated dataset of single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with 8,789 human samples comprising more than 59 million cells or nuclei across 614 biological states, we then embedded each state with a 36-dimensional vector in a unified space of cell-composition change and further deciphered states bridges by analyzing the relationships among the 614 state vectors. As a result, 22,161 significant bridges (P < 0.05) between the 614 states were revealed. Moreover, we successfully identified a number of well-known bridges such as bridge between Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease (P = 2.21e-15), suggesting the effectiveness of the proposed framework. More importantly, we uncovered a number of new bridges. Furthermore, analyses of the number of changed cell types (NCC) and Shannon entropy revealed heterogeneous and tissue-dependent patterns of cellular composition remodeling. This study provides a new strategy for identifying disease associations and potential therapeutic relationships by deciphering bridges between biological states from scRNA-seq landscape.
evidence_items.title: Deciphering state bridges via a single-cell large language model

evidence_items.summary: With the increasing complexity of modern power systems caused by renewable energy integration, distributed energy resources, and cyber–physical interactions, accurate and trustworthy security risk reasoning has become increasingly important. Existing data-driven methods mainly focus on risk prediction based on statistical correlations, while lacking the capability to model causal risk evolution and generate interpretable explanations. This paper proposes a knowledge-augmented large language model framework for power system security risk reasoning (KALLM-PSR). The proposed framework integrates structured power system knowledge with large language model reasoning capabilities to construct knowledge-enhanced representations, perform multi-stage risk propagation analysis, and generate reliability-aware explanations. A consistency evaluation mechanism is further introduced to improve the trustworthiness of reasoning results. Extensive experiments on IEEE 14-bus, 39-bus, and 118-bus systems demonstrate that KALLM-PSR outperforms conventional deep learning models, general large language models (LLMs), and retrieval-augmented approaches in risk identification accuracy, reasoning consistency, explanation quality, and robustness under disturbance conditions. The proposed framework provides an effective approach for intelligent and trustworthy power system security management.
evidence_items.title: A Knowledge-Augmented Large Language Model for Power System Security Risk Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Speech recognizers built on large language models cover dozens of languages but not Tibetan, whose dialects differ widely and whose script their tokenizers split into byte fragments. We adapted Qwen3-ASR-1.7B to transcribe multidialectal Tibetan and identify its dialect in one pass. We extended its tokenizer with 12,341 Tibetan entries and six dialect–source labels, generated before the transcript, and fine-tuned the full model on 2807 h of speech, 1356 h of which was in Tibetan. On 206,969 test utterances, the adapted model reaches a Tibetan syllable error rate (SyER) of 18.65%; with the label prefix constrained during decoding, 99.94% of Tibetan utterances receive the correct label. On the public TIBMD@MUC corpus, whose 87 speakers it never saw, it reaches 22.21% and identifies the dialect group of 85 speakers, albeit only 85.4% of single utterances. Against an ablation that adds only the labels, the extended vocabulary shortens Tibetan sequences 4.4-fold, speeds up decoding 1.79-fold, and lowers the SyER from 19.14%, significantly in all six dialect–source strata. However, under free decoding, it omits the label prefix more often (3.98% against 1.04% of outputs), which constrained decoding prevents. Development loss pointed to a checkpoint that was 3.96 points worse than the final one; development-set decoding leads to one that is 0.04 points better.
evidence_items.title: Joint Dialect Identification and Speech Recognition for Multidialectal Tibetan with a Large Language Model-Based Recognizer

evidence_items.summary: A modelagem da turbulência permanece um desafio na Dinâmica dos Fluidos Computacional (DFC), sendo frequentemente avaliada por meio de casos benchmark. Neste trabalho, o caso clássico de Pitz–Daily, caracterizado por um escoamento interno em uma tubulação retangular com degrau invertido, foi utilizado para a avaliação de modelos de turbulência Reynolds Average Navier-Stokes Equation (RANS). As simulações foram realizadas no OpenFOAM, considerando escoamento incompressível e em regime permanente. Para investigar a influência da malha nos resultados, conduziu-se uma análise sistemática envolvendo diversos níveis de refinamento, com atenção especial às regiões de maior complexidade do escoamento, como a vizinhança do degrau, as camadas de cisalhamento e as zonas de recirculação. Essa abordagem permitiu avaliar a capacidade das diferentes malhas em capturar adequadamente os campos de velocidade e pressão, bem como a extensão das regiões recirculantes e os pontos de reanexação do fluxo. Também foram feitas análises dos modelos de turbulência k-ε, k-ω e k-ω SST e diferentes tratamentos junto à parede em regime de baixo número de Reynolds, especificamente os modelos de Jones-Launder, Launder-Sharma e Lam-Bremhorst. Os resultados foram comparados com dados experimentais da literatura, destacando diferenças na previsão das regiões de recirculação e nos perfis de velocidade. Os resultados reforçam a importância da escolha adequada do modelo de turbulência e do tratamento próximo à parede, confirmando o caso Pitz–Daily como um benchmark relevante para estudos em CFD.
evidence_items.title: O Caso Pitz–Daily como Benchmark para Avaliação de Modelos de Turbulência

organizations: School of Software Technology, DUT-RU International School of Information Science and Engineering, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian, 116600, China
evidence_items.summary: In recent years, large language models have made significant progress in various aspects of natural language processing due to their powerful language understanding and generation capabilities. However, their internal decision-making processes are highly complex and typically "black-box" in nature, which limits their widespread application in fields such as healthcare, finance, and law. This paper primarily discusses the interpretability issue of large language models. First, we define the concept and scope of interpretability from three perspectives: model transparency, comprehensibility, and trustworthiness, while summarizing the challenges faced in interpretability research—such as massive parameter scale, strong emergent abilities, and complex attention mechanisms. Second, based on different approaches, existing interpretability methods are categorized into three types: mechanism-based methods (e.g., attention visualization, neuron activation analysis, circuit discovery), probe-based methods (e.g., linear probes, causal probes), and generation-based explanation methods (e.g., chain-of-thought prompting, self-explanation generation). We introduce the principles, advantages, and limitations of each category. Additionally, we discuss the relationship between interpretability and model performance, safety, and fairness, arguing that enhancing interpretability can effectively detect model biases, prevent hallucinatory outputs, and increase user confidence. Finally, addressing current research issues such as inconsistent evaluation criteria, difficulty in ensuring explanation fidelity, and limited cross-modal interpretability studies, we propose future research directions—including building causal reasoning frameworks, establishing unified standards, and exploring human-machine collaborative explanation—to advance the field of large language model interpretability.
evidence_items.title: Research on Theories and Methods of Interpretability in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Purpose: To evaluate the prediction performance of the newly developed Buonsanti Artificial Intelligence (AI) formula and compare it with seven established new-generation formulas. Setting: Hospital-based academic practice. Design: Retrospective observational secondary analysis. Methods: The analysis included 523 eyes of 523 patients implanted with a Tecnis ZCB00 intraocular lens. Standard keratometry-based predictions from the Buonsanti formula were compared with Barrett Universal II (BUII), Cooke K6, EVO 2.0, Kane, Pearl DGS, Hoffer QST, and Hill RBF 3.0. Eyetemis analysis tool was used to compare trimmed-mean spherical equivalent prediction error (SEQ-PE; trueness), precision, trimmed-mean absolute SEQ-PE (accuracy), and the proportions of eyes within prespecified absolute-error thresholds. Long-eye and short-eye analyses were performed for axial length (AL) >26.0 mm and AL ≤22.5 mm, respectively. Results: For Buonsanti, the trimmed-mean SEQ-PE was -0.094 D (P<0.001), precision was 0.223 D, and trimmed-mean absolute SEQ-PE was 0.232 D. The percentages of eyes within ±0.25, ±0.50, ±0.75, and ±1.00 D were 59.1%, 86.6%, 95.8%, and 98.7%, respectively. EVO 2.0 had a lower trimmed-mean absolute SEQ-PE than Buonsanti (0.216 vs 0.232 D; adjusted P=0.017); comparisons with the other formulas were not significant. No adjusted pairwise threshold comparison involving Buonsanti was significant. Buonsanti showed myopic trimmed-mean SEQ-PEs in short eyes (-0.309 D; n=48, p<0.001) and long eyes (-0.088 D; n=74, p=0.007). In these subgroups, while some pairwise SEQ-PE comparison with other formulas were significant, Buonsanti’s precision and absolute SEQ-PE did not differ significantly from any comparator in either subgroup after adjustment. Conclusion: The Buonsanti AI formula provided high overall prediction accuracy, showing no major statistically significant differences compared with the established formulas in the ESCRS calculator.
evidence_items.title: Prediction Accuracy of the Buonsanti Artificial Intelligence Formula

evidence_items.summary: Typically, quantum genetic algorithms are based on qubits, a two-level quantum system. This work investigates the optimization of Rastrigin, Rosen-Brock and Table Holder Function in comparison with Classical Genetic Algorithm (CGA), using two quantum approaches: Quantum Genetic Algorithm (QGA), and Higher-Order Quantum Genetic Algorithm (HO-QGA) based on qutrits, a three-level system. HO-QGA uses higher-dimensional quantum representations, such as entangled qutrits, to test its capability of enhanced optimization. We show that the QGA convergence rate is higher than the CGA, and the solution quality is considerably improved. Based on this study, a three-state quantum object novelly provides more capabilities than qubits in terms of computational and information resources.
evidence_items.title: A Quantum Genetic Algorithm for Optimization of Benchmark Test Functions using Entangled Qutrits

evidence_items.summary: Objective: Public electronic health record (EHR) databases differ in schema, identifiers, coding systems, units, and event structure, making disease-specific studies across multiple sources difficult to construct and audit. We developed rendehR, a computational pipeline and R package for cohort-centered extraction and harmonization of multi-source EHR data. Materials and Methods: rendehR treats cohort definition as an explicit executable component of dataset construction. Cohorts can be defined using diagnosis codes, identifiers, R callbacks, or source-specific SQL. After cohort selection, linked source tables are restricted to the selected population and can be retained as cohort-specific Parquet datasets or loaded into a persistent database. Clinical concepts are defined using source-aware mappings, generated, or curated SQL and are harmonized into flat, time-series, and duration representations. Configuration, executable SQL, cohort metadata, concept-origin metadata, and source-level values are retained to support inspection and traceability. In the current version rendehR provides interactive R assistant wizards for workflow configuration, a Shiny application for patient-level data visualization, three agent skills for AI-assisted workflow execution and extension, and an MCP server exposing nine read-only tools for AI-assisted configuration, concept discovery, and cohort exploration. The current implementation supports MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU-CRD. We demonstrate rendehR on a reference cohort of spinal cord injury and disease (SCID). Results: Using the reference cohort, rendehR identified 4,320, 39,850, and 2,343 qualifying hospital admissions in MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU-CRD, respectively. Patient-level extraction expanded these cohorts to 5,725, 104,988, and 2,823 hospital admissions, with 5,983, 17,405, and 3,441 associated ICU stays, respectively.
evidence_items.title: rendehR: a cohort-first, provenance-aware, agentic-ready pipeline for harmonizing multi-source electronic health records

evidence_items.summary: Current MLLM methods largely focus on whether models attend to the right visual regions, implicitly treating spatial attention map as the primary key of effective visual perception. To examine this assumption, we introduce a medical VQA dataset with paired non-contrast (NC) and contrast-enhanced (CE) images that share corresponding anatomy while providing different cues. We show that this view is incomplete: across paired NC and CE medical images, MLLMs often exhibit similar attention patterns despite producing contrasting answers, while controlled bidirectional interventions induce substantially larger prediction changes on visual values than attention weights. These results identify the visual content retrieved through values as a critical factor in improving perception beyond spatial attention alone. Guided by this finding, we propose VIVID (VIsual Value Intervention Distillation), which uses enhanced visual values to identify and refine teacher corrections aligned with useful visual evidence to improve on-policy distillation from CE to NC images. Across six internal and external test sets, VIVID consistently outperforms existing on-policy distillation methods across different model scales and architectures, requires only NC images at inference, and maintains strong zero-shot performance on general-domain VQA benchmarks. The project page is available at https://qiuzyc.github.io/VIVID.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Attention Maps: Understanding and Improving Medical MLLMs via Visual Values

evidence_items.summary: Operating in the physical world requires reasoning beyond what cameras directly capture. In a city, radio signals are invisible to the lens, yet their strength is governed by the buildings and streets an image does show. Given only these visible structures, can vision-language models (VLMs) infer the invisible radio field they shape? Probing true physical reasoning requires exact fields in real cities, alongside controlled interventions where a single physical factor changes. We build a label-free engine that turns any coordinate on Earth into a ray-traceable city, simulates matched single-factor counterfactuals, and computes every answer exactly. This yields RadioVISTA, a benchmark and training dataset for visual reasoning about invisible fields. Physically, a radio field is the sum of its propagation paths, yet across six continents we uncover a striking field-path dissociation: frontier VLMs accurately judge where a field is strong, but fail to tell whether a single direct or one-wall path exists. Open models fail even earlier at reading the field itself, and are systematically wrong, scoring below random guessing even when credited for any of four attempts. On unseen cities, fine-tuning brings a 9B open model close to frontier proprietary models on fields, yet neither supervised nor reinforcement fine-tuning improves path tracing. Supervising only final answers teaches models to approximate the field, yet leaves single-path geometry out of reach.
evidence_items.title: Seeing the Invisible: How Vision-Language Models Read, Predict and Trace Radio Fields

evidence_items.summary: Animal re-identification (Re-ID) must distinguish individuals across species and capture conditions. We introduce ApexID, a hierarchical SphereFace2-based loss that integrates global identity discrimination with balanced animal-category supervision. Using 132,533 images curated from 19 public datasets, we evaluate three model families and four objectives on four external datasets with observation-aware retrieval protocols. ApexID achieves a dataset-averaged Rank-1 accuracy of 64.89% with ConvNeXt-Small and an mAP of 32.54% with MIEW-ID, outperforming their pretrained reference models. On elephants, a category absent from animal Re-ID training, our ConvNeXt-Small variant achieves the highest retrieval performance among the fourteen evaluated configurations. Scores vary by backbone and dataset, and open-set evaluation reveals remaining discovery challenges. These findings support hierarchical category-identity learning to improve transfer to unseen datasets and species.
evidence_items.title: ApexID: Hierarchical Learning for Multi-Species Animal Re-Identification

evidence_items.summary: Vision Banana showed that a closed image generator, instruction-tuned to paint perception outputs as RGB images, becomes a generalist vision model. Does this carry over to open generators, and if not, what fails? We answer with Open Vision Banana (OVB), an open framework that adapts the 7B diffusion generator of Qwen-Image-2.1 into one instruction-driven model for metric depth, semantic, instance, and referring segmentation, using a single shared low-rank adapter and public data. Each task is a task contract whose RGB encoder, instruction, and decoder share one specification and are checked before training. Studying 42 externally evaluated checkpoints from two 100k-update runs, six exact weight-space merges, and eight controlled shorter runs, we find that the gap to the closed system is specific and measurable. Geometry is learned early while absolute scale is not: median-aligned NYUv2 δ_1 stays at 0.89--0.93 throughout training as unaligned δ_1 wanders between 0.11 and 0.50. The scale is not committed by a single sample: a ten-seed ensemble lifts unaligned δ_1 from 0.348 to 0.516 without retraining. Depth and 2D segmentation compete for the shared adapter, and weight merging moves along this trade-off without escaping it. Finally, lower validation flow loss comes with lower Cityscapes accuracy (Spearman ρapprox-0.9 between loss reduction and mIoU), so the loss cannot select checkpoints. We release code, contracts, training data, and all evaluation outputs.
evidence_items.title: Open Vision Banana: An Open Framework for Unified Visual Perception through Generation in RGB Space

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy (δ_1) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.
evidence_items.title: StereoVLM: Binocular Vision-Language Models for Metric 3D Spatial Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal foundation models can play video games well when the game waits for them, but often fail when it keeps running. We find that much of this gap lies in the harness, which decides what the model sees, what it remembers, and how its outputs become actions over time. Existing harnesses such as VISTA improve the first two, yet turn each model call into at most one action, so the agent acts only as often as its model thinks. We introduce AutoPILOT, which changes the third: in each model call, the model can send a primitive action, start an open-loop macro, or write a closed-loop controller that keeps playing from the screen without further model calls until it hands control back. To evaluate agents in real-time games, we build AFK-Bench, 120 diverse browser games grouped by how they respond to inaction and playable in real time or with the clock paused. With GPT-6.1 Sol under the same budgets, AutoPILOT reaches 68.6% real-time success against 38.3% for VISTA, and on GameWorld it keeps 80.0% in real time while VISTA drops from 84.1% to 42.9%. Its gains hold across models, and it reaches VISTA's final success rate at a fifth of its API cost. Our results suggest that how a harness turns model outputs into actions over time is a central yet underexplored part of agent design, and we hope AutoPILOT and AFK-Bench will serve as a foundation for agents in a world that does not wait.
evidence_items.title: AutoPILOT: A Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay

evidence_items.summary: We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. Remarkably, our method shows zero-shot generalization to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. We publicly release our code, the NoPeBench benchmark, and model weights. Project Page: https://nopeworld.github.io .
evidence_items.title: Non-penetrating World Models

evidence_items.summary: Hierarchical text detection aims to localize words, text lines, and paragraphs while parsing their structural relationships. It provides essential structural cues for visual text understanding. To maximize accuracy, existing methods typically rely on complex multi-scale feature fusion necks and heavy-weight heads, resulting in bloated architectures and low inference efficiency. In this paper, we argue that a sufficiently pre-trained backbone can effectively replace these sophisticated external modules, while simple geometric inclusion suffices for hierarchical text structural parsing. Thus, we propose Prism, a minimalist framework for hierarchical text detection. Prism performs multi-granularity detection by attaching parallel lightweight heads to a single-scale backbone feature map, covering words, text lines, and paragraphs, and reconstructs the structural hierarchy via an efficient geometric inclusion algorithm. In addition, we systematically compare representative lightweight head archetypes and show that pixel-level regression offers the best accuracy-efficiency trade-off in this setting. Experiments on multiple public benchmarks show that our significantly simplified architecture achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance with remarkable efficiency. Specifically, it runs 1.7times faster than LRANet on CTW1500 while achieving higher accuracy, and surpasses the current SOTA method, OmniParser V2, by over 6 PQ points on the hierarchical HierText dataset. Code will be released soon.
evidence_items.title: Prism: Hierarchical Text Detection with Minimalist Design

evidence_items.summary: Intent contracts are an authorization interface for tool-using LLM agents in which the planning model holds no tools. For each step it submits a short logged contract: a goal, a verbatim quotation of the user, and scope fields. Code validates the contract, and a small trusted model checks it against the user's words and writes the tool call itself. Provided the validation and dispatch code is correct, every executed call is written by the trusted model, the planner's influence on a call is confined to a contract logged before it, and the trusted side decides how much of a request to carry out. We compare contracts with two reviewers of planner-written commands: one sees only the user's words and the command, the information boundary of a reasoning-blind permission classifier, and one also sees the planner's goal and a checked quotation. With gpt-6.1-terra as planner and GLM-5.3-Flash as the trusted model on three AmPermBench task families, every object changed under contracts is named in the goal of the contract that produced the change; under review the planner names objects in its commands and rarely in its goals. When the planner adds work the user never asked for, contracts complete the user's task in 27/30 runs and the intent-visible reviewer in 16/30, because a reviewer can only refuse a whole command. Contracts do not reduce unauthorized actions. They are indistinguishable from blind review, and once the benchmark's environment terms are clarified, every condition that changes state hits a wrong target in 40-49% of those runs. That error is the planner's choice of objects for an ambiguous reference, which no trusted model here can see the environment to check; telling the executor to decline when unsure does not change it. We evaluate benign over-reach with one pair of models, not adversarial planners. We release the plugin and run records.
evidence_items.title: Intent Contracts: Taking Tools Away from Agents

evidence_items.summary: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.
evidence_items.title: Clover-35B-A3B-Preview Technical Report

evidence_items.summary: We present the Autoregressive View Model (AVM), which generates a scene as a stream of views without constructing an explicit 3D representation. Through a unified in-context interface, AVM conditions on images or videos to generate short clips along a requested camera path. Visual context grounds reconstruction and interpolation, while a learned prior enables extrapolation into unseen regions. AVM retrieves relevant views from inputs and generated history to form a bounded active context. We fine-tune a pretrained bidirectional video diffusion transformer with flow matching in an N-in-1-out formulation. We then tune a causal model on its own rollouts to improve photorealism, reduce denoising steps, and limit long-horizon drift. We scale training to approximately 8M scenes and video clips. We evaluate generation capacity and scene persistence across benchmarks for camera control, text control, visual quality, dynamics, sparse and 4D reconstruction, and long-horizon consistency. The results demonstrate that AVM adapts to diverse input and output settings through one in-context interface.
evidence_items.title: Autoregressive View Model

evidence_items.summary: Text-aware image super-resolution (TAISR) aims to recover high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs while preserving textual content. Existing methods treat this as a visual restoration problem, yet severely degraded text often cannot be read from local visual evidence alone. Humans instead read it by reasoning over image context, logical patterns, and prior knowledge. This raises a fundamental question: Does TAISR need reasoning? To answer this, we introduce two diagnostic tools. The first, ReasonText, is a human-curated benchmark that separates reasoning-required text from locally recoverable text. The second, Ground-Truth Text-Crop Accuracy (GTTCA), is a recognition-based metric that measures text restoration quality without text detection errors. Evaluating twelve recent super-resolution (SR) models, we find a consistent and substantial performance drop on reasoning-required text, revealing a systematic blind spot. Two observations point to a remedy. One is that text-conditioned SR models restore text substantially better when given ground-truth text. The other is that multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can read degraded text in low-resolution images through reasoning. We therefore propose Reasoning Transfer via Captioning (RTC), a training-free plug-in that uses an external MLLM to infer the degraded text and feeds the resulting caption to a text-conditioned SR model. RTC consistently improves all six text-conditioned SR models we evaluate, especially on reasoning-required text. Surprisingly, a real-world SR model with RTC can even outperform the TAISR model with RTC, suggesting that reasoning should be a core design axis for future TAISR.
evidence_items.title: Reading the Unreadable: Text-Aware Image Super-Resolution Needs Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Code localizers are usually trained to predict the files a reference patch edits, but the code a fixer needs to read is not the same as the code it changes. We propose Fixer-Guided Localization (FGL): the localizer proposes several localizations, a frozen fixer scores each by how likely it makes a verified patch, and the localizer is trained on these scores with weighted supervised fine-tuning, without running tests and without reinforcement learning. We build the full pipeline on Gemma 4 E4B for the Kaggle Gemma-4 Developer Agent competition, from 1,629 test-verified Kimi K3 trajectories. The FGL target helps the fixer find the bug as often as the teacher's localization while using 27.5% less code. On the development set, one EM round moves the agent in the expected direction compared with a matched control: more tasks reach a patch (53 vs. 46), fewer tasks get stuck reading files that do not exist (43 vs. 54), and more tasks are solved (8 vs. 6). Training also changes how the agent works: trained agents explore about three times more than the base model and write far fewer wrong patches, and the single agent solves up to 11 of 78 tasks, against 8 for the base model. An analysis of 13 evaluation runs identifies what limits a 4B agent under an 8-minute budget (time, repetition loops and edit quality) and gives practical lessons for training small coding agents. All data, code and adapters are publicly available.
evidence_items.title: Let the Fixer Decide: Training a Code Localizer from the Fixer's Likelihood

evidence_items.summary: Background: Large language models (LLMs) may help apply evolving genetic testing guidelines, but their agreement with clinician assessment in community oncology is uncertain. We compared LLM-generated and physician assessments of the prostate cancer risk group and genetic testing eligibility. Methods: We retrospectively studied 691 consecutive patients with newly diagnosed prostate cancer treated across a community oncology network from 2023 to 2025. Physician review served as the reference standard. The 2023 cohort was evaluated using GPT-4o with explicit National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) decision logic; the 2024 and 2025 cohorts were evaluated using GPT-5.2 Thinking with the corresponding NCCN guideline text and structured electronic health record data. The primary outcome was exact agreement with physician review. Results: Exact agreement for germline testing recommendations was 97% (251/259) in 2023 and 100% for the clinicopathologic criteria represented in the structured data in 2024 (255/255) and 2025 (177/177). Somatic testing recommendations had 100% agreement in all three cohorts. Risk-group agreement was 91% (232/255) in 2024 and 100% (177/177) in 2025; none of the 2024 discordances changed genetic testing eligibility. Conclusions: LLM-generated assessments showed high agreement with physician review when applied to available structured clinicopathologic data. Prospective studies should evaluate reproducibility, performance when incorporating unstructured clinical data and the full range of NCCN eligibility criteria, and utility within clinical workflows.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model Assessment of Genetic Testing Eligibility in Prostate Cancer: A Retrospective Community Oncology Study

evidence_items.summary: Materials discovery is an iterative loop: experiments and calculations verify predictions, and each outcome can inform the next. Yet most predictors are specialized single-task models fixed after training. Large language models have recently emerged as predictors across heterogeneous tasks but generally underperform specialized models, and retrieval-augmented variants discard their own outcomes. Benchmarks also score queries in isolation, leaving improvement from outcomes untested. Here we construct MatMemBench, a sequential benchmark of 22 materials tasks that reveals outcomes only after prediction and tests online adaptation, memory retention and cross-task transfer. We present MatRecall, a framework that lets large language models store verified predictions, with evidence, outcome and error, as episodes and recall them without retraining. MatRecall improved median performance by 62% over a memory-free model, exceeded specialized models on 11 tasks, remained useful after feedback stopped and transferred between related tasks. Verified experience could become a reusable resource for self-improving discovery loops.
evidence_items.title: Verified experience improves materials prediction with large language models

organizations: PhD Scholar at National Law University, Delhi, India
evidence_items.summary: Technology has increased and changed the gender-based violence (GBV) faced by women and girls globally. This paper explores the ways in which AI technology causes GBV and evaluates whether current laws address the issue, with a specific focus on India. Four forms of GBV are identified. AI is used to spread disinformation, increasing the vulnerability of women in conflict zones. Deepfake technology is overwhelmingly used to create non-consensual pornography and to silence women in the media and public life. Biometric and facial recognition data are collected and used, for example from Rohingya refugees, and to monitor whether women in Iran are wearing the hijab as required. Women activists are targeted through cyberstalking, defamation and de-platforming. The international framework includes General Recommendations No. 19 and No. 35 of the CEDAW Committee, the Istanbul Convention and Council of Europe standards on sexist hate speech. Within India, the Information Technology Act, 2000, the IT Intermediary Rules, 2021 and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 address the issue. However, although these laws have been extended to cover technology-facilitated GBV, and the Intermediary Rules were amended in 2026 to address synthetically generated content, there is still no law dealing specifically and fully with AI-facilitated GBV. Regulation of AI and protection of gender equality continue to develop separately, so the accountability of platforms and developers is lacking. To improve this, the two can be combined through measures such as safety by design, labelling of deepfakes, red-teaming, clear processes for escalating the cases of vulnerable women, protection for whistleblowers and digital education. National laws need strengthening, institutional capacity should be improved, and societal attitudes towards women in digital spaces must change.
evidence_items.title: Digital Gender-Based Violence in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Objective Since the large language model (LLM) program Chat Generative Pre‐trained Transformer (ChatGPT) was introduced in November 2022, the use of artificial intelligence (AI) expanded rapidly in published writing. This has been quantified in many fields, but not in medical journals that focus on neurology and neuroscience. We sought to characterize the use of LLM in articles submitted before and after ChatGPT became available to the general public, in a neurology journal, Annals of Neurology , that covers all neurology subspecialties. Methods The study evaluated manuscripts submitted on movement disorders, dementia, and vascular neurology before and after ChatGPT became available. AI content was measured with LLM‐detection platforms Pangram, Originality.ai and GPTZero. Substantial AI was defined as ≥20% of content, or >50% likelihood of AI use. Manuscript type, country of author, country, Human Development Index (HDI), AI disclosure, and publication decision were compared with AI detected. Results Of 300 papers submitted after the introduction of ChatGPT, AI was detected by Pangram in 74 (25%) and this was substantial (≥20% of content) in 32 (11%). Substantial AI was more common in brief communications than full research articles (31% vs 10%, p = 0.006) and in vascular neurology articles (17%, vascular; 8%, dementia; and 5%, movement disorders; p = 0.012). Most manuscripts analyzed were submitted by authors from China (37%) and the United States (19%) and each had 11% substantial AI use. Authors from countries with lower levels of development were more likely to use AI (median HDI 0.797, AI ≥20% vs median HDI 0.925, AI <20%, p = 0.033). No AI was found in 60 papers submitted from July 3 to September 14, 2022 (pre‐ChatGPT) by any of the AI‐detection platforms. Of 300 post‐ChatGPT manuscripts, 24 (8%) were accepted. None with substantial AI use were accepted ( p = 0.090; odds ratio [OR] = 0.000, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.000–1.068).
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence‐Generated Content in Manuscripts Submitted to Annals of Neurology

evidence_items.summary: Abstract In the project Smart Urban Traffic Zones [1], Gothenburg city, Sweden, wanted to collect data from trucks to predict where to build loading zones. The city also wished to utilize data from trucks to enhance urban flexibility, transportation efficiency, and traffic safety. This study investigates four possible approaches to collect and share data from a city perspective: (1) the municipality manages all data internally, (2) procuring processed data from private actors, (3) implementing a shared data platform for public-private exchange, and (4) open data publication via national access points. Through literature reviews, interviews, and workshops, we assessed each approach’s viability. Our findings show that no one-size-fits all solution exists; instead, municipalities must tailor strategies to context, resources, and goals – often combining multiple models. While full municipal control ensures oversight, it demands high resources. Outsourcing data processing is simpler but relies on market maturity. Platform-based models are effective where clear use case exists, such as managing e-scooter data. Open publication lacks municipal control and is thus less suited for Smart Urban Traffic Zones. Key insights include the importance of clear needs assessment, high data quality, innovation-friendly procurement, and well-structured incentives. Municipalities must act as coordinators, data consumers, and public value stewards. Regional collaboration is especially valuable for smaller municipalities. Our results offer a framework for data-driven urban policy and decision-making in evolving traffic environments.
evidence_items.title: Data Governance and Data for Governance – A Circulatory and Regulatory Perspective on Data

evidence_items.summary: Mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics is essential for comprehensive protein characterization, yet it relies on multistep computational workflows that typically demand tedious manual parameter tuning and complex software integration. Here, we present MSRyzen, an agent-driven framework that provides automated parameter optimization and extensible tool integration across bottom-up and top-down proteomics workflows. MSRyzen translates natural-language prompts into directed acyclic workflow graphs, optimizes analytical parameters guided by quantitative metrics and user-defined objectives, and incorporates new third-party software through standardized callable interfaces. Across four public top-down datasets, automated parameter optimization increased proteoform identifications by 3.6% to 15.8% compared to default settings at a 1% false discovery rate. To ensure transparent data interpretation, an interactive visualization interface coordinates identification metrics with peak-level spectral evidence and sequence coverage. Integrating adaptive tuning with multi-tiered spectral inspection, MSRyzen delivers an end-to-end, fully automated framework, dramatically reducing the operational barrier to modern mass spectrometry data analysis.
evidence_items.title: MSRyzen: An Agentic Platform for Unified Proteomics Analysis and Evidence-Centric Visualization
